entries.name: Gothic
entries.description: Inheritance, decay, and a crime the building has not finished paying for.
entries.principle: The founding form, and still the most structurally generous: a confined and over-articulated setting, a lineage with something buried in it, and a present-day inhabitant who must excavate the past in order to survive it. The architecture is not backdrop but antagonist — the plot is the house being read. Gothic runs on suspicion rather than confirmation, which is why it survives translation into every later mode.
entries.example: Walpole's The Castle of Otranto assembled the machinery in 1764; Radcliffe rationalised her hauntings and Lewis refused to, establishing the two settlements the genre has alternated between ever since; Maturin's Melmoth the Wanderer pushed the bargain plot to its limit; Poe compressed the whole apparatus into rooms.
entries.application: Give the building a floor plan the reader can hold, then make the plot a route through it. Decide early and permanently whether your supernatural will be confirmed or left suspended, because Radcliffe's settlement and Lewis's produce incompatible endings. The inheritance question — who owns this, and what was done to get it — is the most reliable engine the form has.

entries.name: Southern Gothic
entries.description: The rot relocated to a specific and documented American guilt.
entries.principle: Gothic decay transplanted to the American South, where the buried crime is not invented for the plot but historical, and the grotesque functions as moral diagnosis rather than as spectacle. The mode's distinguishing move is that its monsters are usually people, and its supernatural, where it appears at all, is a pressure reading on a real social order.
entries.example: Faulkner supplies the structural template of a past that will not consent to be past; O'Connor supplies the grotesque as an instrument of judgment rather than of disgust; Morrison's Beloved makes the haunting inseparable from the historical record that produced it; Jesmyn Ward's Sing, Unburied, Sing carries the line into the present.
entries.application: Anchor the decay in an economic history you can name, not in atmosphere — kudzu and heat are not an argument. Let the grotesque character be right about something. If a ghost appears, it should be legible as a consequence of documented harm, which is what separates this mode from a haunted house with an accent.

entries.name: The Female Gothic & Gothic Romance
entries.description: The house as a marriage, and the marriage as a trap with a door.
entries.principle: The strain of Gothic in which the threat is domestic, legal and sexual rather than spectral: a woman is installed in a house that belongs to a man, and the question is whether her perception can be trusted against everyone's insistence that it cannot. Ellen Moers named the tradition in 1976, and the naming clarified what had always been the form's real subject — the gaslighting is the plot.
entries.example: Radcliffe built the template; Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre supplied the attic and, later, the counter-reading that made the attic the point; du Maurier's Rebecca perfected the predecessor-wife structure; Moreno-Garcia's Mexican Gothic re-stages it against colonial extraction rather than English inheritance.
entries.application: The heroine's judgement must be sound and must be disbelieved — if she is actually unreliable you have written a different subgenre. Give the house a legal dimension: who inherits, who signs, what happens to her if she leaves. And decide whether the romance survives the reveal, because the modern reader will not accept the Byronic settlement without argument.

entries.name: The Ghost Story
entries.description: Not a monster but a claim — the dead want something specific.
entries.principle: The form is defined by economy and by restraint: a short arc, a single intrusion, and an apparition that means something rather than merely appearing. The classical ghost story withholds explanation but not motive, and its characteristic pleasure is the slow arrival of a pattern the reader assembles slightly ahead of the narrator. It is horror's most disciplined length.
entries.example: M.R. James set the antiquarian standard, where scholarship disturbs what it catalogues; Edith Wharton and Elizabeth Bowen wrote the domestic and wartime strains with equal precision; Susan Hill's The Woman in Black demonstrated in 1983 that the Edwardian shape still works undiluted; David Lowery's A Ghost Story inverts the form by taking the ghost's side.
entries.application: Establish what the ghost wants before you establish what it looks like. Keep the cast small and the timeframe tight — the form's power is proportional to its compression, and a ghost story extended to novel length usually becomes a haunted-house story instead. End on the implication, not the exorcism.

entries.name: Haunted House
entries.description: A building that has already decided what happens inside it.
entries.principle: Where the ghost story is about a claim, the haunted house is about a place with agency and a set of rules. The form requires the reader to hold a spatial model, because the horror is generated by violations of it — a corridor that is longer than the room it serves, a door where a wall was. Its second engine is the question of whether the house is doing this or the occupant is.
entries.example: Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House made the ambiguity structural rather than coy, refusing to let the reader separate the building's malice from Eleanor's collapse; Matheson's Hell House answered it with machinery and physics; Danielewski's House of Leaves relocated the impossible geometry into the typography; Clayton's The Innocents filmed the ambiguity without resolving it.
entries.application: Draw the plan. The reader needs a stable map before you can profitably break it, and impossible space only registers as horror against a model the reader has already built. Decide whether the house is haunted or the protagonist is, then withhold that answer for as long as the ending will bear — but know it yourself from page one.

entries.name: Folk Horror
entries.description: The old rules were never repealed, and you are standing inside them.
entries.principle: An outsider enters a community whose beliefs are functional rather than quaint, and discovers too late that the local practice has a calendar, a purpose and a role reserved for him. The form's landscape is not scenery but jurisdiction — the further from the road, the less the outsider's law applies. Its horror is procedural: everything that happens is correct by the community's standards.
entries.example: The British cycle of Witchfinder General, The Blood on Satan's Claw and The Wicker Man established the shape between 1968 and 1973; Andrew Michael Hurley's The Loney and Adam Nevill's The Ritual carry the prose line; Ari Aster's Midsommar demonstrated that the form works in daylight and that the outsider can be complicit in her own selection.
entries.application: Build the community's belief as a working system with a season, an obligation and an economy — a folk-horror village that merely seems sinister is a tourist's impression, not a subgenre. The outsider must be given the information in time and must fail to read it. Withhold the ritual's purpose, never its existence.

entries.name: Witchcraft Horror
entries.description: Power held by the wrong people, and the machinery built to find them.
entries.principle: Two opposed traditions share a name. One treats the witch as a genuine supernatural threat and derives its horror from her power; the other treats witchcraft as an accusation and derives its horror from the persecution apparatus, where the monster is the tribunal. The strongest modern work refuses to choose, letting the accusation be false and the power real at once.
entries.example: Christensen's Häxan documented the persecution reading as early as 1922; Argento's Suspiria supplied the aestheticised coven and made the school a jurisdiction; Eggers's The Witch worked from period court records so that the family's theology and the forest's are the same theology; Fleming's The Craft relocated the form to adolescence and the social cost of power.
entries.application: Decide which tradition you are in before you write the trial scene, because the two require opposite structures — one wants the witch's power confirmed, the other wants the accusation's machinery exposed. If you use historical persecution, use the actual record; the real trials are stranger and more damning than invention. Give the witch a motive that predates the plot.

entries.name: Religious Horror & the Demonic
entries.description: A cosmology that turns out to be literally true, and indifferent to your comfort in it.
entries.principle: The form requires a functioning metaphysics: if the demon is real then so is the church, the rite and the hierarchy, and the story becomes a procedural conducted under theological rules. Its central tension is not good against evil but faith against evidence — the priest who has lost belief is more useful than the one who has not, because the form is about what it costs to act on a doctrine you no longer hold.
entries.example: Blatty's The Exorcist grounded possession in medical exhaustion so that the supernatural arrives only after every other explanation is spent; Levin's Rosemary's Baby made the conspiracy domestic and the institution neighbourly; Donner's The Omen ran the same logic as inheritance thriller; Russell's The Devils turned the apparatus itself into the monster.
entries.application: Establish the rules of the rite and then enforce them — a demon that ignores its own stated constraints is a plot device. Exhaust the rational explanations on the page rather than dismissing them. And give your believer a specific doctrine rather than generic faith, because the form's best scenes come from the gap between what the character believes and what the church will authorise.

entries.name: Occult Detective
entries.description: Investigation conducted where the evidence does not obey physics.
entries.principle: Horror's most durable hybrid: the detective structure supplies forward motion and a reason for the protagonist to walk toward the thing, while the supernatural supplies the failure mode the detective's method cannot handle. The form lives or dies on whether the investigator's expertise is real — a specialist who simply improvises is a tourist, and the reader will notice.
entries.example: Le Fanu's Dr Hesselius established the casebook frame in 1872; Blackwood's John Silence and Hodgson's Carnacki formalised the practitioner, Carnacki notably by failing and by finding hoaxes as often as hauntings; Hellblazer's Constantine made the investigator morally compromised and consequential; Butcher's Dresden Files supplied the long-running commercial template.
entries.application: Give the investigator a discipline with limits and let the limits bite — Carnacki's willingness to be wrong is why the character still works. The mixed caseload is a feature: if every investigation ends supernatural, the form collapses into a monster-of-the-week. Keep the fee, the client and the paperwork; the mundane apparatus is what makes the intrusion land.

entries.name: J-Horror & East Asian Horror
entries.description: The curse as contagion — transmissible, indifferent to guilt, and already in the room.
entries.principle: A tradition organised around obligation and pollution rather than around sin and punishment. The vengeful dead of Japanese and Korean horror do not discriminate between the guilty and the incidental; the curse spreads by contact, and encountering it is sufficient to contract it. This removes the moral logic Western horror usually supplies, and with it the reader's assumption that correct behaviour offers protection.
entries.example: Kobayashi's Kwaidan adapted Hearn's collected tales and set the register; Suzuki's Ringu and Nakata's film of it made the transmissible curse a modern media object; Kurosawa's Pulse extended it to network isolation; Kim Jee-woon's A Tale of Two Sisters and Na Hong-jin's The Wailing demonstrate the Korean line's greater interest in family culpability.
entries.application: Do not retrofit a moral cause. The form's distinctive dread comes from the victim having done nothing to deserve it, and Western remakes have repeatedly weakened their sources by inserting one. Give the curse a transmission mechanism specific enough to be reasoned about, then let the characters reason about it correctly and lose anyway.

entries.name: Vampire
entries.description: The predator that must be invited, and the appetite that can be discussed.
entries.principle: The one monster with a conversational register, which is why the subgenre carries more thematic freight than any other and why it periodically collapses under it. The vampire's rules — invitation, threshold, daylight, the specific aversions — exist to make predation negotiable and therefore dramatic. Every era rewrites the vampire as its own anxiety about appetite, class or contagion, and the form absorbs it.
entries.example: Polidori's The Vampyre made the vampire an aristocrat in 1819; Le Fanu's Carmilla introduced the erotic and the female predator decades before Stoker consolidated the apparatus in Dracula; Murnau's Nosferatu supplied the plague reading and the non-seductive body; Lindqvist's Let the Right One In returned the form to the transactional relationship underneath the romance.
entries.application: Fix the rule set and publish it to the reader early — the vampire is horror's clearest example of a threat improved by constraint. Decide what your vampire is an argument about, then keep that argument subordinate to the predation. If seduction is in play, the power differential is the subject whether you intend it or not.

entries.name: Werewolf & Shapeshifter
entries.description: The monster you become on a schedule you cannot negotiate.
entries.principle: Where the vampire converses, the lycanthrope cannot: the form's subject is involuntary transformation and the horror of being responsible for what you did without agency. It is structurally a tragedy on a clock, and its best work treats the transformation as physically costly rather than as an upgrade. The subgenre is chronically weakened by making the wolf cool.
entries.example: Endore's The Werewolf of Paris supplied the literary template in 1933; Siodmak's screenplay for The Wolf Man invented most of the folklore audiences now assume is traditional; Landis's An American Werewolf in London made the transformation itself the set piece and paid for it in screaming; Fawcett's Ginger Snaps rebuilt the form around adolescence and made the metaphor load-bearing rather than decorative.
entries.application: Make the change hurt and take time. The moral engine is the aftermath — what the character finds, and what they must conceal — so budget scenes for the mornings, not only for the nights. Beware inherited folklore: much of what reads as ancient was written for the screen in the 1940s, and the actual traditions are stranger and more usable.

entries.name: Zombie & the Risen Dead
entries.description: An antagonist with no interiority, so the survivors have to supply the conflict.
entries.principle: The only major monster that is structurally a landscape rather than a character. The dead supply pressure and attrition; the story is always about the group, and the form's reliable discovery is that the living are the more dangerous problem. Its rules — bite transmission, headshot, the slow-versus-fast argument — matter because they set the resource economy the survival plot runs on.
entries.example: Romero's Night of the Living Dead severed the figure from its Haitian origins in 1968 and made it a crowd; his Dawn of the Dead added the consumer reading and the fortified position; Brooks's World War Z demonstrated the oral-history structure suits the material better than a single protagonist; Capcom's Resident Evil turned ammunition scarcity into the genre's most efficient tension mechanism.
entries.application: Decide the transmission rule, the movement speed and the noise threshold before you plot, because those three settings determine every scene you can write. Give the group a resource clock. And know the figure's origin: the zombie entered American fiction through the occupation of Haiti and the flattening of vodou, which is a debt the subgenre still mostly declines to acknowledge.

entries.name: Creature Feature & the Monster Movie
entries.description: One organism, established rules, and a cast learning them at cost.
entries.principle: The purest form of horror's engineering problem: a single non-human threat, a bounded environment, and a sequence of encounters that must each teach the audience something new about the creature without exhausting it. The form's discipline is disclosure management — how much of the thing is seen, when, and in what light. Its characteristic failure is the full reveal arriving before the rules are interesting.
entries.example: Honda's Godzilla made the creature an argument about the atomic bomb and lost that reading in export; Spielberg's Jaws demonstrated that mechanical failure and restraint produce a better monster than the monster; Scott's Alien gave the organism a life cycle so that each act faces a different animal; Carpenter's The Thing made the creature's rule set the plot, since the question is not where it is but who it is.
entries.application: Write the creature's biology before its behaviour — appetite, reproduction, limits — and let the cast deduce it in the wrong order. Ration the reveal against the environment's shrinkage. If the creature can be stopped, establish the method early enough that the audience can want it and doubt it.

entries.name: Body Horror
entries.description: The betrayal is interior, and there is nowhere to run to.
entries.principle: Horror sited in the body's own processes — disease, pregnancy, mutation, surgery, appetite — where the threat cannot be escaped because it is the escapee. The form trades startle for dread and works on disgust, which is a separate emotional channel with its own rules: it habituates fast, it is culturally variable, and it does not respond to pacing tricks that work on fear.
entries.example: Cronenberg's Videodrome and The Fly established the modern grammar, the latter by playing transformation as a documented decline rather than a shock; Tsukamoto's Tetsuo pushed it into industrial abstraction; Ito's Uzumaki demonstrated the manga page's advantage in depicting the impossible body; Machado's Her Body and Other Parties relocated the mode into the politics of who is believed about their own body.
entries.application: Choose one process and follow it honestly to its end — the form rewards commitment over variety. Write the body's changes through function rather than appearance: what the character can no longer do is more disturbing than what they look like. And ration disgust, because it dulls faster than fear and cannot be recovered within a single work.

entries.name: Cosmic Horror
entries.description: A universe that is not hostile, which is worse.
entries.principle: The argument that the human frame of reference is provincial and that contact with what lies outside it degrades the observer without malice. Its threat is epistemic: the danger is knowing, and the form's characteristic arc is the erosion of a narrator's capacity to report. The tradition's founding author held racial views that are not incidental to the work — the fear of contamination by the other is the mechanism — and the contemporary form has largely been built by writers arguing with him.
entries.example: Chambers's The King in Yellow established the contaminating text and Hodgson's The House on the Borderland the deep-time vertigo, both before Lovecraft consolidated the mode; Ligotti pursued its philosophical version without the pulp furniture; VanderMeer's Annihilation renewed it by making the incomprehensible ecological; LaValle's The Ballad of Black Tom rebuilt a Lovecraft story from inside the racial politics it depended on.
entries.application: Withhold the explanation permanently — a cosmic horror that resolves has become science fiction, which is a fine outcome but a different contract. Degrade the narrator's language as the story proceeds, since the prose is where the epistemic damage has to be visible. Scale is not achieved by size; it is achieved by indifference.

entries.name: Weird Fiction & the New Weird
entries.description: Estrangement without a taxonomy to file it under.
entries.principle: Broader than cosmic horror and older than its association with it: fiction whose effect depends on a wrongness that resists classification as ghost, monster or delusion. The classical weird tale is short, ambiguous and refuses to resolve; the New Weird of the early 2000s kept the anti-taxonomy and added density, cities and politics. Both reject the reassurance of a named category.
entries.example: Machen and Blackwood wrote the foundational English weird, the latter locating it in landscape rather than in incident; Aickman's self-described strange stories perfected irresolution so thoroughly that summarising one is nearly impossible; Miéville's Perdido Street Station led the New Weird's turn toward the urban and material; Link's short fiction demonstrates the mode operating at domestic scale.
entries.application: Resist the impulse to supply a category — the moment the reader can say "so it's a ghost," the effect is spent. Work from a concrete and precisely observed surface, because the weird needs a solid floor to be wrong against. Accept that irresolution is the form's contract, and signal it early so the reader stops waiting for an answer and starts reading what is actually there.

entries.name: Science-Fiction Horror
entries.description: The threat has a mechanism, and knowing it does not help.
entries.principle: The hybrid in which the horror survives explanation. Where cosmic horror collapses if the anomaly is understood, this form is built so that comprehension increases the dread — the reader learns exactly how the organism reproduces and is more frightened, not less. Its enabling condition is isolation with a technological cause: a crew, a station, a facility, a ship that cannot turn back.
entries.example: Shelley's Frankenstein founded the mode by making the creature's manufacture explicit and the consequences moral; Scott's Alien and Carpenter's The Thing are its two purest screen statements, one built on a life cycle and the other on an assimilation rule; Faber's Under the Skin runs it as sustained procedural estrangement; Visceral's Dead Space demonstrates the form's fit with the survival-horror game.
entries.application: Make the mechanism legible and terrible on the same page. The cast should be competent professionals — incompetence lets the audience off, whereas experts failing correctly is the form's strongest move. Establish why they cannot leave in the first act, and make it structural rather than stubborn.

entries.name: Eco-Horror & Nature's Revenge
entries.description: The environment stops being setting and starts having interests.
entries.principle: Horror in which the non-human world acts, whether as retaliation for a specific harm or as sheer indifferent process. The retaliation strain carries an obvious moral risk — it can flatter the audience with a punishment narrative — while the indifference strain is harder and more durable, because a landscape that simply does not require you is more frightening than one taking revenge.
entries.example: Du Maurier's The Birds offers no cause at all and is the stronger for it, a restraint the film adaptation preserved; Wyndham's The Day of the Triffids ties the catastrophe to cultivation and human blindness; Smith's The Ruins reduces the form to a single plant and a confined space; VanderMeer's Annihilation makes the ecological transformation illegible rather than punitive.
entries.application: Decide whether nature is retaliating or simply operating, and hold the line — mixing them produces a story that seems to be assigning blame and then withdrawing it. Avoid the ledger structure where each death matches a sin. Get the biology right enough that a reader who knows the organism stays inside the story.

entries.name: Psychological Horror
entries.description: The unreliable instrument is the one you are reading through.
entries.principle: Horror generated by interiority under pressure, where the reader's uncertainty about the narrator's perception is the primary source of dread. The form's discipline is fairness: the text must contain enough evidence for the reader to reconstruct what is happening, or the ambiguity reads as evasion. Its usual failure is the late reveal that retroactively cancels the story.
entries.example: Gilman's The Yellow Wallpaper set the template in 1892 and tied the deterioration to a real medical practice; Jackson's We Have Always Lived in the Castle narrates from inside a settled and unsettling logic without ever conceding it; Polanski's Repulsion externalised subjective collapse into architecture; Hitchcock's Psycho made the structural rug-pull a permanent part of the genre's vocabulary.
entries.application: Plant the evidence in plain sight and trust the reader. Keep the narrator internally consistent — unreliability is a stable distortion, not randomness, and the reader is decoding a system. Decide what actually happened and write it down somewhere, because ambiguity written without an underlying answer reads as vagueness on the page.

entries.name: Quiet Horror
entries.description: Wrongness introduced in a subordinate clause and never withdrawn.
entries.principle: A deliberate reaction against escalation, named as an editorial position rather than a content category: horror achieved through implication, domestic scale and an atmosphere that never resolves into an event. The form is technically demanding because it forgoes every reliable tension mechanism — no clock, no chase, no reveal — and must generate dread from tone and from the reader's growing certainty that something is off.
entries.example: Aickman's stories withhold not just explanation but incident, and remain unsettling on rereading precisely because there is nothing to solve; Charles L. Grant edited the Shadows anthologies around the principle and gave the mode its name; Campbell's prose locates dread in ordinary English suburbs and misread perception; Waters's The Little Stranger sustains it across a full novel by keeping the class resentment louder than the haunting.
entries.application: Introduce the wrong detail early, in passing, and never return to underline it. Resist the escalation instinct — the form's power is cumulative and a single loud scene will spend it. This mode requires the most confident prose in the genre, because with the machinery removed there is nothing else holding the reader.

entries.name: Slasher
entries.description: A body count with rules, and an audience that knows them.
entries.principle: The most formally rigid horror subgenre and the most self-aware: an isolated group, a killer with a signature method, a sequence of deaths in an established order, and a survivor whose survival the form has trained the audience to predict. Because the audience knows the rules, tension has to be generated by variation within them rather than by uncertainty about them.
entries.example: Clark's Black Christmas assembled the elements in 1974; Carpenter's Halloween supplied the killer's-eye camera and the suburban setting that fixed the template; Cunningham's Friday the 13th industrialised it and Craven's A Nightmare on Elm Street rescued it by giving the killer a personality and a rule set worth exploring; Craven's Scream made the audience's rule knowledge the text.
entries.application: Vary the order, never the logic — an audience that cannot predict anything stops being tense. Give each death a distinct spatial problem so the sequence teaches rather than repeats. Carol Clover's analysis of the form's viewer identification is now part of the genre's working vocabulary, and writing the survivor without engaging it reads as naïveté rather than as innocence.

entries.name: Splatterpunk & Extreme Horror
entries.description: Transgression as a stated position, and the craft question of what it is for.
entries.principle: A self-declared movement of the mid-1980s defined by refusing horror's traditional restraint: explicit and sustained depictions of torture, mutilation, sexual violence and death, presented without the cutaway. The material is genuinely extreme and a writer should know what they are picking up. Its defensible version uses that refusal to make violence cost something and to deny the reader the comfort of implication; its indefensible version is a catalogue with a plot attached.
entries.example: Barker's Books of Blood combined explicit body horror with genuine formal invention and remains the movement's strongest argument; Ketchum's The Girl Next Door, built on a real 1965 murder case, is unflinching about sustained abuse and is defended and attacked on exactly that ground; Laymon and Lee represent the commercial pulp strain; Laugier's Martyrs pushes the screen version to a point where its own critics disagree about whether the film indicts or supplies its spectacle.
entries.application: Know what the extremity is doing, and be able to say it in one sentence — the form's whole defence is that unmediated violence produces a moral response mediation would soften. Watch who it happens to; a subgenre that concentrates its suffering on women and calls it transgression is repeating a convention, not breaking one. And where the source is a real crime, analyse the published work rather than the case.

entries.name: Home Invasion & Domestic Horror
entries.description: The safe location reclassified, with the audience still inside it.
entries.principle: Horror that attacks the reader's default assumption of sanctuary. Two related modes: the external intrusion, whose power comes from the absence of motive, and the internal one, where the household itself is the apparatus and the threat is a spouse, a neighbourhood or an institution. Both depend on the audience having been shown the space as safe before it is reassigned.
entries.example: Haneke's Funny Games withholds motive deliberately and turns the withholding into an accusation of the viewer; Bertino's The Strangers reduces the form to the sentence about being home; Levin's The Stepford Wives and Rosemary's Baby locate the conspiracy in the marriage and the building, where the horror is the reasonableness of everyone involved; Peckinpah's Straw Dogs made the defence itself the disturbing element.
entries.application: Spend real pages establishing the space as ordinary and known — the intrusion's force is exactly proportional to that investment. Withhold motive if the threat is external; supply it precisely if the threat is domestic. And keep the geography consistent, because in this subgenre the audience is tracking exits.

entries.name: Survival Horror
entries.description: Scarcity as the tension mechanism, competence as the false comfort.
entries.principle: Originating as a game form and now fully portable to prose and screen, survival horror makes resource management the source of dread: limited ammunition, limited light, limited saves, and a threat that cannot be defeated so much as outlasted. Its defining move is denying the audience the power fantasy — the protagonist is capable enough to act and never capable enough to win.
entries.example: Capcom's Resident Evil established the vocabulary in 1996, with inventory limits and the fixed camera doing the work restraint does in prose; Konami's Silent Hill replaced combat competence with psychological terrain; Frictional's Amnesia removed the weapon entirely and proved the form survives without one; Marshall's The Descent transposes the whole structure to film, with the cave as inventory limit.
entries.application: Set the scarcity rules and never relieve them for narrative convenience — a resupply that arrives because the plot needs one destroys the form. Make the protagonist competent and insufficient. If you are writing prose, remember the mechanism is transferable but the pacing is not: what a player experiences as pressure over hours has to be compressed into scene-level decisions.

entries.name: Apocalyptic Horror
entries.description: The end as an ongoing condition rather than an event.
entries.principle: Horror in which the catastrophe is complete or completing, and the subject is what people become inside it. The form's structural challenge is that total collapse removes the stakes escalation depends on, so the best work substitutes a small and specific object of value — a child, a destination, a promise — against which the vastness is measured.
entries.example: Matheson's I Am Legend inverted the vampire story into an argument about who counts as the monster and supplied the template for most of what followed; McCarthy's The Road strips the apparatus to a relationship and a direction; Boyle's 28 Days Later re-timed the form for speed and located its threat in the surviving military; Carey's The Girl With All the Gifts refuses the restoration ending outright.
entries.application: Give the reader one thing small enough to hold. Decide whether your ending restores anything, and commit — the form's most common failure is a bleak novel that flinches in its final ten pages. Keep the catastrophe's mechanism mostly offstage; the survivors' inability to explain it is more convincing than a briefing.

entries.name: Techno-Horror & the Digital Uncanny
entries.description: The haunted medium — the signal that carries something it should not.
entries.principle: Horror that treats a communication technology as the vector rather than the setting: the tape, the broadcast, the network, the feed. The form works because these media already produce uncanny effects honestly — latency, degradation, the recorded voice of the dead — and because each new medium arrives before its social rules do. Its risk is obsolescence: hardware-specific horror dates fast.
entries.example: Cronenberg's Videodrome made broadcast a physical infection years before the network existed to prove the point; Suzuki's Ringu attached a curse to a duplicable object and thereby made transmission the plot; Kurosawa's Pulse used early network isolation to write loneliness as an apocalypse; Brooker's Black Mirror demonstrates the anthology's fit with the material.
entries.application: Anchor the horror to what the medium does rather than to the device — duplication, latency, persistence, the impossibility of deletion — and the story will outlive the hardware. Get the technology right; a reader who works with the system will leave at the first implausible detail. Remember that the medium's own artefacts are free atmosphere and should be used before any invented ones.

entries.name: Found Footage & the Documentary Mode
entries.description: Horror that argues about its own evidence.
entries.principle: A presentation mode rather than a content category: the work claims to be recovered material, and the claim does the work. The form's power is that it supplies a built-in reason for the camera, an implied outcome for the people holding it, and a permanent question about what has been edited. Its constraint is that everything must be justified diegetically, which is a discipline and not a licence for shakiness.
entries.example: Stoker's Dracula is the direct prose ancestor, assembled entirely from documents whose gaps are the point; Myrick and Sánchez's The Blair Witch Project established the modern screen form and its economics; Anderson's Lake Mungo uses the documentary register rather than the recovered-tape one and is the mode's most emotionally serious work; Danielewski's House of Leaves runs the apparatus through three levels of unreliable annotation.
entries.application: Justify the camera in every scene, including the ones where a real person would stop filming — if you cannot, restructure rather than hope. Use the archive's gaps deliberately; missing footage is the form's cheapest and best effect. And decide who assembled this material and why, because that editor is a character whether or not they appear.

entries.name: Analogue, Liminal & Internet-Native Horror
entries.description: Fiction shaped by the platform it circulates on.
entries.principle: The genre's newest formal development: horror written for open, collaborative and often anonymous distribution, where the work presents as an artefact rather than a story — a wiki entry, a corrupted broadcast, a lost episode, an empty photograph. Its native effects are the absence of an author, the absence of an ending, and the reader's uncertainty about the boundary of the text. Curation, not authorship, is the organising skill.
entries.example: The SCP Foundation demonstrates that a shared clinical register can sustain thousands of contributors without collapsing into parody; Straub's Candle Cove established the lost-media form in a few hundred words; the Marble Hornets series adapted found footage to serialised upload schedules; Local 58 built dread almost entirely from the conventions of broadcast interruption.
entries.application: Choose a document type and obey its conventions absolutely — the horror lives in the deviation from a form the reader already knows, so the form has to be right first. Withhold the frame; explaining who found this generally weakens it. And accept that the mode resists the tidy ending, which is why the strongest examples stop rather than conclude.

entries.name: Comedy Horror
entries.description: Two responses to the same stimulus, sequenced rather than blended.
entries.principle: The pairing works because laughter and fright are close physiological neighbours and because comedy requires the same precise timing horror does. The form's non-negotiable rule is that the horror must stay real: once the audience learns that nothing has consequences, the fear cannot be recovered and the film or novel becomes a comedy with monsters. The best work alternates registers cleanly rather than mixing them.
entries.example: Raimi's Evil Dead II found the mode almost by accident and made physical comedy and body horror the same gesture; Landis's An American Werewolf in London holds both registers at full strength and refuses to soften its ending; Wright's Shaun of the Dead keeps its emotional stakes intact underneath the parody; Clement and Waititi's What We Do in the Shadows shows the mockumentary's fit with the material.
entries.application: Establish the threat honestly before the first joke, and make sure someone the audience likes actually dies. Alternate rather than blend — a scene should be funny or frightening, with the switch as the effect. And keep the rules consistent across both registers, because comedy that suspends the monster's logic tells the audience the logic was never real.

entries.name: Dread, Terror and Horror
entries.description: Three different emotions that the genre's name collapses into one.
entries.principle: Dread is anticipatory and sustained, produced by a threat the reader knows about and cannot locate. Terror is acute and forward-facing — the moment before. Horror is retrospective and static, the response to what has already happened. They run on different clocks and cannot be generated by the same techniques, which is why a book that is superb at one is often flat at the others.
entries.example: Radcliffe's distinction between terror as expansive and horror as contracting has survived two centuries because it is descriptive rather than theoretical; James's ghost stories run almost entirely on dread and spend terror once; Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House sustains dread across a whole novel by never confirming its source; the standard creature film front-loads terror and has nothing left for the third act.
entries.application: Name which of the three you are writing before you draft the scene. Dread needs information the reader holds and the character does not; terror needs a clock and a confined space; horror needs consequence and stillness. Most weak horror is a terror scene attempting to do a dread scene's job.

entries.name: The Reveal and the Withheld Monster
entries.description: Showing it is a one-time expenditure, and the exchange rate is bad.
entries.principle: The unseen threat is an imagined threat, and the reader's imagination outperforms any description you can supply. But permanent withholding is not the answer either — a threat never seen eventually stops being believed. The craft is in staging partial disclosures that each add a rule rather than a picture: what it can reach, what it wants, what it leaves behind.
entries.example: Spielberg's Jaws is the standard case, where mechanical failure forced restraint and the restraint made the film; Carpenter's The Thing reveals constantly and stays frightening because each reveal changes the rules rather than satisfying curiosity; Mitchell's It Follows shows its threat plainly in the first act and derives everything from its pace and its single rule; the third act of most creature films demonstrates the failure mode.
entries.application: List your disclosures in order and check that each one adds a constraint, not a detail. Reserve the full view for the point where the reader already knows enough to be frightened by what they see. If you must show early, compensate by making the rules the mystery — Carpenter's route, not Spielberg's.

entries.name: Startle Economics and the False Scare
entries.description: The cheapest effect in the genre, and the one that spends the others.
entries.principle: A startle is a reflex, not an emotion — it is involuntary, it lasts under a second, and it produces relief immediately afterward. Relief is the enemy of dread. The false scare (the cat, the friend in the doorway, the hand on the shoulder) works by paying out that reflex without cost, and each one teaches the reader that alarm signals in your text are unreliable, which is the opposite of what you want them to learn.
entries.example: The Val Lewton unit's bus sequence in Cat People invented the technique in 1942 and used it once; Friedkin's The Exorcist places almost no false scares and is exhausting for exactly that reason; the post-2000 commercial haunting film typically runs a startle every four to six minutes and is frightening while watched and forgettable after; Flanagan's television work notably rations them.
entries.application: Count them. If you have more than two or three in a novel, you are training the reader to discount your alarms. Where you use one, make it cost something — the false scare that reveals the character was right to be afraid, or that moves the plot, buys back what it spends. A startle should never be the highest-tension moment in a chapter.

entries.name: Disgust as a Separate Channel
entries.description: It works fast, it habituates faster, and it does not convert into fear.
entries.principle: Disgust is a distinct emotional system with an evolutionary job — contamination avoidance — and it behaves nothing like fear. It saturates within a few exposures, it varies enormously between readers, and crucially it produces withdrawal rather than attention. A reader who is disgusted looks away; a reader who is afraid leans in. Treating the two as interchangeable is the most common miscalibration in the genre.
entries.example: Cronenberg's The Fly earns its disgust because the transformation is tracked as loss of function rather than as accumulating grotesquerie; Ito's manga uses the still image's permanence to make a single disgusting panel do a chapter's work; Barker's Books of Blood alternate the channels deliberately; the modern extremity film that opens at maximum disgust has nowhere to go by its midpoint.
entries.application: Budget disgust like a finite resource, because it is one. Place it after fear has been established, never before. And prefer disgust that carries information — a detail that tells the reader what the thing does — over disgust that merely describes a state, since the informative kind survives habituation.

entries.name: The Tension Curve and the Release Valve
entries.description: Sustained tension is not a plateau; it is a rising sawtooth.
entries.principle: Readers cannot hold peak tension for long and will disengage rather than endure it. The functional shape is repeated rise and partial release, with each release landing above the previous baseline. What matters is that the releases are partial — a full release resets the curve and you must rebuild from nothing. Comedy, tenderness, exposition and small victories are all valid valves, provided they do not resolve the underlying threat.
entries.example: Levin's Rosemary's Baby releases repeatedly into social comedy and domestic detail without ever lowering the actual threat level; Marshall's The Descent uses each new cave chamber as a partial reset; King's long novels characteristically release into character backstory, which is why they sustain length; a relentless novel like Ketchum's most extreme work achieves its effect by refusing the valve, at the cost of most readers.
entries.application: Chart your novel's tension by chapter and look for flat stretches at the top — those are where readers stop. Install valves that do not touch the threat: a meal, a joke, a small competence. And check that each new peak is higher than the last, because a curve that plateaus reads as repetition regardless of what is happening.

entries.name: Camera Placement on Violence
entries.description: Where the reader is standing when it happens determines what it means.
entries.principle: Prose has a camera whether the writer manages it or not, and its position during violence is the single most consequential choice in the scene. Inside the victim produces sympathy and duration; beside the perpetrator produces complicity; at a distance produces the coldness of documentation; after the fact produces dread and lets the reader's imagination do the work. Each carries an argument, and the reader will infer one whether or not you meant it.
entries.example: Haneke's Funny Games moves the camera off the violence and onto its duration, which is an accusation aimed at the audience; Hooper's The Texas Chain Saw Massacre is remembered as far more explicit than it is because its camera stays close and its sound does the rest; Ketchum's fiction stays with the victim's interiority throughout, which is precisely what makes it contested; police-procedural horror typically adopts the documentary distance and loses the fear.
entries.application: Choose the position deliberately and state to yourself what it argues. Changing position mid-scene is powerful and should be reserved. If you find you have defaulted to the perpetrator's shoulder throughout a manuscript, that is a thematic decision you have made by accident.

entries.name: Sound and Silence on the Page
entries.description: Prose has no soundtrack, so the noise has to be structural.
entries.principle: Screen horror gets its most reliable effects from sound design, and prose writers routinely try to import them by describing noises, which does not work — a described sound arrives at the reader's ordinary reading pace. What transfers is the structure underneath: rhythm, sentence length, white space, the paragraph break as a cut, and the deliberate absence of sensory information. Silence on the page is achieved through omission, not through the word silence.
entries.example: Jackson's prose accelerates and fragments as Eleanor's grip fails, so the reader experiences the tempo rather than reading about it; Danielewski's House of Leaves makes the page's physical layout carry the acoustics of an impossible space; Krasinski's A Quiet Place demonstrates on screen how completely the removal of sound restructures a scene; the standard haunted-house novel writes "a low moaning sound" and produces nothing.
entries.application: Cut sentence length as tension rises and let paragraphs shorten with it. Use a section break where a film would cut. And when you want the reader to hear something, withhold the other senses in that paragraph rather than describing the sound in more detail.

entries.name: The Uncanny as Technique
entries.description: Not a mood but a specific mechanism: the familiar, altered by one degree.
entries.principle: The uncanny is produced by a small deviation in something well known, not by a large deviation in something strange. Its effect depends entirely on the reader's prior model — a face is uncanny because the reader has an exact template for faces, whereas an alien landscape cannot be uncanny because there is no template to violate. This makes the uncanny the most economical effect in horror and the one most often squandered on already-strange material.
entries.example: Gaiman's Coraline builds its central figure by changing one feature of a mother, which is why it disturbs adults as much as children; Ito's work repeatedly applies a single geometric rule to ordinary bodies; Aster's Hereditary derives much of its unease from behaviour that is almost normal; the standard demon design piles on deviations and lands as fantasy rather than as wrongness.
entries.application: Change one thing. Establish the familiar version first and in detail, because you cannot violate a template the reader has not built. And resist adding a second deviation — the uncanny is subtractive, and the moment the thing becomes clearly other, the effect converts into ordinary monster horror.

entries.name: The Approach: Earning Isolation
entries.description: The drive out is not filler; it is where escape gets spent.
entries.principle: Almost every horror plot requires the characters to be beyond help, and the modern reader will not accept isolation asserted. The approach sequence — the road, the trail, the last town, the failing signal — is where the writer converts an assertion into an accumulated fact. It also performs a second job: it is the last stretch in which the reader can enjoy anticipation, which is a pleasure the rest of the book will not offer.
entries.example: The folk-horror tradition treats the journey as jurisdictional, with each stage moving the outsider further from his own law; Nevill's The Ritual spends substantial pages on the walk in and is unbalanced without them; Marshall's The Descent front-loads the descent so that the return becomes arithmetically impossible; the cabin film that arrives at the cabin in two minutes has to invent a reason nobody leaves.
entries.application: Remove one escape option per stage and let the characters notice each one. Make the last point of contact specific — the name of the town, the moment the bars drop — so the reader can locate exactly where rescue stopped. And use the approach for the group's ordinary dynamics, because after this you will not have time.

entries.name: The Investigation Structure
entries.description: The plot shape that makes people walk toward the thing.
entries.principle: Horror's central plotting problem is motivation: sensible people leave. Investigation solves it by giving the protagonist a reason to advance that is stronger than fear — a missing person, a professional duty, a debt, a need to know. The structure supplies its own escalation, because each answer narrows the space and raises the cost, and it converts exposition into action since research is something the character does rather than something the narrator delivers.
entries.example: Stoker's Dracula is assembled almost entirely from investigative documents and moves because its cast are gathering evidence; Blatty's The Exorcist runs a medical investigation for its entire first half; Peele's Get Out uses the protagonist's accumulating observations as the plot's spine; Langan's The Fisherman nests investigation inside investigation as its structural principle.
entries.application: Give the investigator a stake that outweighs self-preservation and state it early. Structure the discoveries so each one closes an exit rather than opening a door. And ensure the investigation's method has limits the supernatural can defeat, or the reader will wonder why the protagonist does not simply keep researching.

entries.name: Escalation Without Inflation
entries.description: Bigger is not the same as worse, and the genre keeps confusing them.
entries.principle: The instinct to escalate by increasing scale — more victims, larger entity, wider threat — usually reduces fear, because fear is proportional to specificity and intimacy rather than to magnitude. Genuine escalation raises the cost to a particular person, narrows the available options, or shortens the time. A threat that grows from one house to a city has often become less frightening, not more.
entries.example: King's Pet Sematary escalates entirely inward, to a smaller and more unbearable domestic unit; Aster's Hereditary escalates by making the family's situation more specific rather than more populous; the later entries of most horror franchises escalate by scale and demonstrate the failure; Boyle's 28 Days Later notably de-escalates its scale in the third act to focus on a single compound, and gains from it.
entries.application: Escalate along cost, constraint or clock — never along body count. Ask what the character now stands to lose that they did not stand to lose in chapter one; if the answer is only "more of the same," you have inflated. Sequels are where this discipline collapses most reliably, so plan the ceiling before you write the first book.

entries.name: The Ensemble Attrition Plan
entries.description: If the deaths are in the wrong order, the whole novel sags.
entries.principle: Any horror story with a group is running an attrition structure, and it needs planning at the outline stage. Each death must cost the survivors a specific capability — the one who could drive, the one who was holding the group together, the one who knew the way — so that the situation materially worsens rather than merely thinning. Deaths that remove no capability read as list-clearing regardless of how well written they are.
entries.example: Scott's Alien assigns each loss a function and the crew's options visibly narrow; Carpenter's The Thing compounds attrition with paranoia so each death also removes trust; Marshall's The Descent removes light sources and expertise in sequence; the standard slasher sequel kills in order of billing, which is why its middle acts are inert.
entries.application: Write the group as a capability list before you write them as people, then decide the order in which those capabilities are removed. Kill the most competent member earlier than instinct suggests. And give at least one death to something the group did rather than to the threat's initiative, because a self-inflicted loss changes the room permanently.

entries.name: Ending Taxonomy
entries.description: Five endings, and the book has been promising one of them since chapter one.
entries.principle: Horror's endings fall into recognisable settlements: survival with cost, the pyrrhic victory, the downer in which the threat wins, the return in which nothing was resolved, and the unresolved in which the reader is denied a verdict. Each is legitimate; the failure is a mismatch between the ending delivered and the one the book's tone, structure and promises have been preparing. Readers forgive bleakness far more readily than they forgive a broken contract.
entries.example: Levin's Rosemary's Baby ends on a settlement so consistent with everything preceding it that it reads as inevitable; McCarthy's The Road delivers a fractional mercy the novel has quietly earned; Boyle's 28 Days Later shot two endings and the choice between them changes what the film argues; the studio-mandated survival ending grafted onto a bleak film is the genre's most recognisable structural failure.
entries.application: Identify which ending your first fifty pages have been promising, then either deliver it or break it deliberately and pay for the break. Write the ending you actually believe before you write the middle. And note that the unresolved ending, which is horror's most common, requires the most careful setup — it must read as a decision, not as an unfinished draft.

entries.name: The Stinger and the False Close
entries.description: The last beat retroactively edits everything before it.
entries.principle: The final-image reversal is horror's signature move and its most abused one. It works when it recontextualises the story the reader has just finished — revealing that the escape was partial, the survivor is carrying something, or the cycle is structural. It fails when it merely appends a shock, because an appended shock tells the reader the preceding resolution was insincere, which retroactively cheapens the whole climax.
entries.example: Carpenter's Halloween ends on absence rather than on an appearance, which is why it still functions; De Palma's Carrie made the grab-from-the-grave a permanent genre convention and most subsequent uses are decorative; Anderson's Lake Mungo places its true reveal in the closing images and the film is entirely rebuilt by it; the franchise-obligation stinger is the clearest case of the failure mode.
entries.application: Test the stinger by asking whether removing it would change the meaning of chapter one. If not, cut it. Prefer the stinger that confirms a suspicion the attentive reader already had over the one that arrives from nowhere — the first rewards rereading, the second punishes trust.

entries.name: The Standalone Discipline
entries.description: Horror is the genre most damaged by continuation.
entries.principle: Most horror's power depends on scarcity of explanation, and continuation is a machine for producing explanation. Each sequel must either repeat the first work's mystery — which the audience has now solved — or expand its lore, which converts dread into cosmology. This is why the genre's canon is overwhelmingly standalone and why its franchises so reliably decline along a predictable curve.
entries.example: Jackson's Hill House has no sequel and could not survive one; Barker's Hellraiser universe demonstrates the lore-expansion decline across a long series; King's The Shining and its much later sequel are instructive precisely because the second book chooses to explain the first's mechanism; the Alien sequence shows both routes, with each explanatory instalment reducing the original organism.
entries.application: Write the standalone as a standalone, with its unexplained material genuinely unexplained rather than reserved. If a sequel is contractually likely, plan what will stay permanently unexplained and defend it. And if you are continuing someone else's work, resist the instinct to answer the original's open question — that question is the property's actual asset.

entries.name: Rules of the Haunting: Hard and Soft
entries.description: How much the reader can predict determines what they feel.
entries.principle: A fully specified threat produces a puzzle and the pleasures of problem-solving; an unspecified one produces dread and the pleasures of dread. Neither is superior, but they are mutually exclusive within a scene, and the choice must be made and held. Horror's default is soft — the entity's rules remain partly unknown — which is why the genre's satisfactions differ so sharply from fantasy's, where hard systems dominate.
entries.example: Mitchell's It Follows publishes one hard rule and derives an entire film's tension from the audience's ability to calculate; the slasher tradition runs hard rules and is enjoyed partly as a game; Aickman's stories operate at the extreme soft end, where no rule is ever confirmed; Wan's Insidious begins soft and hardens as it explains, and the tension moves accordingly.
entries.application: Decide where on the axis you are sitting and audit for drift, because unplanned hardening is the most common structural failure in a horror second act. If you publish a rule, obey it without exception — a hard rule broken once converts the reader from participant to spectator permanently.

entries.name: Source, Cost and Limit
entries.description: Three questions the writer must answer even if the reader never does.
entries.principle: Where does the threat come from, what does acting cost it, and what stops it. The reader may never learn any of these, but the writer must, because the answers determine what can happen in every scene. A limit in particular is what makes survival conceivable and therefore makes suspense possible — a wholly unlimited threat produces despair, which is a much shorter-lived reading experience than fear.
entries.example: Krasinski's A Quiet Place states its limit in the title and builds every scene against it; Suzuki's Ringu specifies a deadline and a transmission mechanism, so the characters can act rationally and still lose; Carpenter's The Thing gives its organism a metabolic cost that the blood test exploits; the omnipotent demon of the generic possession film has no limit and consequently no scenes that can be plotted.
entries.application: Write the three answers down before drafting and keep them beside you. Reveal the limit late and the cost early. And check that your threat has at least one thing it cannot do, because a character who has no possible correct action cannot be written into a tense scene.

entries.name: The Explanation Problem
entries.description: Understanding is the strongest anti-horror force in the genre.
entries.principle: Horror's characteristic arc runs toward knowledge, and knowledge is corrosive to fear. Every explanation converts an unbounded threat into a bounded one, and a bounded threat is a problem rather than a terror. The craft response is not to refuse explanation but to sequence it so that each answer reveals a worse question, or to ensure the explanation arrives too late to be actionable.
entries.example: Friedkin's The Exorcist explains almost everything and stays frightening because the explanation is a theology the characters must act inside rather than a solution; VanderMeer's Annihilation withholds permanently and makes the refusal its subject; the researcher scene in the standard haunting film explains the entity's backstory and is almost always the moment the film stops being frightening; Kubrick's The Shining notably strips the novel's explanations and gains dread while losing coherence.
entries.application: Put the exposition scene where a reduction in tension is affordable, and never immediately before the climax. Make each answer cost something or open something worse. And consider giving the explanation to a character the reader has reason to doubt, which lets you deliver information without conceding it.

entries.name: Monster and Entity POV
entries.description: Inhabiting the thing, and what it costs you.
entries.principle: Writing from inside the threat converts fear into something else — sympathy, revulsion, or the specific unease of alien cognition. It is a legitimate and powerful move that permanently forecloses one option: an entity the reader has inhabited can no longer be unknowable. The calibration problem is that a mind rendered too alien becomes unreadable, while one rendered too human stops being a monster.
entries.example: Shelley's Frankenstein gives the creature the novel's central argument and thereby relocates the horror onto its maker; Harris's Red Dragon alternates into the killer's perspective and makes his interiority coherent without making it sympathetic; Lindqvist's Let the Right One In sits inside a predator's practical routine; the serial-killer thriller that renders its antagonist as pure appetite demonstrates the failure at the alien end.
entries.application: Enter the threat's perspective only if you are prepared to lose its unknowability, and do it early rather than late — a late entry reads as a reveal and deflates the accumulated mystery. Ground alien cognition in a consistent priority rather than in strange syntax. And keep the entity's chapters shorter than the human ones.

entries.name: Withheld Backstory as Dread
entries.description: The unexplained tenth, not the documented nine.
entries.principle: Depth of invention behind the page is only useful if it constrains what happens on it. In horror specifically, the withheld material must remain withheld — the dread is generated by the reader sensing a system they cannot see, and it evaporates when the system is drawn. This is the inverse of the fantasy iceberg, where revealing the submerged mass is usually a reward.
entries.example: Jackson supplies Hill House with a history that is gestured at and never assembled; Danielewski's House of Leaves surrounds its absence with an enormous apparatus of scholarship that explains nothing; Kubrick's The Shining leaves its hotel's chronology deliberately unresolvable; the prequel that documents the entity's origin is the standard demonstration of what the withholding was worth.
entries.application: Build the backstory in full and then plan what will never appear. Let the withheld material leave traces — an inconsistency, an object, a date that does not fit — because dread requires evidence of a system, not merely absence. Never write the prequel chapter, however much you want to.

entries.name: The Threat That Cannot Be Negotiated With
entries.description: The structural difference between horror and every adjacent genre.
entries.principle: Fantasy's monsters can often be reasoned with, bargained with or redeemed; horror's characteristically cannot, and that impossibility is what forces the form's plots into flight, endurance or destruction. Where negotiation is possible, the story converts into dark fantasy or tragedy. This is worth stating plainly because the redemption instinct is strong and arrives late in drafts, usually as an attempt to give the antagonist depth.
entries.example: Carpenter's The Thing offers no communicative channel at all and the film's paranoia follows directly from that; Peele's Get Out makes the antagonists entirely reasonable and entirely unnegotiable, which is the point; Kingfisher's What Moves the Dead keeps its entity outside the terms of any bargain; the third-act scene in which the demon is talked to demonstrates how quickly the register changes.
entries.application: Decide whether a channel exists, and if it does not, remove the scenes where characters attempt one — they read as the writer hedging. Depth for an unnegotiable threat comes from consistency and specificity, not from motive. If you find yourself wanting to redeem the entity, you may have written a different book, which is worth knowing before the final act.

entries.name: The Unreliable Narrator in Horror
entries.description: A stable distortion the reader is invited to decode.
entries.principle: Unreliability in horror is not randomness or concealment; it is a consistent bias whose shape the reader can learn. That learnability is what makes the technique generative rather than merely tricky — the reader's growing comprehension becomes a form of dread, since they see the shape of the danger before the narrator concedes it. The failure mode is the narrator who withholds arbitrarily, which reads as authorial manipulation.
entries.example: Gilman's The Yellow Wallpaper distorts in a single direction and the reader tracks the deterioration precisely; Jackson's We Have Always Lived in the Castle narrates from inside a settled logic and never breaks frame; Clarke's Piranesi turns the reader's comprehension outpacing the narrator's into the book's engine; the twist novel whose narrator simply omits a fact until the last chapter demonstrates the cheat.
entries.application: Define the distortion as a rule — what this narrator systematically cannot see, or reframes — and apply it without exception. Give the reader enough to reconstruct the truth by the two-thirds point; the pleasure is in being ahead, not in being ambushed. Never let the narrator lie about an event they are currently narrating.

entries.name: Found Documents and the Epistolary Chain
entries.description: Horror's native structure, older than the novel's respectability.
entries.principle: Assembled-document narration gives horror four things at once: a reason the account exists, a limit on what can be known, gaps that the reader fills with worse material than the writer could supply, and an implied compiler whose motives are themselves a source of unease. Its discipline is that every document must be plausible as a document — written by someone, for someone, at a moment when writing it made sense.
entries.example: Stoker's Dracula remains the form's most complete demonstration, with its cast's evidentiary compulsion doing the plotting; Blackwood and James used the recovered-account frame to license their narrators' precision; Danielewski's House of Leaves stacks three unreliable compilers; the SCP Foundation shows the form operating natively online with a clinical register and no author at all.
entries.application: Justify each document's existence and its survival. Design the gaps deliberately — missing pages are the form's cheapest strong effect — and decide who assembled the file, because that person is a character even if they never appear. And watch the tense problem: a first-person account of one's own death requires a solution, and the solutions are all visible.

entries.name: Prose Texture and the Flat Register
entries.description: Understatement is not a style choice; it is a load-bearing technique.
entries.principle: Horror's most reliable prose strategy is to report the impossible in the same register used for the ordinary, because the flatness implies a narrator who has accepted what they are describing — and that acceptance is more disturbing than any amount of emphasis. Ornate prose can work, but it must be established from the first page as the book's weather, whereas the flat register is portable and rarely fails.
entries.example: Jackson's sentences deliver appalling information in the cadence of household observation; Aickman's narrators remain courteous throughout events that would justify screaming; Machado's fiction uses the deadpan to make bodily horror read as reportage; the amateur manuscript that reaches for adjectives at the moment of revelation demonstrates the alternative.
entries.application: Cut the intensifiers at the moment of highest tension — very, suddenly, horribly, unspeakable — because they instruct the reader how to feel and thereby do the feeling for them. Report the wrong thing in a subordinate clause. Save your most ordinary sentence for your worst moment.

entries.name: The Scene of First Wrongness
entries.description: The mundane baseline, three exact details, and no comment.
entries.principle: The first intrusion sets the book's contract and is worth disproportionate care. It requires an established ordinary — the reader must have a baseline to measure against — followed by a small, specific, unglossed deviation, followed by the narrative declining to remark on it. The declining is the technique: a narrator who notices and worries has told the reader how frightened to be, whereas one who moves on leaves the reader alone with it.
entries.example: Jackson's opening chapters establish domestic routine so thoroughly that a single wrong detail carries the weight of a scene; Kurosawa's Pulse introduces its wrongness in the corner of ordinary frames; Hill's The Woman in Black places its first sighting in daylight among mourners; the novel that opens on a prologue of atrocity has spent the effect before establishing anything to violate.
entries.application: Spend real pages on ordinary before the first deviation, and make the deviation small enough to be deniable. Give exactly three concrete details, not five. Then change the subject — the reader will not, and that gap is where the dread lives.

entries.name: Comic Relief and the Tonal Contract
entries.description: Humour is a valve; it becomes a leak the moment consequence lapses.
entries.principle: Comedy in horror is legitimate and often necessary as a tension valve, but it operates under one strict condition: the threat's consequences must remain fully intact. Readers infer the contract quickly — if a joke arrives at a moment of danger and the danger then fails to materialise, they conclude that the danger is not real, and that conclusion cannot be reversed within the same work.
entries.example: Wright's Shaun of the Dead keeps its bereavements permanent and its jokes therefore cost something; King's novels use humour extensively while keeping the mortality rate high; Landis's An American Werewolf in London holds both registers without softening either; the horror-comedy that survives its own set pieces demonstrates the collapse, after which no scene can be tense again.
entries.application: Set the contract in the first act and never violate it. Kill someone the reader likes reasonably early if you intend to be funny later. And keep the registers sequential rather than simultaneous — a scene should be frightening or funny, with the transition as the effect.

entries.name: Transgression as Craft
entries.description: Extremity is a technique with a purpose, or it is a catalogue.
entries.principle: Explicit and sustained depiction of violence has a defensible craft rationale: mediation lets the reader off, and refusing mediation forces an unmediated moral response. This is a real argument and the genre's extreme wing rests on it. The test is whether the work knows what its extremity is for and whether removing the mediation actually produces the response claimed — where it does not, the material is functioning as spectacle with a defence attached.
entries.example: Barker's Books of Blood pair explicit body horror with formal invention, so the transgression is doing structural work; Ketchum's The Girl Next Door depicts sustained abuse without cutaway and is defended and attacked on precisely that ground, with both positions arguable; Laugier's Martyrs divides serious critics on whether it indicts its spectacle or supplies it; the direct-to-market extremity title with no argument at all is the honest baseline for comparison.
entries.application: Be able to state in one sentence what the unflinching depiction achieves that a cutaway would not. Check whether the extremity is distributed or concentrated, and on whom. And distinguish the reader's discomfort, which may be the point, from the reader's disengagement, which never is.

entries.name: Writing the Body Without the Anatomy Catalogue
entries.description: Function lost is worse than tissue described.
entries.principle: Detailed anatomical description reliably produces less horror than writers expect, because it engages the reader as an observer of a specimen. What produces horror is the loss of function and the character's relationship to their own altered body — what they can no longer do, what they now have to manage, what they notice themselves getting used to. The second register is also renewable, whereas description saturates.
entries.example: Cronenberg's The Fly tracks its transformation almost entirely through capability and habit; Machado writes the body through what is done to it and believed about it rather than through its surfaces; Ito's manga can afford pure depiction because the still image works differently from prose; the splatter novel that inventories wounds demonstrates how quickly catalogue prose stops registering.
entries.application: Write what the body can no longer do before you write what it looks like. Give the character a practical adaptation — a routine, an accommodation, a concealment — because adaptation implies duration and duration is where the horror sits. Reserve explicit description for one or two moments and let function carry the rest.

entries.name: Sexual Violence: The Field's Standing Failure
entries.description: The genre's most-used and least-examined device.
entries.principle: Horror has relied on sexual violence as a source of threat, motivation and spectacle more than any adjacent genre, and overwhelmingly as something that happens to women in order to generate a plot for someone. The craft objection is not squeamishness: it is that the device is almost always doing work that could be done better another way, and that its ubiquity has made it inert as well as harmful.
entries.example: The rape-revenge cycle of the 1970s is the clearest case, where the assault functions as a permission structure for the second half; du Maurier and Jackson generate sexual threat throughout their work without depicting assault, which demonstrates the alternatives exist; Machado's fiction addresses the subject from the interior of the person it happens to; Peele's Get Out finds bodily violation horror that does not route through it at all.
entries.application: Ask what the scene achieves and whether another violation would achieve it — if yes, the choice was inherited rather than made. If it belongs, write it from inside the person it happens to, give it consequences that persist past the act, and do not make it the engine of someone else's arc. And note that the threat of it is not a free alternative; suspended threat aimed continuously at a woman is its own convention.

entries.name: Cruelty to the Character, Cruelty to the Reader
entries.description: Two different acts, and only one of them is craft.
entries.principle: Horror requires cruelty to characters — that is the form. What it does not require is cruelty to the reader, which is the separate act of extracting distress without offering the compensations reading provides: comprehension, shape, meaning, or the dignity of the thing depicted. The distinction is not about intensity. A very bleak book can be generous, and a mild one can be contemptuous.
entries.example: McCarthy's The Road is relentless and treats its reader as a collaborator throughout; Haneke's Funny Games is deliberately cruel to its audience and says so, which is a coherent position rather than an accident; Ketchum's work divides readers on exactly this line; the film that withholds all meaning from prolonged suffering and calls the withholding realism illustrates the failure.
entries.application: Distinguish discomfort you have designed from disengagement you have caused. Give prolonged suffering a shape — duration the reader can measure, a character who remains a person throughout. And if you are being cruel to the reader deliberately, know it and commit, because the position is defensible and the accident is not.

entries.name: Folklore Research for Fiction
entries.description: Work from the collections, not from other people's monsters.
entries.principle: Most genre creatures have passed through several generations of fiction and gaming until almost nothing of the source survives, and what is left is usually the parts that stat well. Going back to folklore collections, regional ethnographies and archives yields material nobody else is using — and material that is stranger, more local and more usable, because folk tradition is full of specific rules and inconsistencies that genre processing has sanded off.
