entries.example: Hearn's collected Japanese tales continue to supply screen horror a century later because they were gathered rather than invented; Hurley's The Loney works from English regional Catholic practice rather than from folk-horror films; Moreno-Garcia builds from Mexican material directly; the standard genre vampire, four removes from any source, demonstrates what the sanding costs.
entries.application: Read the collections and the ethnographic scholarship rather than encyclopedias of creatures. Keep the locality — one valley, one rule, one season is more convincing than a species. And preserve the inconsistencies and the cruelty, because those are precisely the features that got removed and precisely where the fresh material is.

entries.name: Borrowing Across Living Traditions
entries.description: The difference between a dead corpus and someone's current religion.
entries.principle: Folklore is not uniformly available. Some traditions are historical and unowned; others are living practice with adherents, and rendering them as horror casts real people as monsters. The distinction is not about permission in the abstract but about consequence: horror is the genre most likely to take a community's sacred material and reissue it as a threat, and the record of that is long and specific.
entries.example: The screen zombie's derivation from vodou under the American occupation of Haiti is the genre's foundational case, and the tradition it flattened is a functioning religion; King's Pet Sematary attaches its burial ground to a named Indigenous people and is regularly cited as the template for a device that has since become generic; Rose's Candyman is argued over precisely because it engages the racial history of its setting rather than merely using it; Stephen Graham Jones writes Blackfeet material from inside the tradition, which is a different transaction entirely.
entries.application: Establish whether the tradition is living and whether its practitioners have said anything about outside use — often they have, in writing, and it is findable. Apply the equivalence test: would this treatment of a religion you belong to read as respectful? Consult and credit and pay where you can. And if the answer is that you should not write it, that is a legitimate outcome rather than a failure of nerve.

entries.name: Trauma Representation and Its Ethics
entries.description: Horror is the genre best suited to it, which raises rather than lowers the standard.
entries.principle: Horror's native techniques — intrusion, repetition, unreliable perception, the past refusing to stay past — map unusually well onto how trauma is actually experienced, which is why the genre has become a primary vehicle for writing about it. That fit creates an obligation: the metaphor should be accountable to the condition it borrows from, and the resolution should not imply that recovery works the way plot resolution does.
entries.example: Kent's The Babadook makes grief structurally inseparable from the entity and refuses the ending where it is destroyed; Morrison's Beloved holds the historical and the supernatural in the same frame without letting either become a device for the other; Aster's Hereditary makes inherited illness and inherited curse indistinguishable, which is either the film's strength or its problem depending on the reader; the horror film that resolves a character's trauma by killing the monster demonstrates the standard failure.
entries.application: Decide whether the supernatural is a metaphor for the condition or a separate thing the condition sits beside, and hold that line. Do not let the exorcism double as a cure. And if you are writing a specific diagnosis, get the phenomenology right, because readers who have it will be the ones who notice.

entries.name: Real Crime as Source Material
entries.description: The case belongs to the people it happened to.
entries.principle: A substantial part of the horror canon derives from real crimes, often loosely and often without acknowledgement. The craft position is that the published work is fair ground for analysis and the case is not: the writer's obligations run to accuracy about what they are inventing, to the victims' families where they are identifiable, and to not laundering documentary claims through fiction. Recency and identifiability are the two variables that matter most.
entries.example: Bloch's Psycho and the several films drawing on the same Wisconsin case took a set of details and invented outward, which is the defensible pattern; Ketchum's The Girl Next Door stays close to a 1965 murder and its closeness is exactly what the argument about it concerns; the dramatised-investigation subgenre routinely presents invention in a documentary register, which is where the real harm concentrates.
entries.application: Invent outward from a detail rather than dramatising a case. Change what identifies real people, and assume surviving family will read it. Do not adopt a documentary register for invented material. And when you write about such a work, analyse the book or film's craft rather than relitigating the crime.

entries.name: YA and Middle-Grade Horror: Voice and Agency
entries.description: The protagonist's choices must cause the resolution, or the book is about adults.
entries.principle: Horror for younger readers is not diluted adult horror; it is horror in which the protagonist's limited power is the premise. Adults must be handled structurally — absent, disbelieving, complicit or overwhelmed — because an available competent adult removes the plot. The voice constraint is real but narrower than commonly assumed: the vocabulary bends, the emotional sophistication does not.
entries.example: Gaiman's Coraline gives its protagonist a problem adults cannot perceive and a solution only she can execute; Arden's Small Spaces builds its danger around a group whose isolation is age-appropriate and complete; Schwartz's Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark, with Gammell's illustrations, demonstrated how much unmediated dread the readership actually tolerates; the middle-grade horror rescued by a parent in the final chapter demonstrates the structural error.
entries.application: Remove or discredit the adults in the first act, and do it plausibly rather than by contrivance. Make the protagonist's decisive action require something only they have. And write down rather than simplify — young readers detect condescension faster than they detect difficulty.

entries.name: YA and Middle-Grade Horror: Darkness Calibration and the Hope Requirement
entries.description: Bleakness is permitted; futility is not.
entries.principle: The genuine constraint on horror for young readers is not intensity but implication. Frightening material, permanent loss and unresolved endings are all available and widely used. What the readership is poorly served by is the argument that action is pointless — the ending in which nothing the protagonist did mattered. The adjustment is to move the camera rather than the subject: the same event, witnessed from a different distance.
entries.example: Gaiman's The Graveyard Book opens on a family's murder and handles it by camera placement rather than by omission; Arden and Black both permit real and permanent losses; Hahn's Wait Till Helen Comes deals directly with a child's death without softening it; the young-adult horror that ends on total futility is rare precisely because the readership's response to it is not productive fear but discouragement.
entries.application: Keep the events and adjust the vantage — what is shown, from how far, and with what aftermath. Ensure the protagonist's agency produced something, even if it did not produce safety. And be honest about aftermath rather than about spectacle; young readers accept that a thing happened far more readily than they accept that it did not matter.

entries.name: Rules-of-the-Threat Audit
entries.description: For any story with a supernatural, non-human or non-negotiable antagonist.
items: Can you state the threat's source, its cost and its limit in one sentence each?
Is the limit established on the page before it becomes load-bearing in a scene?
Does the threat acquire a new capability at the climax? (If so, cut it — the reader will register it as cheating even if they cannot name why.)
Could the threat have solved an earlier problem in a way it inexplicably did not?
Would fully explaining the threat make it less frightening? (If yes, do not fully explain it.)
Are you writing hard rules or soft, and does the manuscript drift from one to the other in the second act?
If you published a rule to the reader, is it obeyed without a single exception?
Is there at least one correct action available to a character in each threat scene? (If not, you have written despair rather than suspense.)

entries.name: Dread-Budget & Tension-Curve Audit
entries.description: Run this on a chapter-by-chapter tension chart before the final draft.
items: Which of dread, terror and horror is each major scene attempting, and does its technique match?
Are there flat stretches at the top of the curve where tension is sustained rather than rising? (That is where readers stop.)
Does each release land above the previous baseline, or does any release resolve the underlying threat?
How many startles and false scares are there in total, and does each one cost something or move the plot?
Is disgust placed after fear is established rather than before, and is it used sparingly enough to still register late in the book?
Does sentence and paragraph length actually shorten as tension rises?
Is the highest-tension moment in each act something other than a jump?
Where is the reader permitted to breathe, and have you written those moments deliberately?

entries.name: Reveal & Setup Ledger
entries.description: The anti-cheat pass. Run it as a two-column list: every reveal, and where it was planted.
items: Is every reveal traceable to something established earlier in the text?
Does each disclosure about the threat add a constraint rather than merely a detail?
Is the full view of the threat held until the reader already knows enough to fear what they see?
Does the ending's reversal change the meaning of the first chapter? (If removing it changes nothing, cut it.)
Is every planted object, name, date or inconsistency eventually used or deliberately left as a trace?
Does the narrator ever withhold a fact about an event they are currently narrating? (That is concealment, not unreliability.)
Can an attentive reader reconstruct the truth by the two-thirds point?
Does the exposition scene sit somewhere a drop in tension is affordable — and not immediately before the climax?

entries.name: Lore-Delivery Pass
entries.description: For every scene in which someone explains the threat.
items: Does anybody explain something to a character who already knows it?
Is there a paragraph of history delivered as speech that could be delivered as disagreement instead?
Does the explanation scene defuse the threat? (The single most common way a horror second act loses its grip.)
Does each answer open a worse question, or does it close the subject?
Is the information given to a character the reader has reason to doubt, where that would help?
Does the researcher or expert have limits the threat can defeat?
How much of the backstory you invented is on the page, and is the withheld portion still leaving traces?
Have you written the prequel chapter that explains the entity's origin? (Cut it.)

entries.name: Ensemble Attrition Audit
entries.description: For any story where a group is reduced.
items: Does each death remove a specific capability the group needed?
Is the situation materially worse after each loss, or merely less populated?
Are the deaths ordered by dramatic function rather than by how minor the character is?
Does the most competent member die earlier than instinct suggested?
Is at least one loss caused by something the group did, rather than by the threat's initiative?
Does the reader know each victim well enough for the loss to cost them something?
Does the group's decision-making stay plausible, or do people split up because the plot needs them to?
After the final death, does the survivor have a different problem than they had at the start?

entries.name: Cultural Borrowing & Living-Religion Check
entries.description: Run before drafting, not after. Any single "no" is a stop, not a note.
items: Can you name the specific culture, region and period, rather than a continent or an era?
Have you worked from primary sources, collections or ethnography rather than from other genre fiction?
Is the tradition living practice with adherents today, or a historical corpus?
If it is living: have its practitioners said anything about outside use, and have you looked? (Often they have, in writing, and it is findable.)
Is a real religion, ethnicity or community functioning as the monster in your story?
Would this treatment of a tradition you belong to read as respectful? (The equivalence test.)
Have you consulted, credited and where possible paid someone from the tradition?
Is the sacred element being used as belief with its own logic, or as an aesthetic?
Are you aware of the genre's own record here — the zombie's derivation from vodou under the occupation of Haiti, the "ancient burial ground" device and its source — and are you repeating it?
Why this material, and why you? (If you cannot answer the second half, that is an answer.)

entries.name: Violence & Taste Pass
entries.description: For any scene of sustained violence, assault or bodily harm.
items: Can you state in one sentence what the unflinching depiction achieves that a cutaway would not?
Where is the camera — inside the victim, beside the perpetrator, at documentary distance, or after the fact — and what does that position argue?
Is the suffering distributed across the cast or concentrated on one demographic?
If the scene is sexual violence: would another violation achieve the same plot work? (If yes, the choice was inherited rather than made.)
Does the harm have consequences that persist past the scene, or is it reset by the next chapter?
Is the violence generating discomfort you designed, or disengagement you caused?
Does the character remain a person throughout, or become a body partway through?
Is any of this drawn from a real crime, and if so have you invented outward rather than dramatised?

entries.name: YA & Middle-Grade Horror Calibration
entries.description: For horror aimed at younger readers. Age brackets, not a genre — the craft standard does not drop.
items: Do the protagonist's own choices cause the resolution?
Are the adults removed, discredited, complicit or overwhelmed — and plausibly rather than by contrivance?
Does the decisive action require something only this protagonist has?
Are the frightening events intact, with the calibration handled by camera placement rather than by omission?
Are there permanent losses, and does the book treat them as permanent?
Does the ending imply that what the protagonist did mattered, even if it did not produce safety?
Is the aftermath given more attention than the spectacle?
Have you written down to the reader anywhere? (They detect condescension faster than difficulty.)

entries.name: The Rules Learned Too Late
entries.description: The information that would have saved them arrives after it can be used.

examples.text: Every piece of information Howie needs is given to him openly and in good time, and his own certainties make each one unreadable, so the failure is his frame of reference rather than the community's deception.
Suzuki structures the whole book as rule-acquisition against a deadline, so the reader learns the mechanism at the same rate as the characters and can calculate the shortfall.
Nevill lets the group misidentify what they are dealing with for most of the book, and the correction costs them the only advantage they had.

entries.name: The Thing That Must Not Be Seen
entries.description: Perception as the trigger; looking is the fatal act.

examples.text: Malerman makes sight itself the vector, which converts every ordinary action into a procedure and gives the blindfold a permanent narrative cost.
Blackwood's presences remain almost entirely unglimpsed, and the narrator's growing conviction that attention itself attracts them is the story's engine.
A perception rule announced rather than demonstrated: the prohibition has no observable mechanism, so the audience has nothing to reason with.

entries.name: The Invitation
entries.description: The threshold that must be crossed voluntarily, by the victim.

examples.text: Lindqvist makes the invitation rule physically consequential rather than symbolic, and the scene demonstrating what happens without one converts folklore into biology.
Stoker establishes that the threat requires permission and then makes the granting of it a matter of ordinary hospitality, which is what puts the whole household at risk.
Invitation is invoked as a term of art in the exposition and then never constrains anything the entity does.

entries.name: The Survivable Clause
entries.description: One narrow escape written into the curse, and the cost of using it.

examples.text: James builds the entire story on returning a slip of paper, so the escape is a physical object that must be passed to someone who will then die.
The transmission clause is stated early and turns survival into a moral problem the film refuses to resolve on the protagonist's behalf.
The clause exists to generate a sequel hook rather than to constrain anyone's choices, so it produces no dilemma.

entries.name: It Knows Your Name
entries.description: Naming as the proof that this is personal and already underway.

examples.text: James makes the apparitions' specific interest in named children the governess's evidence and the reader's grounds for doubting her, doing double work with a single device.
Rose ties summoning to speech and repetition, so the protagonist's scholarly interest in the legend is indistinguishable from participation in it.
Naming and summoning are present as ritual furniture with no rule attached; nothing follows from having spoken.

entries.name: The Threat That Mimics
entries.description: It can be anyone, so trust becomes the resource that runs out.

examples.text: Carpenter derives everything from one rule — perfect imitation at the cellular level — so that the plot is not where the creature is but who it is, and every test scene is a genuine deduction the audience can follow. The organism's assimilation logic makes paranoia structurally correct rather than a character flaw, and no film since has improved on the design.
Siegel makes the replacement undetectable except by intimacy, which relocates the horror into marriages and friendships rather than into the creature.
Iwaaki gives the mimics a biology and a learning curve, so their imperfect early imitations are both comic and genuinely unnerving.

entries.name: The Countdown
entries.description: A deadline the characters can measure and cannot extend.

examples.text: Nakata's seven-day limit converts investigation into a resource problem and makes every scene of research legibly expensive.
An application that names the hour of death supplies a number without a mechanism, so nothing the characters do can spend or save the time they have been shown.
The sequence of deaths supplies order without pressure, since knowing you are next produces no action the characters can meaningfully take.

entries.name: The Sound That Precedes It
entries.description: An audible signature that arrives before the thing does.

examples.text: Krasinski inverts the trope by making the characters' own sound the summons, so the signature belongs to the victims rather than to the threat.
Marshall's creatures announce themselves by clicking in total darkness, which gives the audience directional information the characters cannot use.
King attaches a recurring auditory motif to the entity across four decades of story time, so the sound functions as continuity rather than as a jump cue.

entries.name: The Thing in the Periphery
entries.description: Seen at the edge of the frame, gone when looked at directly.

examples.text: Aster stages figures in the deep background without musical emphasis, so the audience does the discovering and cannot be sure they did.
Anderson buries its apparitions in amateur footage at a resolution that makes verification impossible, which is the film's whole argument about grief.
The fixed camera converts the entire lower half of the frame into a region the audience polices, achieving with framing what most films attempt with score.

entries.name: It Was Always Here
entries.description: The threat predates the house, the town and the deed.

examples.text: Lovecraft's contaminant arrives and simply persists in the soil, indifferent to ownership and to the family's attempts to farm around it.

The film's claims were marketed as documented fact and have been extensively disputed since, and its use of an invented Indigenous burial site as the source of the haunting supplied the template for a device that spread across the genre and remains in use. It teaches the wrong lesson twice: that a documentary claim can be asserted rather than earned, and that another people's dead are available as set dressing.
Jones writes consequence arriving out of the past from inside the tradition it belongs to, which is precisely the transaction the burial-ground device counterfeits.

entries.name: The Protection That Fails
entries.description: The salt line, the circle, the charm — and the moment it does not hold.

examples.text: Eggers lets the family's prayer and doctrine function as their entire defensive apparatus, and the film's horror is that the theology is correct and does not protect them.
Barker gives the puzzle box a set of operating rules that work exactly as described, which is what makes the summoners' confidence fatal.
Ritual protections are deployed and breached without any established rule governing either, so the failures read as pacing rather than as events.

entries.name: The Rule Broken by Accident
entries.description: Not transgression but ignorance, which is worse for being undeserved.

examples.text: Kobayashi's Hoichi is protected by inscription and doomed by an omission nobody notices, which locates the failure in diligence rather than in sin.
Kurosawa's characters breach a boundary they had no way of knowing existed, and the film's refusal to assign fault is what makes its dread ambient.
Contact is sufficient to condemn, which is faithful to the source's logic, but the remake supplies an investigative frame that keeps implying a culpability the rules do not support.

entries.name: It Cannot Be Killed, Only Delayed
entries.description: Victory as postponement, and the sequel written into the premise.

examples.text: Carpenter ends on the absence of a body rather than on a return, which is the restrained version and the reason the ending still functions.
King's incursion is survived rather than resolved, and the novella's power comes from ending while the situation is still ongoing.

examples.work: Friday the 13th Part VIII: Jason Takes Manhattan
examples.text: Repeated resurrection without cost converts an unkillable antagonist into a scheduling convention.

entries.name: The Threat That Chooses You
entries.description: Selection without merit — the opposite of the chosen one.

examples.text: Kent makes the entity's attachment inseparable from a specific bereavement, so selection is legible without ever being deserved.
The entity's criteria are discovered through archival research and turn out to be procedural, which makes the protagonist's own choices retroactively catastrophic.
The American adaptation adds a maternal-sympathy motive to a curse whose original power was its complete indifference to who watched.

entries.name: The Slow Approach
entries.description: Something coming at a pace that cannot be outrun forever.

examples.text: Mitchell's single rule — always walking, always toward you — generates an entire film's tension without a chase, and makes rest the scarcest resource.
Romero's dead are individually trivial and collectively arithmetic, which turns the farmhouse into a countdown rather than a battle.
The pursuer's speed varies to suit each scene, which removes the audience's ability to estimate and therefore the dread.

entries.name: The Threat With a Territory
entries.description: Safe here, not safe there, and the line is not marked.

examples.text: Blackwood's island is superbly rendered but its boundaries are never established firmly enough for the reader to know when the characters have crossed back.
VanderMeer's Area X has a hard perimeter and wholly unreadable interior rules, so the border is the only thing the expedition can be certain of.
Team Silent makes the town's extent a psychological rather than geographic fact, and the fog boundary doubles as the medium's own draw distance.

entries.name: The Revenant
entries.description: The dead who return in a body, with a grievance and a route home.

examples.text: King's returned come back wrong in ways that are specific and domestic, and the novel's cruelty is that the mechanism works exactly as promised.
Kingfisher works from documented folk material rather than genre convention, so her returning dead obey rules that feel found rather than designed.
Shimizu's revenant is a property of the house rather than of the wronged woman, which detaches the grievance from any possibility of satisfaction.

entries.name: The Double
entries.description: Your own face, doing something you would not.

examples.text: Machen's transformation material is foundational, but the doubling is reported at several removes and never staged where the reader can feel it.
Peele gives the doubles an entire underground society and a grievance, converting a private uncanny device into a structural one.
Clark Ashton Smith stages the following shadow as an inexorable geometric fact, and the story's brevity is what makes it land.

entries.name: The Possessed Child
entries.description: Dependency inverted — the thing you must protect is the thing in the room.

examples.text: Friedkin exhausts every medical and psychiatric explanation on screen before conceding the supernatural, so the theology arrives as a last resort rather than as a premise, and the film's horror rests on a mother's total inability to act. The performances make the child's deterioration a matter of loss rather than of spectacle, which is why the imitators reproduce the effects and not the effect.
Donner runs the same premise as an inheritance thriller, where the horror is the parents' slow arrival at a conclusion the audience reached in the first act.
Gran relocates possession into an adult woman's first-person account and makes the reader complicit in her rationalisations.

entries.name: The Thing Wearing a Face
entries.description: Someone you love, returned, and not returned.

examples.text: Gaiman changes one feature of a mother and produces a figure that disturbs adult readers as reliably as children, which is the uncanny at its most economical.
Carpenter's imitations are perfect until they are not, and the reveal is always a failure of the copy rather than a discovery by the cast.
The substituted-child premise is set up carefully and then resolved by confirming the mother's suspicion, which spends the ambiguity that was the film's asset.

entries.name: The Swarm
entries.description: An antagonist with no individual to defeat.

examples.text: Du Maurier supplies no cause, no negotiation and no centre, so the story is pure attrition against weather that has developed intentions.
Cutter makes the swarm internal and biological, which removes even the possibility of a perimeter.
The collective is given a controlling intelligence, which converts an unbeatable distributed threat back into a single killable antagonist.

entries.name: The Thing in the Water
entries.description: A medium you cannot see into and cannot stay out of.

examples.text: Spielberg's mechanical failures forced a submerged antagonist, and the resulting discipline made the water itself the threat for two thirds of the film.
Lovecraft establishes the ocean as a lid over deep time, an association the subgenre has drawn on ever since.
Levinson's waterborne parasite is well researched, but the found-footage frame keeps cutting away from the water to explain it.

entries.name: The Vampire's Hunger
entries.description: Predation with a conversational register, and the problem of consent.

examples.text: Le Fanu establishes the predator's intimacy with her victim decades before Stoker, and the relationship's mutuality is what makes it unsettling rather than merely violent.
Lindqvist makes the vampire's logistics — the servant, the blood, the disposal — the actual subject, which strips the figure of glamour without stripping it of pathos.
King transplants the Stoker apparatus to a small American town and uses the vampire's spread as a map of the community's existing rot.

entries.name: The Wolf Inside
entries.description: Transformation on a schedule, and responsibility without agency.

examples.text: Fawcett ties lycanthropy to puberty so precisely that the metaphor carries the plot rather than decorating it, and the sisters' relationship supplies the cost.
Landis plays the transformation as sustained physical agony in full light, which permanently raised the genre's standard for what the change should cost.
Lycanthropy is treated as an upgrade with an inconvenient schedule, so nothing is at stake in either state.

entries.name: The Reanimated Corpse
entries.description: The body without the person, and what the living owe it.

examples.text: Shelley makes the creature articulate and the horror entirely moral, which is why every subsequent version that silences him weakens the argument.
Lovecraft's serial was written to a comic brief and shows it, but its industrial approach to reanimation established a durable template.
Gordon's adaptation keeps the medical procedure central, so the body horror follows from a stated method rather than from spectacle.

entries.name: The Doll That Moves
entries.description: An object built to resemble a person, doing what it was not built to do.

examples.text: Holland withholds confirmation for a full act so the film is genuinely about whether a child is believed, and the doll's stillness does the work before it moves.

The doll never moves on screen in any consequential way; menace is supplied entirely by score and framing around an object that does nothing. It teaches that the uncanny can be asserted through presentation alone, when the effect actually requires a violated template — the film has a prop where it needs a deviation.
Black keeps the doll's agency ambiguous throughout and lets the children's own conviction carry the dread, which is the middle-grade form doing something the adult version rarely risks.

entries.name: The Faceless Figure
entries.description: Featurelessness as the point — nothing to read, nothing to appeal to.

examples.text: The series established the modern faceless figure and its distribution model, but the entity's rules shift across entries in ways that dissipate the early episodes' precision.
Del Toro's Pale Man is a single sustained scene built on a stated prohibition, and the creature's design puts perception in the wrong place entirely.
Faber's predator is described with clinical exactness and remains unreadable, which makes the reader's inability to find a face in it structural.

entries.name: The Monster That Was a Person
entries.description: Sympathy and threat held in the same figure, without cancelling.

examples.text: Cronenberg tracks the transformation as accumulating loss of function and keeps Brundle articulate long enough for the audience to grieve someone still on screen.
Siodmak's screenplay invented most of the folklore audiences assume is traditional, and its central figure is defined by dread of what he will do rather than by what he does.
Whale gives the creature articulacy and a want, which converts Shelley's moral argument into something a film audience can watch happen.

entries.name: The Old God
entries.description: Something worshipped rather than fought, and indifferent to both.

examples.text: Lovecraft's entity is dangerous chiefly as a fact about the universe rather than as an actor, and the story's structure — fragments assembled by an executor — exists to keep it offstage.
FromSoftware makes cosmic scale playable by tying comprehension to a stat, so the player's growing insight literally reveals more of the world and makes it worse.
Carpenter's old god is genuinely unknowable but arrives with an explanatory apparatus that keeps translating it into plot mechanics.

entries.name: The Predator That Hunts by Sound
entries.description: A sensory rule that rewrites every ordinary action.

examples.text: Krasinski converts the entire domestic surface of the film into a procedure, so nails, sand paths and board games all become plot.
Creative Assembly built an antagonist that learns the player's habits, which makes the sound rule adaptive rather than exploitable and is the medium's strongest use of the trope.
The reversal of putting the blind man in the predator's role is genuinely clever, but the film's sound rules bend whenever a scene needs a character to be heard or not heard.

entries.name: The Creature Beneath
entries.description: Something older under the floor, the town, or the ice.

examples.text: Marshall's crawlers are the least of the film's horrors until they are the only one, and the cave's geology does more work than the creature design.
The series keeps its creature almost entirely subordinate to scurvy, lead and command failure, which is what makes its appearances register.
Underwood makes the subterranean threat's rules fully legible and the film becomes a puzzle the characters solve competently, which is a rarer pleasure than it sounds.

entries.name: The Thing That Should Be Extinct
entries.description: Deep time as the threat's alibi — it was here first.

examples.text: Lovecraft's survival is hereditary rather than zoological, which is where the story's racial anxieties become inseparable from its mechanism and must be read rather than inherited.
Ito's revived sea life arrives on mechanical legs and the absurdity is precisely what makes the escalation unbearable.
Extinction is used as a size justification and nothing follows from the creature's antiquity; it is a large animal with a date attached.

entries.name: The Bad House
entries.description: A building that has already decided what happens inside it.

examples.text: Jackson refuses to separate the house's malice from Eleanor's need, so every apparent haunting is simultaneously an accurate reading of a lonely woman's psychology and neither reading can be discarded. The opening and closing paragraphs make the house a subject with its own sentence, and seventy years of the subgenre have been arguing with it rather than improving on it.
Matheson answers Jackson with physics, apparatus and a stated mechanism, which is the useful counter-position even where it is the lesser book.
McDowell puts his third house half-buried in sand and lets the family's ordinary Southern manners continue around it, which makes the encroachment domestic rather than gothic.

entries.name: The Room That Should Not Exist
entries.description: A door in a wall the occupants know the far side of.

examples.text: Danielewski makes the extra space a measurable fact, so the horror is arithmetic before it is anything else and the reader checks the numbers.
The single hotel room is established as ordinary in exhausting bureaucratic detail before anything happens, which is why the turn works.
The discovery of the impossible lower floor is superbly staged, but the film keeps extending the space until it stops being an anomaly and becomes a level.

entries.name: Impossible Geometry
entries.description: Space that violates the model the reader has been made to build.

examples.text: Ito takes a single shape and treats it as contagious, so the spiral propagates through hair, pottery, bodies and finally the town's architecture with the remorselessness of a proof. The manga page's fixed panel grid makes the deformation measurable in a way no other medium achieves, and the final chapters resolve into a structure the reader has been assembling unknowingly since page one.
Kojima Productions built an entire form out of one corridor that loops with alterations, which made repetition itself the mechanism.
Clarke's endless halls are rendered with such affection that the dread comes entirely from the reader's comprehension outpacing the narrator's.

entries.name: The Town That Watches
entries.description: A whole population in on it, behaving normally.

examples.text: Aster stages the community's observation in daylight and open air, which removes the concealment the trope usually depends on and replaces it with hospitality.
King maps the infection onto the town's existing gossip networks, so the spread follows social lines that were already there.
Peele makes the observers uniformly polite and complimentary, and the accumulating wrongness is carried almost entirely by tone.

entries.name: The Road at Night
entries.description: Transit as the least defensible position.

examples.text: Spielberg gives the pursuer no face and no motive, so the road becomes a corridor with one exit and the film never needs anything else.
McDonald confines the whole outbreak to what can be heard down a phone line from a church basement, which makes the world beyond the road purely inferential.
A stalled bus is a sound premise, but the antagonist's ability to be anywhere collapses the geography the trope depends on.

entries.name: The Threshold Crossed Unknowingly
entries.description: You are already inside, and there was no sign.

examples.text: VanderMeer withholds the moment of entry from the expedition's own record, so the crossing has to be reconstructed rather than experienced.
Hurley's field is entered by ordinary agricultural work, and the novel's dread accumulates through soil samples and small domestic failures.
The crossing is signposted with an explicit ritual, which removes exactly the unknowingness the trope names.

entries.name: The Basement
entries.description: Downward as a one-way commitment.

examples.text: Romero makes the cellar argument the film's real conflict, and the ending confirms that both positions were wrong for different reasons.
Frictional removed the player's ability to fight and made descent the only progress mechanic, so every stairway is a decision.
An impossible staircase with a mathematical rule is a strong premise the film explains fully by its midpoint, after which the descent is procedure.

entries.name: The Institution
entries.description: Asylums, hospitals and homes — architecture built to contain people.

examples.text: Anderson shot in a genuinely decommissioned hospital and lets its documented history and asbestos remediation supply the dread, so the building's real institutional violence is the subject.

The psychiatric hospital functions purely as gothic set dressing and its patients as ambient menace, with the institution's actual history of confinement and abuse reduced to texture. It teaches a convention the field had already inherited and has kept using: that mental illness is a haunted-house surface rather than a thing that happens to people, which is both an ethical failure and, in craft terms, a waste of the most frightening real material available.
Flanagan's expansion works because it treats the family's psychiatric and addiction histories as load-bearing rather than as atmosphere.

entries.name: The Hotel
entries.description: Transience as vulnerability — nobody here belongs here.

examples.text: King makes the Overlook's guest register its haunting, so the hotel's power is the accumulated residue of people who passed through and were not changed by it.
Lynch and Frost use the Great Northern's ordinary hospitality rhythms as the surface that the series' dread deforms.
The motel's found tapes are a strong opening device that the film abandons for a chase once the premise is established.

entries.name: The Woods That Keep You
entries.description: Terrain that returns you to where you started.

examples.text: Myrick and Sánchez make the map itself the horror, and the argument over the discarded map is the film's central scene.
Nevill's forest is navigable in principle and unnavigable in practice, and the group's deteriorating competence tracks their deteriorating relationships.
Acid Wizard makes the forest reshuffle nightly, so the player's accumulated map knowledge is a resource that decays.

entries.name: The Empty Place
entries.description: A space designed for people, with none in it.

examples.text: The film commits fully to a house rendered as unattended corners and ceilings, which is the purest realisation of the trope and also demonstrates how little narrative the effect can carry.
Team Silent turned a hardware draw-distance limit into fog, and the resulting emptiness became the series' defining texture rather than its compromise.
Hendrix stages his haunting in a flat-pack showroom after closing, where the emptiness is a designed retail condition before it is a supernatural one.

entries.name: The Place That Repeats
entries.description: The same room again, altered, and no exit from the loop.

examples.text: Smith builds a closed causal loop the audience can chart, so the horror is the protagonist's growing understanding of her own position in it.
Bloober's rooms reconfigure constantly and impressively, but with nothing to deduce the reconfiguration becomes a corridor with better scenery.
The series repeats returns across an entire town without ever explaining the mechanism, which keeps the loop a condition rather than a puzzle.

entries.name: The House That Wants You
entries.description: Not hostile but acquisitive — it is recruiting.

examples.text: Marasco makes the house's restoration and the family's deterioration the same process, tracked in fresh paint and new wallpaper.
Mitchell runs the same predation on a schedule across decades, so the reader learns the pattern and watches each new visitor fail to.
Del Toro's house is magnificently realised and its appetite is stated, but the ghosts spend the film warning rather than acquiring.

entries.name: The Sealed Room
entries.description: Something closed off, and the decision to open it.

examples.text: Waters keeps the nursery's history and the family's class decline inseparable, so opening the house at all is the fatal act.
Hill and Rodríguez make each locked door a specific and rule-bound capability, which turns the trope into a system without defusing it.
Flanagan seals the room with equipment and documentation, and the mirror defeats the apparatus rather than the people.

entries.name: The Infection
entries.description: A rule of transmission, and a clock that starts at contact.

examples.text: Matheson gives his plague a bacteriology and lets the protagonist do the research, which makes the last man a scientist rather than a survivor.

examples.work: The Girl With All the Gifts
examples.text: Carey builds his contagion from a real parasitic fungus and follows the biology to a conclusion that refuses restoration.
The asymptomatic carrier is a strong idea introduced to justify a reinfection the plot has already decided on.

entries.name: The Parasite
entries.description: Something living in you, with its own interests.

examples.text: Scott gives the organism a full life cycle so each act faces a different animal, and the host's body is a stage in it rather than a victim of it.
Cutter's worm is described with clinical patience and the novel's structure — interleaved inquest documents — makes the outcome known and the reading unbearable anyway.
Cronenberg's parasite spreads through a single apartment block and rewrites its residents' desires, establishing his career's central preoccupation in one building.

entries.name: The Body Changing Without Consent
entries.description: Transformation tracked as accumulating loss of function.

examples.text: Cronenberg charts the change through capability and habit rather than appearance, and keeps Brundle articulate long enough for the audience to grieve someone still on screen.
Power distributes the transformation across a whole school so that adaptation becomes social, and the girls' accommodations are more disturbing than the mutations.
Ducournau ties the change to an initiation and a family history, so the body's new appetite arrives as inheritance rather than as accident.

entries.name: The Monstrous Pregnancy
entries.description: Gestation as occupation, and the loss of standing to object.

examples.text: Levin's horror is procedural and social — the obstetrician, the neighbours, the husband — and the supernatural conspiracy is indistinguishable from ordinary medical dismissal.
Cronenberg's externalised gestation is a striking image attached to an argument about a specific divorce, and the film never resolves whether it is diagnosing anything beyond that.
Ducournau pushes the premise past metaphor into a sustained physical fact the film simply refuses to explain.

entries.name: The Surgeon and the Clinic
entries.description: Medical authority as the thing you cannot refuse.

examples.text: Cronenberg locates the horror in instruments, credentials and access rather than in violence, and the profession's ordinary authority does all the work.
Brandon Cronenberg builds a clinic whose product is infection itself, which makes consent the film's actual subject.
The premise is a single surgical conceit with no second act; the film's notoriety exceeds anything it does with the idea.

entries.name: The Appetite That Grows
entries.description: Hunger as a progressive condition rather than a state.

examples.text: Bazterrica's society has industrialised the appetite and the novel's flatness of register is what makes the processing scenes land.
Katsu attaches the appetite to a documented historical crossing, so starvation and the supernatural cannot be separated.
The escalating appetite is handled as farce with real consequences deferred, which is a legitimate comic choice and removes the trope's pressure entirely.

entries.name: The Skin Taken
entries.description: The surface removed, worn, or exchanged.

examples.text: Harris keeps the skinning offstage and makes the investigative reconstruction the horror, which is why the novel is more restrained than its reputation.
Faber's exchange is industrial and unglamorous, and the protagonist's discomfort in her own altered body is the book's centre.
The bandaged face is a superb sustained image, and the film's late reveal converts it retroactively into a device.

entries.name: The Wound That Will Not Heal
entries.description: Damage that persists past the scene, and past the plot's convenience.

examples.text: Barker makes flayed incompleteness a permanent condition requiring maintenance, which is what gives Frank's storyline its logic.
Injury is thematically central and mechanically reversible, and the tension between the two is never quite resolved.
Carroll's wounds stay open across her stories and the artwork's colour choices make them structural rather than incidental.

entries.name: The Body Under Another's Control
entries.description: Awake, present, and not driving.

examples.text: Peele's Sunken Place makes retained consciousness the point of the procedure rather than a side effect, which is what converts the premise into an argument.
Tremblay keeps possession and adolescent psychiatric crisis in permanent superposition, mediated through a reality television production.
Heinlein's controllers are a strong central image serving a Cold War allegory that keeps overriding the bodily horror.

entries.name: The Bodies Merged
entries.description: Two or more, joined, and the question of who is left.

examples.text: Yuzna withholds the merge until a single final sequence and lets an hour of class satire earn it.
Tsukamoto fuses flesh with industrial material at a pace that makes the process illegible, which is the film's argument about the city.
Otomo's late-volume expansion of a single body into architecture is the trope's most extended statement in any medium.

entries.name: Accelerated Decay
entries.description: Time applied to a body at the wrong rate.

examples.text: Wilde externalises the decay onto an object and makes the deferral itself the corruption, which is why the final reversal needs no explanation.
Tecmo ties the player's only weapon to photographing the dead, so capturing decay is the mechanic rather than the imagery.
The creature's periodic renewal is a rule stated in dialogue and never made physically consequential on screen.

entries.name: The Missing Sense
entries.description: A channel removed, and the compensations that arrive with it.

examples.text: Malerman makes voluntary blindness a discipline with a failure rate, so every journey is a procedure the reader can audit.
Flanagan builds a home invasion around a deaf protagonist without ever treating the deafness as a deficiency the plot corrects.
The staged loss of each sense is a strong structural idea used almost entirely for romance rather than for dread.

entries.name: The Body as Meat
entries.description: The person reduced to material, and the industry that does it.

examples.text: Bazterrica's processing plant is written in the register of a compliance manual, which is what makes the reduction total.
Hooper frames his family as workers with a trade, and the abattoir logic makes the violence procedural rather than passionate.
The reveal is the entire film and the industrial process it names is never shown operating on anyone the audience knows.

entries.name: The Transformation Welcomed
entries.description: The subject consents, which removes the audience's last refuge.

examples.text: Cronenberg's protagonist adopts his own transformation as a programme rather than suffering it, and the film gives him the vocabulary to advocate for it.
Ito's townspeople increasingly pursue the spiral rather than flee it, and the collectors and the obsessed are more disturbing than the victims.
Consent to bodily transformation is the film's explicit subject and is discussed more than it is dramatised.

entries.name: The Party Picked Off
entries.description: Reduction as structure, and each loss narrowing the options.

examples.text: Natali lets the structure itself do the removing, so each loss subtracts a specific skill the group needed to solve the next room.
Supermassive makes the attrition order a consequence of player choices, so the group's composition at the end is an argument about the player's decisions.
Cunningham orders his deaths by screen prominence rather than by capability, which is why the middle stretch has no accumulating pressure.

entries.name: The Sceptic
entries.description: The one who is wrong, and whose wrongness has to be earned.

examples.text: Friedkin makes the sceptical position the medically responsible one and keeps it credible for half the film, so its defeat costs something.
Carter institutionalised the sceptic as a permanent structural counterweight rather than a first-act obstacle, which is why the dynamic sustained nine seasons.
The sceptic exists to be corrected on schedule and holds no position the film takes seriously enough to argue with.

entries.name: The One Who Knows
entries.description: Local knowledge, delivered early, disregarded.

examples.text: Spielberg splits the knowledge across three men who each know something incompatible, which turns exposition into a working conflict.
Carpenter gives the knowledge to a priest who is also the inheritor of the guilt, so disclosure and confession are the same act and both come late.
Whedon and Goddard make the knowing party an entire off-site department, which converts the trope into the film's premise.

entries.name: The Sacrifice Vote
entries.description: The group deciding, out loud, who is spent.

examples.text: King lets the decision be made by a congregation rather than by individuals, so the horror is deliberative and procedurally correct.

examples.work: The Cabin at the End of the World
examples.text: Tremblay builds the entire book on a demand for a chosen sacrifice and refuses to confirm whether the demand was real.
The family's collective decision is played for satire, which is effective and removes the deliberation's weight.

entries.name: The Final Girl
entries.description: The survivor the form has trained the audience to identify in advance.

examples.text: Carpenter codified the figure so precisely that Laurie Strode's competence, watchfulness and social separation became the template every subsequent slasher either follows or argues with. The film gives her the discovery of the bodies, the improvised weapons and the ending's ambiguity, and the fact that Carol Clover's later analysis of viewer identification could be built almost entirely from this one performance is the measure of it.
Ripley arrives at the same position from a professional rather than a moral route, which is the more durable version and the one science-fiction horror has kept.
Craven's survivor knows the convention she is inside, and the film's tension comes from whether the rules she has learned from films actually hold.

entries.name: The Survivor Who Is Not Believed
entries.description: The aftermath in which testimony is the second ordeal.

examples.text: Tremblay's survivor gives her account through a blogger and a television edit, so the reader receives it already contested.
Anderson's family are believed and still cannot make their experience mean anything, which is the harder version of the trope.
Aster puts the disbelief inside the family, where it is indistinguishable from ordinary grief and ordinary blame.

entries.name: The Group Splits Up
entries.description: The decision the audience has been trained to shout at.

examples.text: Separation happens through exhaustion, argument and lost equipment rather than by decision, which is why it does not read as contrivance.
Capcom splits the team in the opening minutes to justify a solo protagonist and a partially explored mansion, making the trope a structural necessity of the form.
The deliberate split is the series' engine and its entire comic apparatus depends on the danger being fraudulent, which is the convention's origin point for a generation of audiences.

entries.name: The Leader Who Fails
entries.description: Competence that turns out to be the wrong competence.

examples.text: The series makes command failure the actual antagonist and keeps the creature as an aggravating factor rather than a cause.
Cameron gives command to an officer whose training is real and entirely wrong for the situation, and the squad is destroyed in minutes by correct doctrine.
Smith's group has no leader at all and the novel is a study of what that absence costs, hour by hour.

entries.name: The Betrayer Inside
entries.description: Someone in the group is already working for the other side.

examples.text: Levin makes the betrayal marital and entirely explicable by ordinary careerism, which is why it does not require a supernatural motive.
Kusama keeps the hosts' complicity deniable for almost the entire running time, so the protagonist's suspicion is indistinguishable from unresolved grief.
Rodriguez signals the betrayer early through behaviour the film treats as a clue rather than as character, which converts the trope into a guessing game.

entries.name: The Child in the Group
entries.description: A member who cannot be asked to carry their share.

examples.text: Cameron makes Newt a survivor with genuine tactical knowledge, so protection and dependence run in both directions.

examples.work: The Girl With All the Gifts
examples.text: Carey makes the child the group's greatest asset and its greatest hazard simultaneously, and never resolves the tension in the adults' favour.
Naughty Dog builds an escort structure and then progressively transfers agency, so the protection premise is dismantled by the mechanics.

entries.name: The Expert Who Arrives Too Late
entries.description: Authority summoned, and outmatched on arrival.

examples.text: Blatty's specialist arrives with the correct diagnosis and the correct procedure, and the procedure kills him.
Delano and successors made the arriving expert habitually complicit in the disaster he is called to fix, which is the character's defining structure.
The expert is reconceived as an action protagonist, which removes the trope's central irony that expertise is insufficient.

entries.name: The One Who Is Already Gone
entries.description: A member the reader realises has been absent, or dead, for some time.

examples.text: Shyamalan's reveal is fair on rewatch because the rules are stated early and the staging never cheats, which is what separates it from its imitators.
The series inverts the trope by making the returned know they are returned and the living slow to accept it.
Amenábar builds his household's rules — the light, the doors, the keys — so that the reversal reinterprets a system rather than a fact.

entries.name: The Pact
entries.description: Terms agreed, and enforced to the letter.

examples.text: Benét makes the contract genuinely litigable and the escape a matter of jurisdiction, which is the American folk version of the form.
King distributes small individual bargains across a whole town so the settlement is collective rather than personal.
The bargain is stated in a lengthy closing monologue rather than enforced across the film, so the terms never bind anything.

entries.name: The Wish Granted Exactly
entries.description: Getting what you asked for, in the words you used.

examples.text: Jacobs establishes the mechanism, the price and the horror in a few thousand words, and the story's final act consists entirely of a sound at a door and a decision not to open it. The wish is granted exactly and the granting is never shown, which is the definitive demonstration that the trope's power lies in what the reader is left to supply.
King runs the same logic at novel length and adds the crucial refinement that the bargainer knows the outcome and proceeds anyway.
The wishes are granted with an accounting the film explains immediately, so the mechanism becomes arithmetic rather than dread.

entries.name: The Rite Performed Correctly
entries.description: Everything done properly, and the result is what was promised.

examples.text: Eggers derives his rite from period court testimony, so the ceremony's efficacy and the family's theology are the same theology.

Adapted from an ethnobotanist's account of Haitian pharmacology, the film converts a living religion with millions of adherents into a horror apparatus of zombification and torture, with its priests as antagonists. It is the clearest single instance of the genre's oldest structural failure — the same appropriation that produced the screen zombie in the first place — and its commercial success helped keep the device in circulation for another generation.
Flanagan stages Catholic liturgy accurately and lets the horror emerge from the congregation's sincerity rather than from any distortion of the rite.

entries.name: The Rite Performed Wrongly
entries.description: A small procedural error with disproportionate consequences.

examples.text: Kobayashi's protective inscription is complete except for the ears, and the omission is administrative rather than moral.
Raimi's incantation is played from a recording by people who do not understand it, which makes the summoning careless rather than ambitious.
Philippou and Philippou build a rule set with a stated time limit and let the breach be social pressure rather than curiosity.

entries.name: The Cult
entries.description: A community whose beliefs are functional, and which has a role reserved for you.

examples.text: Hardy's islanders have an economy, a calendar and a theology that all cohere, which is why nothing they do reads as arbitrary.
Wheatley withholds the cult almost entirely until the final act, so the film's earlier procedural violence is retroactively reframed.
West's fictionalised mass-suicide compound follows a documented historical case closely enough that the invention adds little and the framing device adds less.

entries.name: The Offering
entries.description: Something given, and the community's agreement about who supplies it.

examples.text: Jackson makes the ritual's purpose entirely unstated and its administration entirely bureaucratic, so the horror is the paperwork.
The offering's terms are announced rather than practised, and the film's community has no visible economy the sacrifice could serve.
Clark makes the offering explicitly political and historical, with the Klan's own rituals functioning as the summoning apparatus.

entries.name: The Curse's Terms
entries.description: A contract nobody signed, with clauses discoverable by experiment.

examples.text: Shimizu's curse attaches to a location and propagates by presence, so the terms are geographic and cannot be negotiated.
Raimi gives the curse a deadline, a transfer clause and a documented procedure, all of which the protagonist tests in order.
The mirror's terms are established through an elaborate experimental protocol that the film then allows it to violate at will.

entries.name: Forbidden Knowledge
entries.description: Information that damages the person who acquires it.

examples.text: Chambers never reproduces the play and lets its effects be reported by people already damaged, which is why the device still works.
Moore and Burrows build a research narrative where the protagonist's diligence is precisely what completes the catastrophe.
The recovered recording is a strong single scene attached to a ship whose supernatural physics are otherwise unexplained.

entries.name: The Summoning
entries.description: Deliberately calling the thing, and the moment before it answers.

examples.text: Rose makes summoning a matter of speech and repetition, so scholarly interest in the legend is indistinguishable from participation in it.
The board is operated repeatedly with no rule governing what answers, so summoning becomes an activity rather than a transaction.
Petersen's sanity mechanic made the cost of successful summoning a tracked statistic, which fed back into forty years of prose.

entries.name: The Convert
entries.description: Someone who came to argue and stayed.

examples.text: Aster's protagonist is recruited through grief and hospitality rather than coercion, and the final image treats the conversion as relief.
Ruff's characters engage with the lodge's cosmology instrumentally, which makes conversion a tactical rather than spiritual question.
The conversion arc is driven by a rendering of Afro-Caribbean practice that the film treats as inherently sinister rather than as belief.

entries.name: The Prophecy Fulfilled
entries.description: Foreknowledge that turns out to have been the mechanism.

examples.text: Donner stages the prophecy as documentary evidence assembled by a journalist, which converts foreknowledge into investigation.
King makes the foreseen outcome contingent on the protagonist's own decision, so the prophecy is a moral problem rather than a schedule.
The premonition supplies an ordering device without giving the characters any action that could alter it.

entries.name: The Faith Tested
entries.description: Belief as an instrument that may or may not still function.

examples.text: Flanagan gives his priest a sincere and articulate theology and lets the horror follow from taking it seriously rather than from corrupting it.
Glass keeps devotion and pathology in permanent superposition, so the film cannot be resolved into either a religious or a clinical reading.
Blatty's own sequel argues its theology at length in dialogue rather than staging it, which makes the test rhetorical.

entries.name: The Found Tape
entries.description: Recovered footage whose existence implies what happened to the operator.

examples.text: Balagueró and Plaza justify the camera through a working news crew, so the recording continues for reasons the audience never has to grant.
Derrickson makes the tapes an archive with a pattern, which converts viewing from an event into research.
The recovered material stops mid-incident and directs the audience to a website, which abandons the frame's central promise that someone assembled this.

entries.name: The Archive
entries.description: An institution that catalogues what should not be catalogued.

examples.text: Sims builds an entire cosmology out of filed witness statements, and the archivist's growing implication in what he reads is the series' actual plot.
A clinical containment register written by thousands of anonymous contributors, whose deadpan format holds because deviation from it is the only available effect.
The catalogue of dangerous objects is played as adventure, which demonstrates how much of the archive's dread lives in the register rather than in the premise.

entries.name: The Researcher
entries.description: Diligence as the mechanism of the catastrophe.

examples.text: Moore and Burrows make the protagonist's methodical enquiry the thing that completes the event he is investigating.
Files ties film-historical research to a mother's exhaustion and a child's needs, so scholarship competes with ordinary life for the protagonist's attention.
Kostova's archival apparatus is meticulous and the research consistently arrives at conclusions the reader reached several hundred pages earlier.

entries.name: The Epistolary Chain
entries.description: A story assembled from documents by someone with a reason to assemble it.

examples.text: Stoker's cast are compulsive recorders — journals, phonograph cylinders, shorthand, telegrams, newspaper cuttings — and the novel's plot is literally the collation of those records into a usable weapon. The gaps between documents do the work no narrator could, the technology is contemporary and specific rather than decorative, and every found-footage film since has been rebuilding this structure with a camera.
King interleaves commission testimony and published extracts so the outcome is known from the first pages and the reading becomes a matter of watching it arrive.
Brooks's oral-history structure lets him cover a global event at human scale, and the interviewer's near-silence is what keeps it from becoming a chronicle.

entries.name: The Recording That Keeps Playing
entries.description: A signal that continues past the point where anyone should be sending it.

examples.text: Kane builds dread almost entirely from the conventions of broadcast interruption, so the horror arrives inside a format the audience already trusts.
Visceral scatters the crew's audio logs through the ship so the dead keep explaining, in order, exactly how the player's current situation was arrived at.
McDonald confines an entire outbreak to what can be heard down a phone line, so broadcasting becomes both the transmission vector and the only evidence.

entries.name: The Diagnosis
entries.description: Medical language applied to something it cannot hold.

examples.text: Blatty spends half the book on neurology and psychiatry, so the supernatural arrives only after the medical apparatus is genuinely exhausted.
Gilman's narrator is under an actual prescribed treatment, so the diagnosis is the confinement and the deterioration is iatrogenic.
The courtroom frame stages the medical and religious readings as competing testimony and then resolves in favour of one, which spends the ambiguity it built.

entries.name: The Photograph
entries.description: An image containing something nobody saw at the time.

examples.text: Amenábar makes a book of post-mortem portraits the film's evidentiary turn, and the Victorian practice does the explaining without a word of exposition.
Tecmo makes photographing the dead the only weapon, so the player must frame and hold what they would otherwise avoid looking at.
Spirit photography is established as a rule and then used chiefly to deliver reveals on schedule.

entries.name: The Translated Text
entries.description: Meaning arriving through a chain nobody can audit.

examples.text: Chambers keeps the play untranslated and unquoted, so its effects are reported only by people already damaged by reading it.
Carpenter makes a popular novelist's prose the vector and the reader's comprehension the infection route.
Polanski's textual detective work is meticulous and its supernatural payoff arrives untethered from the bibliography that preceded it.

entries.name: The Interview
entries.description: Testimony given to someone whose purpose is unclear.

examples.text: The statement format is the series' engine and also its constraint, since a hundred episodes of first-person testimony flattens the individual voices.
Fuller makes the therapeutic interview a predation in both directions, so every session advances an investigation and a grooming simultaneously.
Rice frames the entire confession as a transaction with a journalist who wants something, which makes the narrator's self-presentation the actual subject.

entries.name: The Map
entries.description: A representation the territory declines to honour.

examples.text: Team Silent lets the protagonist annotate his own map as he goes, so the record of blocked doors becomes the player's only reliable memory.
Clarke's narrator indexes his halls with scholarly care, and the catalogue's completeness is precisely what conceals the thing it cannot represent.
Acid Wizard reshuffles the forest nightly so accumulated map knowledge decays, which makes cartography a depreciating asset.

entries.name: The Missing Person
entries.description: An absence that gives the protagonist a reason to walk toward it.

examples.text: Sluizer gives the audience the answer early and makes the film about the obsession, so the search is pathology rather than suspense.
Lemire and Sorrentino split the search across two protagonists whose panels are formally incompatible until they are not.
The disappearance is meticulously procedural and the film's supernatural register never quite arrives, which leaves the dread unattached.

entries.name: The Redacted Document
entries.description: Removal as evidence — the shape of what was taken out.

examples.text: Redaction is the site's most reliable single device, because a blacked-out clause implies an authority, a policy and a reason all at once.
Moore's appendices document exactly which claims are invented, and the transparency makes the speculative sections more disturbing rather than less.
Sollazzo and Bodner build their found-tape restoration around what the restorer chooses not to include, which makes the archivist a suspect.

entries.name: The Witness Who Recants
entries.description: Testimony withdrawn, and the reader left holding both versions.

examples.text: James's framing device puts the governess's account at two removes and lets her own qualifications do the undermining.
The series stages evidentiary collapse procedurally, so a confession and an alibi can both be documented and both be true.
Perkins withholds the chronology rather than the testimony, which produces confusion in place of doubt.

entries.name: The Thing Discovered in the Data
entries.description: A pattern nobody was looking for, in a dataset nobody suspected.

examples.text: Frictional makes the scanned mind a data object with copies, and the horror is entirely a consequence of what the file format implies.
Kurosawa's network traffic is the first evidence and remains the most frightening, because the images arrive without an interpretive frame.
The desktop conceit is executed with real discipline and the entity behind the data behaves like a conventional slasher.

entries.name: The Frame Story
entries.description: Someone is telling you this, and their reason matters.

examples.text: Shelley nests the creature's account inside Victor's inside a sea captain's letters, so the most morally serious voice is the one furthest from the reader.
Straub's frame is a message-board thread, and the format supplies the corroboration, the drift and the final post without a narrator.
Dougherty interlocks his segments so the frame is chronological rather than narrational, which is the harder version and pays off on rewatch.

entries.name: The Cold Open
entries.description: A death before the title, establishing the rules and the stakes.

examples.text: Argento opens on a murder staged as choreography and colour, which sets a contract about style over causality that the film then honours.
Craven spends a recognisable star in the first sequence, which tells the audience the ordinary protections do not apply here.
The opening pair establish the curse efficiently and also front-load the film's best scare, leaving the second act to explain rather than escalate.

entries.name: The False Ending
entries.description: Resolution offered, accepted, and withdrawn.

examples.text: De Palma's grave sequence made the device a permanent genre convention, and it works because the preceding scene is a sincere attempt at closure.
Laugier ends his first film entirely at the midpoint and begins a second one, which is the most extreme legitimate use of the structure.
The lake sequence is effective and unearned, since nothing in the film has established that the drowned boy is anything other than backstory.

entries.name: The Stinger
entries.description: A final beat that either rewrites the film or advertises the next one.

examples.text: The theatrical ending's final movement toward the camera works because ninety minutes have trained the audience to police exactly that part of the frame.
Craven's closing reversal was a studio requirement he disliked, and it contradicts the resolution the film had just earned.
Snyder and Jock close on an image that reframes the family's bargain rather than promising a continuation.

entries.name: The Return Home Changed
entries.description: Survival, and the discovery that the ordinary world has no slot for you.

examples.text: Weekes makes the haunting inseparable from asylum housing policy, so the return is to a place actively refusing to accommodate them.
Lyne's veteran returns to a city that keeps failing to stay solid, and the film treats the impossibility of coming home as a medical fact.
King's continuation gives the survivor a functioning adult life and a support structure, which is humane and dissolves the trope it inherits.

entries.name: The Cycle Restarting
entries.description: The mechanism was never interrupted, only delayed.

examples.text: Suzuki's transmission clause means the protagonist's survival is arithmetically identical to propagating the curse.
Ito builds every story on the same regeneration, so the collection's structure is the cycle rather than a depiction of one.
Lynch and Frost close their second season by transferring the entity to the investigator, so the cycle resumes with the audience's own point of identification.

entries.name: The Twist of Identity
entries.description: The person you have been watching is not who you were told.

examples.text: Hitchcock spends his star at the midpoint and then reassigns the protagonist role to her killer, and the identity reveal that follows is staged so that every earlier scene remains literally accurate. It established both the structural rug-pull and the genre's habit of building a film's marketing around withheld information, and sixty years of imitation have not produced a version that plays as fairly.
Parker plants the reveal in names, songs and dates from the first reel, so the detective's investigation is genuinely of himself.
Peele's reversal is well planted and asks the audience to reinterpret a character's entire arc in the closing seconds, which is more weight than the runtime supports.

entries.name: The Survivor's Epilogue
entries.description: The scene after, where the cost is counted rather than shown.

examples.text: Harris gives his survivor a professional future and a permanent correspondent, so the epilogue is an ongoing condition rather than a resolution.
rose-engine offers multiple closing states that differ in what the survivor is permitted to keep, which makes the epilogue the game's actual subject.
Twenty years of aftermath are summarised in dialogue and then discarded for a confrontation the film was always going to stage.

entries.name: The Cost That Persists
entries.description: Damage the plot cannot reverse and declines to reverse.

examples.text: Morrison makes the haunting's departure a beginning rather than a resolution, and the cost stays distributed across a community.
King's writer survives with permanent injuries and a permanent creditor, and the book he produced under duress is the one that works.
Armfield gives her returning partner a change that cannot be reversed or named, and the novel stays entirely inside the domestic accommodation of it.

entries.name: The Unresolved Ending
entries.description: No verdict, by design — and the difference between a decision and a shrug.

examples.text: Lindsay withholds the explanation completely and the withholding is structural, which is why the book survives being unsolvable.
Aickman withholds not merely the explanation but the incident, and the story's refusal is so complete that summarising it is nearly impossible.

The film stops mid-scene and displays a web address inviting the audience to learn how the case concluded, which converts an unresolved ending into an unfinished one and a marketing asset. It teaches that irresolution is an absence of work rather than the hardest ending to earn, and the audience response was severe enough that it stands as the genre's clearest cautionary case.

entries.name: The Last Line
entries.description: A closing sentence that reassigns the meaning of everything before it.

examples.text: Jackson closes by repeating her opening paragraph with one clause altered, which resolves the house's ownership question without stating it.

examples.work: We Have Always Lived in the Castle
examples.text: Jackson ends on contentment, and the reader's recognition of what that contentment consists of is the entire effect.
Harvey's final image supplies the explanation and simultaneously makes the preceding film unrewatchable in its original register.

entries.name: The Downer Ending
entries.description: The threat wins, and the book has been honest about that from the start.

examples.text: Darabont's altered ending is crueller than the novella's and works because the protagonist's decision is competent, reasonable and wrong.
Fincher lets the antagonist's plan complete on schedule and gives the detectives the choice of participating in it or not, which is worse than defeat.
Sluizer's ending is the logical terminus of the obsession the film has documented, delivered without music or emphasis.

entries.name: The Revenant
entries.description: The medieval European corpse that walks home, and the practical measures taken against it.

examples.text: William of Newburgh reports four revenant cases as news rather than legend, with named parishes and the remedies applied, which is the register modern folk horror keeps trying to reproduce.
Kingfisher works from documented English folk material rather than genre convention, so her returning dead obey rules that feel found rather than designed.
