Jacobs never shows what is at the door, which is the folkloric position exactly: the tradition is far more concerned with prevention than with description.

entries.name: The Draugr
entries.description: The Norse barrow-dweller: physically present, territorial, and immensely strong.

examples.text: The Glámr episode is the tradition's fullest surviving account, and its detail that the curse is delivered by the draugr's dying words rather than by its violence is the part fiction consistently drops.
The Fróðá hauntings are settled by a formal court summons issued to the dead, which is the single most usable and least used idea in the entire corpus.
Draugr are reduced to barrow-dwelling encounter fodder, retaining the location and the name while discarding the property dispute that gave the tradition its logic.

entries.name: The Jiangshi
entries.description: The Chinese hopping corpse, animated by unsettled remains and unfinished transit.

examples.text: Sammo Hung fused the tradition with martial-arts comedy and established the talisman, the breath-holding and the Taoist priest as a working rule set.
Ricky Lau codified the rules so thoroughly that most subsequent Chinese and Western treatments cite this film rather than the folk tradition, which is a useful caution about how fast a canon forms.
Juno Mak returns the figure to a public housing block and treats the 1985 conventions as a lost world, which is the rare case of a homage that adds an argument.

entries.name: The Yūrei
entries.description: The Japanese dead held in place by an unresolved obligation.

examples.text: Hearn collected rather than invented, and his versions preserve the tradition's insistence that the ghost's grievance is specific, contractual and usually satisfiable.
Mizoguchi lets the encounter proceed for a long stretch before the audience is given grounds to reclassify it, which is the tradition's own narrative shape.
Nakagawa's version of the most-adapted Japanese ghost narrative keeps the wronged wife's claim legally precise, so the haunting reads as enforcement.

entries.name: The Ghoul
entries.description: The Arabic ghūl: a desert predator on travellers, and a grave-eater by later accretion.

examples.text: The ghūl of the compiled Arabic manuscripts is a shapeshifting road hazard rather than a cemetery scavenger, a distinction almost entirely lost in transmission westward.
Vipul Amrutlal Shah's series returns the figure to a South Asian and Islamic frame and makes it an interrogator, which restores the tradition's association with deception.
Lovecraft's ghouls are a wholly new species sharing only a name, and the story's own quality has helped keep the Arabic tradition invisible in anglophone horror.

entries.name: The Woman Who Died in Childbirth
entries.description: A cross-cultural class of returning dead — churel, pontianak, la Llorona — defined by a death the community failed to prevent.

examples.text: Anvita Dutt keeps the churel's grievance rooted in the specific domestic violence that produced her, so the supernatural and the social explanation never separate.
Shuhaimi Baba treats the pontianak as a figure with a biography and a community that remembers her, rather than as a jump-scare delivery system.

A Mexican tradition with four centuries of regional variation is compressed into a franchise monster with a haunting schedule, stripped of the drowning, the river and the maternal grief that constitute the entire figure. It is the clearest recent demonstration of a living folk tradition being mined for a name and a silhouette, and its placement inside a shared-universe brand made the flattening commercially permanent.

entries.name: The Unquiet Grave
entries.description: Burial that did not take, and the customs designed to make it take.

examples.work: The English and Scottish Popular Ballads
examples.text: Child's collection preserves the ballad in which excessive mourning is itself the thing preventing the dead from resting, which inverts the modern assumption that grief is the sympathetic force.
Hurley builds his dread from English regional Catholic practice and shore ritual rather than from folk-horror cinema, and the difference is legible on every page.
The resurrection rite is given exact terms and a time limit, and the film then spends its second half on a conventional pursuit that the rules did not require.

entries.name: Corpse Roads and Wake Customs
entries.description: The procedures around a body between death and burial, and what they are protecting against.

examples.text: Westwood and Simpson map corpse ways, coffin stones and lych paths to actual places, which is exactly the local specificity that makes invented folklore convincing.
Hurley's excavations proceed through ordinary agricultural and archaeological work, so the customs are encountered as artefacts rather than explained as lore.

Frazer's comparative method has been rejected by anthropology for a century, and the volume remains the single most common source of confidently wrong folk detail in genre fiction — read it as a document of Victorian thought, not as a reference.

entries.name: The Ghost That Wants Something Specific
entries.description: The tradition's default: an apparition with a claim, not an atmosphere.

examples.work: Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad
examples.text: James attaches the haunting to a retrieved object and a summoning, so the ghost's interest is precisely bounded and its behaviour follows from it.
Hill gives her revenant a grievance, a pattern and a cost to the town, which is why the novel sustains a shape the short form usually carries.
The unfinished business is stated in the first act and resolved on schedule, which is the tradition's logic emptied of the ambiguity that made it frightening.

entries.name: The Dead Who Are Expected
entries.description: Festivals of return, where the dead arrive by invitation and on a date.

examples.text: Rulfo lets the reader discover the town's population by degrees, and the Mexican festival logic underneath it is never explained because the narrator has no reason to explain it.
Unkrich and Molina make remembrance load-bearing rather than sentimental: the dead persist exactly as long as someone alive keeps the obligation, which is the tradition's actual mechanic.
The same festival supplies a visual palette and a plot device while the reciprocal obligation between living and dead, which is the whole point of it, goes largely unused.

entries.name: The Changeling
entries.description: A child substituted, and a belief with a documented body count.

examples.work: Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry
examples.text: Yeats's collection records the tests and the remedies, and reading them alongside the 1895 killing of Bridget Cleary — burned by her husband as a changeling — is the clearest available lesson in folklore as a live social instrument.
LaValle builds the tradition into contemporary New York parenthood and makes the substitution question inseparable from postpartum illness and paternal denial.
The substitution premise is established with real patience and then resolved by confirming the mother's suspicion, which spends the deniability the tradition depends on.

entries.name: The Aswang
entries.description: The Philippine shapeshifting predator, and the manananggal that separates at the waist.

examples.text: Maximo Ramos catalogues the regional variants and their incompatibilities, which is precisely the local inconsistency that genre processing removes.
Tan and Baldisimo place the creatures inside a working Manila with jurisdictions and politics, so the folklore is civic rather than exotic.
Prime Cruz relocates the figure to a condominium and treats its bisection as a physical logistics problem, which is the tradition taken seriously.

entries.name: The Strigoi
entries.description: The Romanian returning dead, and the source Stoker actually used.

examples.text: Emily Gerard's essay is the direct documentary ancestor of the modern vampire, and reading it shows how much Stoker invented and how much he simply transcribed.
Murnau's plague-carrier is closer to the Eastern European tradition than to Stoker's aristocrat, and the association of the revenant with epidemic is the folkloric core.
Del Toro and Hogan attach the Romanian name to a parasitic biology that owes nothing to the tradition, which is the standard modern transaction: keep the word, discard the belief.

entries.name: The Nachzehrer
entries.description: The Germanic corpse that chews in the grave and draws the living after it.

examples.text: Ranft's treatise argues against the belief while documenting it in detail, and the sceptical framing preserves more usable specifics than any credulous account.
The Grimms collected the regional variants with sources attached, and the entries are far stranger and more locally bounded than the composite creature genre fiction assembled from them.
Niles and Templesmith produce an excellent siege story with a vampire that has no regional derivation at all, which is a fair choice and a good illustration of what gets lost by default.

entries.name: The Rougarou
entries.description: The Louisiana loup-garou, enforced by Lenten observance and swamp geography.

examples.text: The Louisiana Writers' Project collection records the rougarou as a behavioural sanction tied to Lent, which is a social function the creature retains nowhere in modern fiction.
Jeremy Love places folk creatures inside Jim Crow Mississippi so the supernatural and the historical violence operate on the same terms.
The name is imported into an existing supernatural hierarchy and the regional Catholic observance that defined the figure is entirely absent.

entries.name: The Kitsune
entries.description: The Japanese fox: shapeshifter, wife, trickster, and eventual local deity.

examples.text: The Heian anthology's fox tales are matter-of-fact about transformation and preoccupied with the resulting marriages and lawsuits, which is a register almost nothing in modern fiction attempts.
Yangsze Choo keeps the fox's own perspective and the human investigation in parallel, so the tradition's ambivalence about whether the fox is a threat survives intact.
The nine-tailed fox is reduced to a sealed power source, retaining the tail-count grading of the tradition and discarding the shapeshifting, the marriage and the shrine.

entries.name: The Selkie
entries.description: The seal-wife, the hidden skin, and a story that is mostly about coercion.

examples.text: David Thomson collected the tellings directly in the Hebrides and Ireland, and his versions retain the discomfort that later retellings smooth: the marriage begins with a theft.
Tomm Moore keeps the coat as a physical object with a location, so the family's grief and the folkloric mechanism are the same problem.
Jordan supplies a rational explanation that resolves the ambiguity, which is a defensible choice that leaves the tradition functioning only as misdirection.

entries.name: The Water Horse
entries.description: Kelpie and each-uisge: a beautiful animal at the water's edge, and a skin that will not release you.

examples.text: Douglas records the adhesive hide and the liver washed ashore, details grisly and specific enough that no invented creature needs to be built.
Mollie Hunter writes the creature as a Highland neighbour with terms of engagement, which is the folk position rather than the monster position.
King-Smith's domesticated water horse is a fine children's book and completes the tradition's century-long conversion from drowning hazard to pet.

entries.name: The Huli Jing
entries.description: The Chinese fox spirit: seductress, scholar's companion, and moral test.

examples.work: Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio
examples.text: Pu Songling collected and rewrote several hundred tales in which fox spirits, ghosts and demons behave with more integrity than the officials and scholars around them, and the satire is inseparable from the supernatural. It remains the single richest source of usable supernatural material in any language — specific rules, unresolved endings, and a consistent refusal to make the non-human the villain — and almost every Chinese ghost film of the last fifty years is drawing on it directly.
Ching Siu-tung adapts a Pu Songling tale while keeping its central inversion, that the human institutions are the greater danger.
Gordon Chan turns a story about a demon wearing a woman's flayed skin into a romantic triangle, and the source's central image survives as an effect rather than as an argument.

entries.name: The Wendigo
entries.description: An Algonquian concept about famine and the cannibalism taboo — and the genre's most thoroughly rewritten borrowing.

examples.text: Basil Johnston, an Ojibwe scholar writing from inside the tradition, presents the wendigo as an account of insatiable consumption and winter starvation with a moral and economic argument attached. This is the source a writer should start from, and the contrast with everything below is the card's actual lesson.

Blackwood's story is a genuine achievement of landscape dread and is also where the detachment begins: the name and the northern setting are retained while the famine ethic that gives the figure meaning is replaced with a generic wilderness summons.

The film's antlered deer-skull creature has no basis in Algonquian tradition and appears to originate in twenty-first-century screen and game design, yet it is presented as the wendigo's authentic form while the culture's name and a Native character's exposition supply the authenticity. It teaches the most damaging version of the borrowing failure — not omission but confident substitution, delivered with enough production value to become the reference image for a generation of writers.

entries.name: The Skinwalker
entries.description: Diné witchcraft belief, and the case where the first craft question is whether to write it at all.

examples.text: Stephen Graham Jones writes Blackfeet material from inside the community it belongs to, with consequence arriving out of a specific broken obligation; it is the model for what Indigenous-authored horror does that extraction cannot.

Hillerman wrote his Navajo-set novels with sustained consultation and was recognised by the Navajo Nation for it, which is the consultation standard the borrowing checklist asks for and almost nobody meets.

Kluckhohn's monograph remains the most-cited outside source and was assembled by pressing informants for material many Diné hold should not be discussed with outsiders at all; a writer who uses it should know they are working from a document its own subjects objected to, and should weigh the substantial body of Diné opinion that this subject is not available.

entries.name: Sleep Paralysis and the Old Hag
entries.description: A documented physiological event that produces the same intruder across unrelated cultures.

examples.work: The Terror That Comes in the Night
examples.text: Hufford's study established that the experience precedes and shapes the folklore rather than the reverse, which is the most useful single fact in this cluster: the tradition is a report, not an invention.
Ascher's documentary reconstructs subjects' accounts as staged scenes, and the near-identical figures arriving in unconnected testimonies do the argument's work.
The condition is used as a delivery mechanism for a conventional pursuing entity, which discards the immobility that is the experience's defining and most frightening feature.

entries.name: The Mara and the Night-Rider
entries.description: The Germanic and Norse pressing spirit that gave the nightmare its name.

examples.text: Snorri records a king killed by a mara sent by a woman he abandoned, which ties the visitation to an unpaid obligation rather than to random malice.
Christensen stages the night-rider material as historical reconstruction and connects it directly to the persecutions it was used to justify.
A sleep clinic supplies an efficient premise and the entity behaves as a standard possessing demon once the setting has been established.

entries.name: The Incubus and the Succubus
entries.description: A demonology of unwanted nocturnal visitation, and its use as an instrument of prosecution.

examples.text: The text's Lilith narrative is the earliest developed account of the figure and is preoccupied with a dispute about equality, which is a motive later demonology removed entirely.
Kusama and Cody make the predatory succubus a consequence of what was done to the girl, so the appetite has a documented origin rather than an essential nature.

Kramer's manual codified the incubus into a testable legal charge and was used to prosecute and execute women for decades; it is essential reading for the tradition and worthless as an account of belief, since much of what it describes was produced under torture.

entries.name: The Baku and the Eaten Dream
entries.description: A creature summoned to consume the nightmare rather than to cause it.

examples.text: Terajima's illustrated encyclopedia fixes the baku's composite anatomy and its function, and the tradition's key term is that it must be invited — protection here is a request, not a ward.
Shin Mashiba builds an episodic structure entirely from the transaction, so each client's dream is both the case and the payment.
Tsutsui's dream-intrusion apparatus is technological and rigorous, and the folk tradition survives only as a naming gesture.

entries.name: The Black Dog
entries.description: An omen animal on the road, the churchyard and the parish boundary.

examples.text: Fleming's pamphlet reports the Bungay church appearance as a news event with casualties and property damage, which is the register that makes the tradition frightening rather than quaint.
Doyle deploys the local legend, honours its atmosphere completely, and then rationalises it, which is the Radcliffean settlement executed at its highest level of craft.

examples.work: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban
examples.text: The Grim is used as a death omen and then resolved as a misidentification, retaining the tradition's silhouette while discarding its finality.

entries.name: The Knock
entries.description: Sound at a threshold, and the decision that follows it.

examples.text: The Grimms' knocking-spirit entries are consistently about counting: how many raps, at what hour, on which wall, and what each combination obliges the household to do.
Hooper and Spielberg keep the early manifestations auditory and domestic, so the family's incremental normalisation of the noise is the film's most disturbing stretch.
Shyamalan's arrival is superbly staged and the film then explains its cosmology at length, which converts an unanswerable knock into a negotiation.

entries.name: The Visitor at the Foot of the Bed
entries.description: Presence without approach — the figure that is simply there, watching.

examples.text: James's pursuing figure is glimpsed at distance and never closes, and the story's dread is entirely a function of that maintained interval.
The hearse-driver segment establishes the warning-visitor structure that British horror has drawn on ever since, in under four minutes.
Wan's figure behind the shoulder is one of the genre's best single images, deployed in a film that then explains its realm in detail and dissolves the effect.

entries.name: The Fetch and the Vardøger
entries.description: Your double, seen elsewhere — as an omen, or as an arrival ahead of you.

examples.work: Fairy and Folk Tales of the Irish Peasantry
examples.text: Yeats records the fetch as timing-dependent: seen in the morning it means long life, seen at night it means death, which is a precision modern doppelgänger fiction never bothers with.
Henry James makes the double the self that would have existed on a different decision, and the confrontation is entirely a matter of accounting.
Villeneuve's double is deliberately unresolvable and the film's interest is psychoanalytic throughout, which leaves the omen tradition's timing rules entirely unused.

entries.name: The Rusalka
entries.description: The Slavic water spirit: a drowned woman with a season and a jurisdiction.

examples.text: Afanasyev's collection ties the rusalka to Rusalka Week and to fields as much as to water, which is the agricultural dimension almost every retelling drops.
Dvořák and Kvapil keep the bargain's terms and its cost intact, and the heroine's muteness is a contractual penalty rather than a plot device.
Sapkowski's Slavic creatures are precise and vivid, and the monster-contract frame converts them into a bestiary with rates.

entries.name: Jenny Greenteeth and the Water That Takes Children
entries.description: A named hazard invented, or maintained, to keep children away from open water.

examples.text: Harland and Wilkinson record the figure alongside the duckweed she supposedly hides under, which shows the tradition doing its actual job: making a specific pond frightening.
Westwood and Simpson tie the regional variants to named waters, and the local specificity is what a writer should be stealing rather than the creature.

examples.work: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire
examples.text: Grindylows appear as an examination hazard in a controlled lake, which is the cautionary function of the tradition inverted into a school sport.

entries.name: The Ningyo
entries.description: The Japanese merfolk whose flesh confers a lifespan nobody wants.

examples.text: Takahashi builds an entire series on the tradition's actual proposition, that eating the flesh usually kills and occasionally curses you with centuries, and treats immortality as a chronic condition.
The encyclopedia's ningyo is an omen creature whose appearance predicts disaster, a function entirely separate from the immortality tale and rarely combined with it.
Miyazaki's transformation is joyful and the tradition's cost structure is deliberately absent, which is a legitimate choice and worth noticing as a choice.

entries.name: The Bunyip
entries.description: An Aboriginal Australian water being, and a textbook case of collection without consent.

examples.text: Ryan Griffen created the series specifically so his son would have Aboriginal heroes drawn from Dreaming traditions, developed with community involvement; it is the model this card exists to point at, and the contrast with what follows is the lesson.

K. Langloh Parker's collection preserved Yuwaalaraay narratives that might otherwise be lost and did so on settler terms, without consent frameworks and with framing that treated the material as vanishing curiosities; use it knowing what it is.
Wagner's picture book is charming and completed the figure's conversion into a harmless national mascot, which is how a water spirit with a serious warning function ends up on a lunchbox.

entries.name: The Leshy
entries.description: The Slavic forest lord who moves the path rather than attacking.

examples.text: Afanasyev's leshy misleads, swaps sizes and can be escaped by reversing your clothing, and that specific remedy is worth more to a writer than any description of the creature.
Arden works from the household and forest spirits as a functioning system of obligations, so neglect of the domestic ones has forest consequences.
CD Projekt Red's leshen keeps the territorial logic and the village's negotiated accommodation with it, which is closer to the source than most prose treatments.

entries.name: The Wild Hunt
entries.description: A procession in the sky that sweeps up whoever it passes.

examples.text: Jacob Grimm's chapter assembles the regional versions and their leaders, and the variation between them is the point: the Hunt is a shape that local tradition fills differently everywhere.
Cooper stages the Hunt as a force neither side controls, which restores the tradition's indifference to whether you deserve it.
Folk hunts and their leaders are absorbed into a monster-of-the-week hierarchy where every entity has a weakness and a kill method.

entries.name: The Forest That Keeps You
entries.description: Woodland as a jurisdiction with its own law and its own time.

examples.work: The English and Scottish Popular Ballads
examples.text: Child's Tam Lin texts make the wood a place with an owner, a toll and a rescue procedure with exact conditions, which is a complete plot machine sitting in the public domain.
Novik's Wood is a hostile polity rather than a setting, with territory, strategy and a grievance, and the villagers' defence is organised accordingly.
Perkins produces an exceptional-looking forest with no rules attached, so the wood is a design language rather than a jurisdiction.

entries.name: The Bog
entries.description: Ground that preserves rather than consumes, and gives its dead back intact.

examples.text: Glob's account of the Iron Age bodies, with their preserved faces and evidence of ritual killing, is the single most productive source in this cluster and reads like horror because it is reporting.
Heaney's bog poems connect the preserved dead to contemporary political violence, which is the model for how a folk artefact carries a present-day argument.
Doyle's Grimpen Mire is a landscape that kills by procedure and requires local knowledge to cross, which is the bog's actual folkloric function.

entries.name: The Deep
entries.description: Water as a lid over depth, and what the tradition assumes is under it.

examples.text: Lovecraft establishes the ocean floor as a place where deep time is stored and occasionally surfaces, an association the subgenre has drawn on for a century.
Armfield keeps the descent almost entirely offstage and locates the horror in what came back, which is the folk position on the sea exactly.
Eubank's trench creature is revealed at full scale in the final minutes, which converts an unbounded depth into a bounded animal.

entries.name: The Field Spirit and the Corn Mother
entries.description: Agricultural belief about what the harvest owes and who pays it.

examples.text: Tryon builds an entire New England community around a corn rite with a calendar, an economy and a role for the newcomer, and it remains the most complete American folk-horror novel.
Evans makes his island's fertility arrangement a resource extraction with a supplier who is visibly running out, which is the tradition's transactional logic taken literally.

The corn-spirit and dying-god material is Frazer's most influential and least reliable, and its comparative method — which flattened unrelated practices into one imagined universal rite — is the direct ancestor of the composite-folklore problem this collection exists to correct.

entries.name: The Crossroads Bargain
entries.description: A place of decision where something is available to meet you.

examples.text: Irving makes the bargain a mortgage negotiation conducted in a swamp, which is the American form's founding move: the devil as a counterparty with terms.

examples.work: The Land Where the Blues Began
examples.text: Lomax documents the crossroads tradition's West African and Haitian derivation, which matters because the Robert Johnson legend is largely posthumous invention layered onto a real practice by people who did not know it was one.
The Coens invoke the guitarist's bargain as a joke the film never returns to, which is a fair comic choice and leaves the tradition as a reference rather than a rule.

entries.name: The Faustian Contract
entries.description: A term of years, agreed knowingly, with the terms honoured.

examples.text: The anonymous Faustbuch is blunt about the arithmetic — twenty-four years, itemised services, no renegotiation — and its lack of literary ambition makes the mechanism unusually visible.
Benét's contribution is jurisdiction: the contract is real, enforceable and litigable, which relocates the horror into procedure.
Donen's wish comedy demonstrates the loophole structure with great precision and no stakes, which is instructive about how thin the line is.

entries.name: Djinn and Their Law
entries.description: Beings with their own legal and religious standing, not wish-dispensers.

examples.text: The djinn of the Arabic manuscripts have faiths, obligations and grievances, and the fisherman's bottled ifrit negotiates from a position of law rather than gratitude.

examples.work: The Djinn Falls in Love and Other Stories
examples.text: Murad and Shurin's anthology gathers writers from cultures where djinn belief is current, and the range of the resulting stories is itself the argument against the single Western template.
The djinn becomes a wish-granting slasher whose Islamic legal framing is replaced with a loophole-hunting kill mechanic, which is the tradition's most commercially successful misreading.

entries.name: The Imp in the Bottle
entries.description: A contained servant, a price, and a resale clause.

examples.text: Stevenson builds a perfect small machine: the bottle grants any wish, damns you if you die holding it, and can only be sold for less than you paid. The horror is entirely arithmetic and entirely legible to the reader, the currency-conversion sequence is one of the great problem-solving passages in the genre, and the story demonstrates conclusively that a supernatural threat with fully published rules can be more frightening than a mystery.
King distributes the same containment logic across a whole town, so the imp is a retail operation and the price is always paid by a neighbour.
The object's accounting is explained on screen almost immediately, which turns the resale problem into a countdown.

entries.name: The Fairy Debt
entries.description: Obligation incurred without agreement, and collected without appeal.

examples.text: Evans-Wentz's interviews record the etiquette in force: what is left out, what is not thanked for, what is never named, and the consequences of each lapse.
Clarke restores the tradition completely, with bargains honoured to the letter by a creature that is charming, entirely without malice as he understands it, and catastrophic.
Del Toro's fae have a treaty and a grievance, and the film resolves them by combat, which is the one method the tradition's own rules do not support.

entries.name: The Exact Wording
entries.description: The clause honoured precisely, against the plain intention.

examples.text: Gaiman's Other Mother proposes a game with stated terms and keeps them, and the child's counter-move is to find the ambiguity first.
Langan's bargain is transacted through a nested story whose terms the reader must reconstruct, so the wording problem operates on the reader as well as the characters.
The three-wish structure with published exclusions is the most influential softening of the djinn contract ever produced, and most modern audiences now take it for the tradition.

entries.name: The Price Named Late
entries.description: Payment specified after the service, when refusal is no longer available.

examples.text: The Grimms' Rumpelstiltskin makes the deferred price a firstborn and the escape a matter of correct naming, which is a two-clause contract with a documented loophole.
The Philippou brothers establish a time limit and a social pressure to exceed it, so the real price is only legible after the group has already incurred it.
Raimi states the terms and the deadline early with unusual clarity, which makes the film a superb chase and removes this particular mechanism from it.

entries.name: The Signature
entries.description: The physical mark that makes the pact enforceable, and locatable.

examples.text: Guazzo's manual specifies the pact's form, the renunciation, the mark on the body and the register it is entered in; as demonology it is worthless and as a source of contractual detail it is unmatched.
Parker makes the signed contract the literal object of the investigation, so the detective story and the pact story are the same story.
The arrangement is never reduced to a document, so nothing is enforceable and the film's climax is a change of mind rather than a breach.

entries.name: The Evil Eye
entries.description: Harm transmitted by attention, usually envious and often unintended.

examples.text: Dundes assembles the belief across the Mediterranean, South Asia and beyond, and its central finding is that the eye is most dangerous when the admiration is sincere, which is a far better engine than malice.
Isaac Ezban keeps the belief inside a Mexican family's ordinary intergenerational suspicion, so the curse is diagnosed the way an illness would be.
The nazar is invoked as an inherited maternal anxiety and then resolved through a reincarnation plot that the folk belief does not require.

entries.name: The Transferable Curse
entries.description: Affliction that can be passed on, which makes survival a moral act.

examples.text: James reduces the curse to a slip of paper that must be handed to someone who accepts it, with a deadline and a demonstrated fatality, and the entire second half is a logistics problem about returning it without the recipient noticing. It is the direct structural ancestor of every transmission curse since, and it remains the most efficient: the rules fit in a sentence, the horror is arithmetic, and the moral cost of surviving is unavoidable rather than debated.
Tourneur's adaptation keeps the runic transfer exact and adds a sceptic whose profession commits him to disbelief, which sharpens the deadline.
The transfer condition is stated clearly and the film spends its running time on startles rather than on the arithmetic the rule sets up.

entries.name: The Cursed Object
entries.description: A thing with terms attached, which can be given away but not destroyed.

examples.text: King's toy has no motive and no negotiation, only a correlation the protagonist establishes over decades, and disposal repeatedly fails as a strategy.
Remedy builds an entire bureaucracy around containing ordinary household objects whose properties are catalogued but not explained, which is the tradition rendered as institutional practice.
The object's terms are never stated, so it can neither be obeyed nor broken and functions purely as a locus for events happening nearby.

entries.name: The Chain Letter and the Copied Curse
entries.description: Transmission by duplication, where the medium's own logic does the spreading.

examples.text: Straub's thread propagates by corroboration, with each poster's confirmation making the false memory more real, which is the chain letter's mechanism relocated into collective recall.
The upload schedule and the response videos made the audience part of the transmission, which no prior medium had allowed the form to do.
The premise is taken literally and attached to a conventional killer, so the duplication rule never generates a decision anyone has to make.

entries.name: Contagion by Contact
entries.description: The folk intuition that touch transfers essence, prior to any germ theory.

examples.text: Cronenberg confines his parasite to one apartment block so transmission is a matter of corridors, lifts and neighbourly proximity, which is the contact principle rendered as architecture.
Power distributes the contagion across a quarantined school so proximity becomes social as well as biological, and the accommodations are more disturbing than the symptoms.
Roth's transmission is vivid and inconsistent, and characters contract or avoid it according to the scene's requirements rather than a rule.

entries.name: Contagion by Resemblance
entries.description: Like affects like — the poppet, the photograph, the effigy.

examples.text: Zora Neale Hurston's fieldwork records the practice from inside the communities that held it, with the practitioners named and their reasoning intact, which is the ethnographic standard this collection keeps pointing at.
Holland withholds confirmation for a full act, so the resemblance principle operates first as a child's claim that adults dismiss.
The film borrows hoodoo's correspondence logic and its material culture while treating the practice itself as inherently sinister, which is the borrowing without the framework.

entries.name: The Tainted Place
entries.description: Ground that has been altered and now alters what enters it.

examples.text: Lovecraft's contaminant persists in soil and water, indifferent to ownership, and the family's attempts to farm around it are the story's actual tragedy.
The Strugatskys make the Zone's rules discoverable only by fatality, so knowledge of the place is an accumulated casualty list.
The house's taint is asserted through claims presented as documented fact and later extensively disputed, which is how a contested account became a template.

entries.name: The Name Written Down
entries.description: Inscription as a binding act, distinct from speech.

examples.text: Ohba and Obata build an entire legal and moral system out of one writing rule with published exceptions, and the exceptions are where the series lives.
Burton splits the tradition cleanly, with the written name in the handbook binding and the spoken name summoning, so two different taboos operate side by side.
The prohibition on saying or thinking the name has no observable mechanism, so the audience is told a rule exists without ever being able to reason with it.

entries.name: The Invitation and the Doorway
entries.description: Permission as the condition of entry, and the household that grants it.

examples.text: Gerard records the threshold conditions as domestic procedure rather than as magic, which is why they read as rules a family could plausibly follow every night.
Holland makes the invitation a matter of suburban neighbourliness, so the fatal permission is granted by ordinary politeness.
The film's opening is built entirely on a threshold decision and then abandons the logic once the house's lower levels open up.

entries.name: Salt and Iron
entries.description: Materials that hold a line, and the tedium of maintaining one.

examples.text: Evans-Wentz's informants describe protections as daily upkeep rather than as one-off wards, which is the detail that turns a charm into a routine a character can fail at.
Kripke's series codified salt lines and iron for a generation of viewers and, to its credit, kept them physical and breachable rather than absolute.
Protective materials appear as set dressing in a house whose entity moves without reference to them.

entries.name: The Circle
entries.description: A boundary that protects by containing the summoner as much as the summoned.

examples.text: Guazzo specifies the circle's construction, its inscriptions and the fatal consequence of stepping outside during the working, which is a complete scene structure sitting in a demonology manual.
Carpenter treats containment as a physics problem staffed by graduate students, so the boundary has instrumentation and a failure mode.
Raimi's summoning is careless rather than ceremonial, which is an excellent choice for that film and leaves the circle tradition entirely unused.

entries.name: Mirrors and Their Covering
entries.description: Reflective surfaces as apertures, and the mourning custom of shutting them.

examples.text: Simpson and Roud trace the covering custom and its stated reasons across regions, and the variation in what people thought they were preventing is more useful than any single explanation.
Carpenter's closing image uses the mirror as a two-way surface and declines to resolve which side the audience is on.
Aja's reflections operate by inconsistent rules that permit whatever the scene requires, which is precisely what a threshold device cannot survive.

entries.name: The Thing Not Said Aloud
entries.description: Naming as summoning, and the community that agrees on a silence.

examples.text: The entries on avoidance names record communities substituting euphemisms for animals, illnesses and the dead, which is a functioning taboo system a writer can lift wholesale.
Hill makes the villagers' refusal to discuss her the protagonist's first real evidence, so the silence is both an obstacle and a disclosure.
The summoning ritual is explicit and instructional, which removes the taboo's central feature that nobody will explain it to you.

entries.name: The Number
entries.description: Counts that carry obligation — three knocks, the thirteenth, the fourth.

examples.text: The Thai anthology's structure is built on tetraphobia, and the number's dread is culturally specific in a way that shows how local these systems are.
Fincher lets a count organise the entire structure, so the audience knows how many remain and can measure the distance to the end from the first body.
Numerological obsession is presented as pattern-finding without any tradition behind it, which leaves the audience watching arithmetic rather than a taboo.

entries.name: Hospitality Law
entries.description: Guest and host obligations, and the catastrophe of breaching them.

examples.text: Xenia is the poem's operating law, breached by suitors and monsters alike, and every violation is punished on terms the audience is expected to already know.
Aickman's traveller is fed, accommodated and never permitted to leave, and the story's dread is entirely a matter of hospitality exceeding its bounds.
The wedding-night hunt inverts host obligation neatly and plays it as satire, which keeps the mechanism visible and drains its pressure.

entries.name: The Protection That Fails
entries.description: The ward correctly applied, with one omission.

examples.text: Hearn's Hoichi is inscribed with protective text everywhere except his ears, and the omission is clerical rather than moral, which is the tradition's cruellest and most usable idea.
Carpenter puts the town's survivors inside a church and lets the sanctuary hold against everything except the debt the church itself incurred.
Wards are deployed and breached without any established rule governing either, so the failures register as pacing rather than as events.

entries.name: The Ritual Year
entries.description: A calendar of obligations, and the date that cannot be moved.

examples.text: Hutton documents the British ritual year with its actual histories, including how much of it is Victorian invention, which is the single best corrective to confident seasonal folklore in fiction.
Tryon's community runs on a seven-year cycle with roles assigned in advance, so the newcomer's arrival is a scheduling event.

examples.work: Halloween III: Season of the Witch
examples.text: The film ties its scheme to a specific date and a mass broadcast, and the folk calendar underneath is asserted rather than built.

entries.name: The Boundary Stone and the Parish Edge
entries.description: Where one jurisdiction stops, and what waits in the gap.

examples.text: Hutton's account of beating the bounds shows a community physically re-establishing its perimeter each year, which is a ready-made folk-horror set piece almost nobody has used.
Hurley's tidal causeway is a boundary with a timetable, so access and isolation alternate on a schedule the characters can read and still misjudge.
Wheatley establishes a perimeter and a folkloric guardian and then resolves the film through pharmacology and light, which leaves the boundary as scenery.

entries.name: The Object That Must Be Returned
entries.description: Removal as the offence, restoration as the only remedy.

examples.text: James's crown has a hereditary guardian and a precise obligation, and the story's horror is that returning it is necessary and insufficient.

examples.work: Oh, Whistle, and I'll Come to You, My Lad
examples.text: The retrieved whistle is an ordinary archaeological find, which is what makes the summoning feel like an administrative error.
Removal and restoration are present as plot furniture inside an adventure structure where the obligation is never binding on anyone.

entries.name: Working from Ethnography
entries.description: Going to the collections and the fieldwork rather than to other people's monsters.

examples.text: Basil Johnston writes from inside the tradition with the moral argument intact, which is what a writer should be reading before a single creature description is drafted.
Hurston's method — extended residence, named practitioners, reasoning recorded rather than summarised — is the standard, and the material she gathered is unmatched precisely because of it.

Graves's poetic synthesis is presented as scholarship, was never accepted as such, and has been mistaken for a source by three generations of writers; it is a fine book about Robert Graves and worthless as ethnography.

entries.name: Living Traditions and Dead Corpora
entries.description: The difference between a historical corpus and somebody's current religion.

examples.text: Griffen developed the series with community involvement so that Dreaming figures appear as living belief with contemporary political stakes, not as a bestiary.
Clark works from Gullah Geechee tradition and makes it the source of the protagonists' power rather than the source of the threat, which inverts the genre's default arrangement.
Afro-Caribbean practice is rendered as inherently sinister and its adherents as antagonists, which is the arrangement this card exists to name.

entries.name: The Composite Monster Problem
entries.description: Regional variants flattened into one creature with a stat block.

examples.text: Ramos preserves the regional incompatibilities rather than resolving them, which shows what a composite entry destroys: the aswang of one province is not the aswang of the next, and the difference is the material.
Borges compiles across cultures and is explicit that he is compiling, with sources named and no pretence of a unified taxonomy — the honest version of the same act.
The bestiary format required one entry per creature with fixed abilities, and its enormous influence made the composite the default form in which most writers now first encounter folklore.

entries.name: The Record of Real Harm
entries.description: What the genre has already done with other people's beliefs, and why the checklist exists.

examples.text: Hurston's fieldwork in Haiti and Jamaica documents Vodou as a functioning religion with theology, clergy and social obligations; read alongside the film below, it is the clearest possible demonstration of the gap between a tradition and its horror export.

LaValle rebuilds a Lovecraft story from inside the racial politics that story depended on, which is the most productive available answer to inheriting a compromised canon: argue with it in its own form.

Released during the American occupation of Haiti, the film took a religion practised by the people then under that occupation and converted it into imagery of mindless coerced labour, inventing the screen zombie in the process. Nearly a century of the genre's most commercially successful monster descends from it, almost none of it acknowledging the source, and the pattern it established — take the name and the silhouette, discard the belief, keep the menace — is the single most consequential borrowing failure in horror's history.

entries.name: The Deep Roots
entries.description: Horror's inherited furniture, assembled long before anyone called it a genre.
entries.principle: The form's oldest materials are not literary but documentary and devotional: the returning-dead accounts in medieval chronicles, the murder ballad, plague literature, execution broadsides, and the hagiographic torture narrative. These were not written to frighten as entertainment, which is precisely why they retain a matter-of-fact register the genre keeps trying to recover.
entries.example: William of Newburgh reports revenants in the 1190s as parish news with named locations and applied remedies; the Child ballad corpus preserves the returning dead, the drowned and the murdered with no supernatural framing offered; execution broadsides sold the condemned's confession as a consumer product for three centuries.
entries.application: Read the chronicle and the broadside rather than the Gothic novel when you want a register that assumes belief. The reporting voice — dates, parishes, remedies attempted — is the single most transferable thing in the entire pre-history, and it is what found-footage and epistolary horror are still imitating.

entries.name: The Gothic Revival and the Graveyard Poets
entries.description: A mid-eighteenth-century taste for ruins, mortality and the sublime that made the Gothic novel possible.
entries.principle: Before Walpole there was a poetic vogue for graveyards, night, decay and the contemplation of one's own death — a deliberate cultivation of gloom as an aesthetic and moral exercise. Burke's account of the sublime supplied the theory, arguing that terror at a safe distance produces the strongest emotion art can reach, which is the genre's founding intellectual justification.
entries.example: Young's Night Thoughts and Blair's The Grave established the mode in the 1740s and Gray's Elegy popularised it; Burke's A Philosophical Enquiry supplied the argument in 1757; Walpole built Strawberry Hill as a Gothic house before writing a Gothic novel in it.
entries.application: Note that the aesthetic preceded the fiction rather than following it. When you want to justify horror as a serious activity rather than a guilty one, Burke's distinction between pain experienced and pain contemplated is still the strongest available case and predates every modern defence of the genre.

entries.name: The Fairy-Tale Collectors and the Cruelty They Edited Out
entries.description: A century of collection that preserved the material and progressively softened it.
entries.principle: The nineteenth-century collectors gathered oral tradition and then edited it across successive editions toward respectability, removing sexual content, softening violence, and — most consequentially — converting cruel mothers into stepmothers. The result is that the versions in circulation are already sanitised, and the harder material sits in the early editions and the field notes rather than in the famous ones.
entries.example: The Grimms revised Kinder- und Hausmärchen across seven editions between 1812 and 1857 with the changes running consistently in one direction; Afanasyev's Russian collection and Asbjørnsen and Moe's Norwegian one preserved rougher material that anglophone readers rarely meet; Perrault had already moralised the French corpus a century earlier.
entries.application: Go to the first edition, not the seventh. The excised material is where the usable horror is, and the pattern of what was removed is itself a map of what an era found unbearable — which is worth knowing when you are deciding what your own era will not tolerate.

entries.name: Poe and the Invention of the Modern Short Form
entries.description: One writer defining the shape horror still uses, and arguing for it in print.
entries.principle: Poe's contribution is structural rather than atmospheric: he established that a short story should be readable in a single sitting and constructed so that every element serves one predetermined emotional effect. He also, in the same decade, invented the detective story, which is why horror and mystery share a spine — both are engines for the controlled release of information.
entries.example: Poe set the argument out explicitly in The Philosophy of Composition in 1846, and demonstrated it across the 1840s in a body of work in which unity of effect governs length, incident and even word choice; his prize-winning MS. Found in a Bottle had already appeared in 1833.
entries.application: Decide your single intended effect before drafting and cut anything that does not serve it — the discipline is nearly two centuries old and remains the most reliable short-horror method available. Note also that Poe's own life has been so heavily mythologised by a hostile executor that most biographical detail attached to him should be checked rather than repeated.

entries.name: The Victorian Ghost Story and the Christmas Annual
entries.description: A commercial slot that produced a canon.
entries.principle: The ghost story became a mass form because periodicals wanted seasonal content, and the Christmas number created steady paid demand for short supernatural fiction. That commercial container shaped the product: a length that fits a magazine, a frame that suits reading aloud, and an ending that lands rather than lingers.
entries.example: Dickens's Christmas numbers institutionalised the practice from the 1850s and his own The Signal-Man appeared in one; Gaskell, Collins, Riddell, Broughton and Edwards all published ghost fiction in periodicals; the tradition survived into the twentieth century as a broadcast fixture rather than a printed one.
entries.application: Study the form's length discipline, which is a market constraint that turned out to be an aesthetic virtue. And note the delivery assumption — these were written to be read aloud in a room — which is why the strongest examples front-load atmosphere and place the reveal where a reader would have to look up.

entries.name: The Edwardian Masters
entries.description: A short, extraordinarily concentrated period in which the modern supernatural story was finished.
entries.principle: Between roughly 1890 and 1914 a small group of British writers established almost every technique the field still uses — the antiquarian intrusion, landscape as an agent, the contaminating text, deep-time dread, and the refusal to explain. They were largely amateurs by profession, which may be why the work is so unhurried and so unconcerned with plot machinery.
entries.example: M.R. James read his stories to friends at Cambridge before publishing them; Machen's The Great God Pan and The White People pursued a theology of evil; Blackwood's The Willows located dread in landscape; Hodgson worked deep time and the sea; Chambers's The King in Yellow made a text the vector.
entries.application: These are the field's technical textbooks and most are out of copyright. Read James for structure and disclosure management, Blackwood for landscape, Machen for the sense that the world's ordinary surface is a courtesy, and Chambers for the contaminating artefact — then notice how little any of them explain.

entries.name: The Lovecraft Circle and the Correspondence Network
entries.description: A genre built by letter, between writers who mostly never met.
entries.principle: The American weird tale developed through an amateur-press and correspondence network rather than through publishers or institutions, with writers exchanging manuscripts, lending each other invented names, and building a shared apparatus by mutual citation. This is an unusually well-documented case of a genre being made by a distributed group, and the shared-world habit it established has never left the field.
entries.example: Lovecraft corresponded voluminously with Robert E. Howard, Clark Ashton Smith, Frank Belknap Long, Robert Bloch and August Derleth; the borrowed pantheon circulated between their stories by agreement; Derleth subsequently systematised the material into a tidier cosmology than Lovecraft had written, which is its own cautionary tale about posthumous editing.
entries.application: The lesson is that shared apparatus is generative and codification is not — the loose borrowing produced the interesting work and the systematised version produced the pastiche. Note also that this network's central figure held racial views that are not separable from the fiction's mechanism, which is why the contemporary form has largely been built by writers arguing with him.

entries.name: Weird Tales and the Pulps
entries.description: The magazine that paid badly, late, and made the genre.
entries.principle: From 1923 a single low-paying magazine provided the only sustained American market for supernatural fiction, and its editorial appetite — for the strange rather than the merely frightening — shaped what got written for two decades. The pulps also established horror's enduring economic pattern: the form's centre of gravity is the short story, and it has almost always paid less than adjacent genres.
entries.example: Weird Tales published Lovecraft, Howard, Smith, Bloch and Bradbury while frequently paying on publication rather than acceptance and sometimes not at all; the same years saw horror become a broadcast staple, with Lights Out from 1934 and Suspense from 1942 developing an audio grammar of silence, sound effect and the unseen that the modern fiction podcast has revived almost unchanged.
entries.application: Read the pulps for pace and for the discipline of a market that would not pay for length. And take audio seriously as a horror medium rather than a delivery format — the radio drama solved the problem of the unseen threat decades before film worked out how to withhold.

entries.name: Arkham House and the Preservation of the Weird
entries.description: A small press founded to stop one writer's work disappearing.
entries.principle: Horror's canon survives largely because of small-press and specialist publishing rather than trade houses, and the pattern established in 1939 still holds — the field's preservation, its anthologies and much of its new talent run through operations of a handful of people. This makes the genre unusually dependent on individual editors and unusually vulnerable when one retires.
entries.example: Derleth and Donald Wandrei founded Arkham House to collect Lovecraft's magazine fiction in hardcover and went on to preserve Machen, Blackwood and Hodgson for American readers; the pattern repeated through Charles L. Grant's Shadows anthologies from 1978, Ellen Datlow's decades of year's-best and original anthologies, and a current small-press ecosystem where most short horror still first appears and where the field's new names are still made.
entries.application: If you write short horror, the market is the anthologies, the small presses and the magazines rather than the trade houses — that has been true since 1923 and is more true now. Read the current year's-best volumes to see who is buying what, and note that the form's centre of gravity has stayed short while almost every adjacent genre's has moved to the novel.

entries.name: The Paperback Boom
entries.description: A decade in which horror became a mass-market shelf.
entries.principle: Between the late 1960s and the mid-1980s horror moved from a specialist interest to a bestseller category, driven by a few enormous crossover successes and then by publishers commissioning to their shape. The boom professionalised the field, made novel-length horror commercially normal for the first time, and established the genre's modern celebrity author.
entries.example: Levin's Rosemary's Baby in 1967 and Blatty's The Exorcist in 1971 demonstrated the crossover audience, both amplified by their film adaptations; King's arrival from 1974 turned that demonstration into a permanent category; Straub, Herbert, Campbell and Rice built careers inside the space it opened.
entries.application: Note what the boom changed structurally — horror learned to sustain four hundred pages, which required the character depth and community-building that the short form had never needed. King's method of spending a third of a book on people before anything happens is a direct response to that commercial requirement and remains the most reliable solution to it.

entries.name: The Template and the Bust
entries.description: Publishing to a proven shape, until the shape stopped selling.
entries.principle: Success produced imitation and imitation produced a formula — embossed foil covers, a skeletal or child-shaped silhouette, a haunted house, an evil child — commissioned to fill shelf space rather than because anyone wanted to write it. The market collapsed at the turn of the 1990s, horror lines were shut down, and writers found their work relabelled as thriller or suspense to stay in print.
entries.example: Zebra and other mass-market lines ran the template through the 1980s; Dell's Abyss line launched in 1991 as an explicit attempt at literary horror against the trend; the bust nonetheless pushed the field back into small press and specialist publishing for most of a decade.
entries.application: The cycle is the most instructive commercial fact in the genre's history and it has repeated in smaller form since. The relevant craft point is that a category dies of sameness rather than of exhaustion — the audience did not stop wanting horror, it stopped being able to tell one book from another.

entries.name: Call of Cthulhu and the Sanity Mechanic
entries.description: A game that gave cosmic horror a rule set, and fed it back into prose.
entries.principle: The 1981 tabletop game translated the weird tale into a playable structure and made two decisions that propagated far beyond it: investigation rather than combat as the core activity, and a numerical sanity score that decreases as the player learns. Making comprehension itself the cost was a genuine design insight, and it has been borrowed by prose, film and video games ever since.
entries.example: Sandy Petersen's design for Chaosium established the investigative structure and the sanity track; the mechanic recurs across four decades of horror video games, most visibly in survival horror's willingness to make knowledge dangerous; the game also introduced Lovecraft to a large audience that had not read him.
entries.application: Steal the design principle rather than the score. If your threat becomes more dangerous as it is understood, you have solved horror's explanation problem structurally rather than by withholding — and note that the game's own history shows how quickly a systematised mythos becomes a catalogue.

entries.name: The Tie-In Economy
entries.description: The invisible majority of horror publishing.
entries.principle: Licensed fiction attached to film, television and game properties constitutes a large share of horror in print and is almost entirely absent from the field's critical conversation. It is where a great many working writers actually earn, it operates under genuine craft constraints, and the skills it demands — voice matching, continuity discipline, working inside someone else's rules — transfer.
entries.example: Franchise novelisations and original tie-in novels have accompanied nearly every major horror property since the 1970s, with substantial lines attached to screen and game franchises; several established horror novelists have written tie-in work under their own or other names.
entries.application: Treat it as a craft discipline rather than as a lesser category — writing convincingly inside a fixed rule set is the exact skill that makes original horror's threats consistent. If you take the work, read the property's existing material as a rule set first and a story second.

entries.name: Splatterpunk's Turn and the Quiet Counter-Swing
entries.description: An explicit movement against restraint, and the immediate reaction against it.
entries.principle: The mid-1980s produced a self-named movement rejecting horror's traditional cutaway in favour of explicit and sustained violence, arguing that mediation lets the reader off the moral hook. Almost simultaneously an opposite tendency organised itself around implication, domestic scale and atmosphere, and the two positions have alternated as the field's dominant register ever since.
entries.example: The term was coined at a 1986 convention and attached to Schow, Skipp and Spector, and to Barker's contemporaneous Books of Blood; Charles L. Grant edited the Shadows anthologies from 1978 around the opposite principle and gave quiet horror its name; the argument recurred in the 2000s extremity cycle and its counter-swing.
entries.application: Recognise which side of this argument your book is on and commit — the failure mode is a novel that flinches at the moment it has spent two hundred pages promising not to. Both positions are defensible and each produces its own dishonesty: unearned explicitness on one side, coyness dressed as restraint on the other.

entries.name: Comic Horror
entries.description: A register that arrived early, was dismissed, and turned out to be durable.
entries.principle: Horror and comedy have been paired since the genre's first decade and the pairing works because both depend on identical timing and on the audience's expectations being managed and then broken. The mode's discipline is that consequences must remain intact — comic horror fails at the moment the audience concludes that nothing in the film can hurt anyone.
entries.example: Universal was parodying its own monsters within a decade of establishing them; Landis's An American Werewolf in London in 1981 and Raimi's Evil Dead II in 1987 established the modern balance; Wright's Shaun of the Dead in 2004 demonstrated that the emotional stakes could be kept fully serious underneath the comedy.
entries.application: Establish the threat honestly and kill someone the audience likes before the first extended joke. And note that comic horror is where a great deal of formal innovation happens, because a mode nobody takes seriously is a mode nobody polices.

entries.name: The Franchise Treadmill
entries.description: The genre's characteristic commercial shape, and its characteristic decline curve.
entries.principle: Horror produces sequels more readily than any adjacent genre because its properties are cheap, its antagonists are marketable, and its endings are traditionally unresolved. It also degrades under sequels more reliably, because each instalment must either repeat a mystery the audience has solved or expand a lore that converts dread into cosmology.
entries.example: The major slasher properties of the 1980s each ran to seven or more instalments with a visible decline; the pattern repeated with the possession and haunting cycles of the 2010s, which added shared-universe construction; the exceptions are almost always films that change form rather than escalate.
entries.application: If a continuation is likely, decide in advance what will stay permanently unexplained and defend it — the property's unexplained material is its actual asset. And note the one reliable escape: the sequels that work change the genre they are in rather than doing the same thing larger.

entries.name: YA Horror
entries.description: A readership the field discovered it already had.
entries.principle: Horror for young readers moved from a niche to a publishing phenomenon in the early 1990s and demonstrated a tolerance for fear that adult gatekeepers had consistently underestimated. The category has cycled since — a boom, a retreat, and a current resurgence with markedly more literary ambition — but the underlying finding has held: young readers want the frightening material and detect condescension faster than they detect difficulty.
entries.example: Stine's Goosebumps from 1992 and the Point Horror line established the mass market; Schwartz and Gammell's Scary Stories collections had already shown in the 1980s how much unmediated dread the readership would accept, and became among the most-challenged books in American libraries as a result; the current wave runs to considerably darker and more formally ambitious work.
entries.application: Write down in vocabulary, never in emotional sophistication. The one genuine constraint is not intensity but implication — young readers accept that terrible things happened far more readily than they accept that nothing anyone did mattered.

entries.name: Elevated Horror and the Prestige Turn
entries.description: A commercial and critical reclassification, and an argument about the label.
entries.principle: From the mid-2010s a body of formally ambitious horror achieved critical standing and awards recognition that the genre had rarely received, supported by a distribution model built on low budgets and directorial control. The term attached to it is contested from inside the field, on the grounds that it implies the rest of horror needs elevating and quietly relabels good work as not-really-horror.
entries.example: Blumhouse's micro-budget model from the 2000s made director-led horror commercially safe; A24's output from 2012 gave it a critical identity; Peele's Get Out won the Academy Award for Original Screenplay in 2018, the genre's most significant such recognition.
entries.application: Take the craft lesson and leave the label. What actually changed was budget structure creating room for ambiguity, slow pacing and unresolved endings — the commercial conditions permitted the technique. Treating "elevated" as a genre rather than as a marketing term will lead you to imitate a tone instead of a set of choices.

entries.name: The Reckoning and the Retired Trophy
entries.description: The field confronting its founding figure's politics, in public and by vote.
entries.principle: Horror's central American ancestor held documented white-supremacist views that are not incidental to his fiction, since the fear of contamination by the other is the mechanism his cosmic horror runs on. The field's response through the 2010s was not to discard him but to argue with him in the work — and, institutionally, to stop making his face the trophy.
entries.example: Campaigning by Nnedi Okorafor, Daniel José Older, China Miéville and others led the World Fantasy Award to announce in late 2015 that it would replace its Lovecraft bust, with a new design following; LaValle's The Ballad of Black Tom and Ruff's Lovecraft Country in 2016 rebuilt Lovecraft material from inside its racial politics; Moreno-Garcia, Jones, Clark, Machado and Solomon reshaped the field's centre in the same decade.
entries.application: The productive move with a compromised inheritance is to argue with it in its own form rather than to ignore it or to launder it. Note also that the strongest of these books are not corrections but genuinely better cosmic horror, because writing from inside the thing Lovecraft feared produces a sharper account of it.

entries.name: Survival Horror at the Centre
entries.description: Games as a primary site of horror craft rather than an adaptation target.
entries.principle: Interactive horror developed its own solutions to the genre's core problems — scarcity as a tension mechanism, denied competence, the antagonist that cannot be defeated, and the removal of the weapon entirely — and those solutions have flowed back into prose and film rather than the other way round. For a large part of the current audience, games are the primary contact with the genre.
entries.example: Capcom's Resident Evil in 1996 established inventory scarcity as tension and Konami's Silent Hill in 1999 replaced combat competence with psychological terrain; Frictional's Amnesia in 2010 removed the weapon altogether; the tradition continues through Alien: Isolation, Bloodborne and a substantial independent scene.
entries.application: Play the canonical ones and steal the pacing logic, not the imagery. The transferable insight is that dread scales with what the protagonist cannot do, and games are forced to be explicit about that in a way prose can leave vague and usually should not.

entries.name: The Globalized Genre
entries.description: The end of the anglophone default.
entries.principle: Horror's most productive traditions are no longer predominantly British or American, and translation, subtitled streaming and international co-production have made national horror cinemas and comics traditions directly available rather than filtered through remakes. The practical effect for writers is access to rule sets that anglophone horror has not exhausted.
entries.example: Japanese horror's transmissible curse and Junji Ito's manga; Korean horror's interest in family culpability; Mexican, Spanish and Latin American horror across film and prose; Nordic, Indonesian, Thai and Nigerian production; the two-decade run of anglophone remakes that consistently weakened their sources by adding moral causation.
entries.application: Watch and read in the original wherever you can, and pay particular attention to what a tradition assumes about causation — the single most repeated failure in adaptation is inserting a reason the victim deserved it, into traditions built on the opposite premise.

entries.name: The Web-Native Tradition
entries.description: Horror written for platforms rather than for publication.
entries.principle: The most significant formal development of the last two decades happened outside publishing entirely: collaborative, anonymous, artefact-shaped fiction presented as documents rather than stories, distributed on forums, wikis and video platforms. Its native effects — no author, no ending, no clear boundary to the text — are not available to print, and it has produced a genuinely new set of techniques.
entries.example: Creepypasta as a forum form from the mid-2000s; the SCP Foundation's collaboratively written containment register sustaining a clinical house style across thousands of contributors; Marble Hornets adapting found footage to serialised upload; the analogue-horror wave building dread from broadcast conventions.
entries.application: Study it for the artefact discipline — choose a document type and obey its conventions absolutely, because the horror lives in the deviation from a form the reader already trusts. And note that the mode resists the tidy ending, which is why the strongest examples stop rather than conclude.

entries.name: Benign Masochism and the Safe-Threat Account
entries.description: Why anyone would choose to be frightened on purpose.
entries.principle: The most durable explanation is that humans learn to enjoy negative experiences the body treats as dangerous once the mind is confident they are not — the same account that covers chilli, bitter drinks and roller coasters. The pleasure depends on a maintained double awareness: the threat must register as real enough to produce the response and be reliably contained.
entries.example: Rozin's work on benign masochism documents the pattern across unrelated domains and finds that enjoyment tracks the gap between the body's alarm and the person's knowledge of safety; the same logic explains why horror consumption drops when the audience's real-world threat level rises, and why a text that seems to threaten the reader rather than the characters loses them.
entries.application: Protect the container. Anything that makes the reader feel personally unsafe rather than vicariously endangered — sustained cruelty with no shape, or an implication that the book is contemptuous of them — collapses the mechanism the whole genre runs on.

entries.name: Excitation Transfer
entries.description: Arousal outlasts its cause, and colours whatever comes next.
entries.principle: Physiological arousal decays more slowly than the emotion that produced it, so residual activation from a frightening scene intensifies the next emotional response regardless of its valence. This is why relief after fear feels disproportionate, and why the placement of a tender or funny scene immediately after a frightening one changes how strongly it lands.
entries.example: Zillmann's excitation-transfer work established the effect and it has been applied extensively to media response, including the finding that satisfaction with a frightening film is highest when the resolution is prompt and complete enough to convert lingering arousal into relief.
entries.application: Use the residue deliberately. The scene after the worst scene is doing more work than its content suggests, which is an argument for placing your most emotionally significant material there rather than treating it as recovery time.

entries.name: Approach and Avoidance Escapism
entries.description: Two different motives that look identical from outside.
entries.principle: Immersive fiction can be sought to expand experience or to suppress an unwanted state, and the two motives predict very different outcomes — the first associates with wellbeing and the second with rumination and worse mood afterward. The distinction matters to horror because the genre is unusually often assumed to serve the second when the evidence points to the first for most of its audience.
entries.example: Stenseng's work separates self-expansion from self-suppression escapism and finds them dissociable in their correlates; survey work on horror audiences during periods of collective threat found frequent consumers reporting greater psychological resilience, though the causal direction remains genuinely open.
entries.application: Take seriously that most of your readers are doing something adaptive, and stop apologising for the genre in your own framing of it. Note also the honest limit: the correlational evidence cannot tell you whether horror builds coping capacity or whether people with that capacity choose horror.

entries.name: Why Bleakness Also Sells
entries.description: Sad, frightening and unresolved fiction is valued differently from enjoyable fiction, not less.
entries.principle: Audiences report two distinct kinds of positive response to fiction: hedonic enjoyment, and a separate appreciation that attaches to work experienced as meaningful, moving or true. Appreciation is what bleak and unresolved work earns, it predicts recommendation and rereading rather than immediate pleasure, and it is the reason a downer ending can be a commercial asset.
entries.example: Oliver and Raney's work distinguishes enjoyment from appreciation as independent dimensions of media response, with appreciation tracking perceived meaningfulness rather than positive affect; horror's most durable canon is disproportionately made of books and films audiences describe as devastating rather than fun.
entries.application: Stop treating a bleak ending as a commercial risk to be mitigated and start treating it as a different contract. The failure is not bleakness but incoherence — an ending that betrays what the book promised loses both dimensions at once.

entries.name: Disposition and the Broken Contract
entries.description: Audiences keep moral accounts, and notice when the book does not settle them.
entries.principle: Enjoyment of narrative is substantially predicted by whether outcomes match the moral standing the audience has assigned to characters — approving of good outcomes for liked characters and bad ones for disliked. Horror routinely violates this, which is the source of both its strongest effects and its most common accusations of nihilism.
entries.example: Affective disposition theory, developed by Zillmann and Cantor, accounts for the pattern across genres; horror's unpunished antagonist and its arbitrary victim are direct violations, and the audience response — that something "isn't fair" — is the mechanism registering rather than a failure of the work.
entries.application: Know when you are violating the contract and make the violation the point. Arbitrary death lands hardest when the book has established that it keeps accounts elsewhere; a story in which nothing is ever deserved has no baseline against which the arbitrary can register.

entries.name: Who Horror Is For
entries.description: Stable individual differences, not a single audience.
entries.principle: Preference for frightening media tracks measurable traits — sensation seeking most consistently, alongside lower trait empathy for victim suffering in some samples and higher curiosity or need for cognition in others. There is no single horror audience, and the sub-audiences want incompatible things, which is why register decisions are also market decisions.
