His reputation for total reclusiveness is overstated: he wrote publicly about Alfredo Ballí Treviño, the imprisoned Mexican surgeon he met as a young reporter and has identified as a source for Lecter, and gave interviews around Cari Mora.
entries.knownFor: Making forensic procedure a horror engine, and creating the antagonist against whom every subsequent articulate monster is measured.
entries.signature: Clinical exactness about method, withheld interiority for the killer, and a protagonist whose competence is real and insufficient.

works.title: Red Dragon
works.note: where Hannibal Lecter first appears, and not The Silence of the Lambs, as is constantly claimed

entries.name: Joyce Carol Oates
entries.description: The reverse of the expected case: a literary novelist with the stronger genre award record.
entries.meta: American, born 1938. **Five competitive Bram Stokers** — Best Novel for 1995 work for Zombie, and four further wins for collections and short fiction, including taking two categories in a single year for 2016 work — plus Lifetime Achievement for 1993. World Fantasy Award 2011 for Short Fiction. A Shirley Jackson Special Award 2011. **National Book Award 1970 for them — one win**, with five further finalist placings. **She has never won the Pulitzer, having been a Fiction finalist four times, and has never won the Nobel.** Nobel nomination records are sealed for fifty years, so any count of her modern nominations is unverifiable by definition and should not be printed. She has written as Rosamond Smith and Lauren Kelly.
entries.knownFor: Sustained, unsentimental attention to American violence, and a body of horror that is not a sideline — five competitive Stokers and a World Fantasy Award is a stronger competitive record than several of this category's better-known names combined.
entries.signature: Present-tense proximity to a mind in the act of harming or being harmed, with the prose refusing to look away or to editorialise.

works.title: The Corn Maiden and Other Nightmares

entries.name: Robert Aickman
entries.description: Wrote stories that cannot be summarised, and was right to.
entries.meta: English, 1914–1981. **World Fantasy Award 1975 for Best Short Fiction** at the award's first ceremony — for a single story, not for the collection it later appeared in, which is the standard error. He was nominated but did not win that year's Life Achievement award. British Fantasy Award 1981 for Best Short Fiction. He co-founded the Inland Waterways Association in 1946 and regarded canal preservation as his principal life's work.
entries.knownFor: The "strange story" as he named it — a form that withholds not merely explanation but incident, and remains unsettling on rereading precisely because there is nothing to solve.
entries.signature: A courteous, faintly antiquated narrator maintaining social composure through events that would justify screaming, with the wrongness never once acknowledged.

works.title: We Are for the Dark
works.note: with Elizabeth Jane Howard, published without individual story credits

entries.name: Charles L. Grant
entries.description: Named quiet horror, edited its defining anthologies, and argued its case in public.
entries.meta: American, 1942–2006. Author and editor records are routinely merged and should be kept apart. **As author:** two Nebulas, at the 1977 and 1979 ceremonies, and a World Fantasy Award for Best Novella in 1983, shared as a tie with Karl Edward Wagner. **As editor:** World Fantasy Awards in 1979 for Shadows and 1983 for Nightmare Seasons. **His only Bram Stoker of any kind is Lifetime Achievement 2000** — the widely repeated claim that he won one for "This Old Man" is false, as it was a nominee and McCammon's "The Deep End" took the category. Three World Fantasy wins from twenty-three nominations, among the highest nomination counts in the award's history.
entries.knownFor: The Shadows anthologies, which gave a generation of quiet horror a market, and for being the position the splatterpunks defined themselves against.
entries.signature: Small-town New England rendered in a deliberately low register, with the supernatural implied through weather, sound and absence.

works.title: The Hour of the Oxrun Dead
Shadows
works.note: as editor, the first of ten volumes running to 1991

entries.name: Charles Beaumont
entries.description: A career of about fifteen years, ended by an illness nobody could name.
entries.meta: American, born Charles Leroy Nutt, 1929–1967, at thirty-eight. **Every major horror award postdates him**, and his sole award is a posthumous Bram Stoker for a 1988 collection. From about 1963 he suffered an undiagnosed degenerative brain disease producing catastrophic premature aging and cognitive decline; **Alzheimer's and Pick's disease have both been proposed and neither is confirmed**, so no diagnosis should be stated. Several Twilight Zone scripts credited to him in 1963 and 1964 were ghostwritten by friends, notably William F. Nolan and Jerry Sohl, as the illness advanced. "It's a Good Life" is Jerome Bixby's story, not his.
entries.knownFor: A body of short fiction, most of it sold to men's magazines, that brought genuine literary ambition to the American fantastic short story.
entries.signature: A clean, unshowy line and a premise pushed exactly one step past the point most writers would stop.

works.title: "The Devil, You Say?"
works.note: Amazing Stories, his first professional sale

works.title: "The Howling Man"
works.note: Rogue, November, and not 1960, which is the television adaptation

entries.name: T.E.D. Klein
entries.description: Very little published, almost all of it essential.
entries.meta: American, born 1947. World Fantasy Award 1986 for Best Novella; British Fantasy August Derleth Award 1986 for The Ceremonies. World Horror Grandmaster 2012. Seven World Fantasy nominations and one win — and **The Ceremonies did not win the World Fantasy Award**, which is a common error; it was nominated and lost. He was editor-in-chief of Rod Serling's The Twilight Zone Magazine from 1981 to 1985, the venue that first published David J. Schow's award-winning "Red Light".
entries.knownFor: An unusually small body of work whose influence far exceeds its size, and for the proposition that a novel of cosmic horror can be built out of a rural summer and a reading list.
entries.signature: Slow accumulation across ordinary days, with the horror arriving through a scholar's misreading of something he has correctly transcribed.

works.title: "The Events at Poroth Farm"
works.note: and not 1975, which is its award-nomination year

works.title: Dark Gods
works.note: four novellas, containing "Nadelman's God", which had no prior magazine appearance

works.title: Providence After Dark and Other Writings

entries.name: Susan Hill
entries.description: A mainstream literary novelist who wrote the most durable ghost story of the last fifty years.
entries.meta: English, born 1942. **She has never won a genre horror award.** Her record is entirely mainstream: Somerset Maugham Award 1971, John Llewellyn Rhys Prize 1972, Whitbread Novel Award 1972, and a Booker shortlisting in 1972 that she did not convert. CBE 2012 and DBE 2020, both for services to literature.
entries.knownFor: The Woman in Black, which demonstrated in 1983 that the undiluted Edwardian ghost-story shape still worked without irony or updating.
entries.signature: Period pastiche executed so precisely that the reader stops noticing it, with the apparition's grievance withheld until it explains everything.

works.title: I'm the King of the Castle
In the Springtime of the Year
The Woman in Black
works.note: the novel, which precedes Stephen Mallatratt's 1987 stage adaptation rather than deriving from it

entries.name: Sarah Waters
entries.description: Wrote a ghost story about the collapse of a class, and let the ghost stay arguable.
entries.meta: **Welsh**, born 1966 in Neyland, Pembrokeshire — she is frequently listed as English, and "Neath" is a persistent transcription error for her birthplace. **She has never won the Booker Prize**, having been shortlisted three times. Her wins include the Betty Trask Award 1999, the Somerset Maugham Award 2000, a Stonewall Book Award 2001 and the CWA Ellis Peters Historical Dagger 2002; OBE 2019. Neither Affinity nor The Little Stranger has ever been nominated for a horror award, so genre recognition should not be implied.
entries.knownFor: The Little Stranger, in which the haunting and the post-war destruction of the gentry are the same event, and the narrator's reliability is the book's real subject.
entries.signature: Immaculate period research carrying a class argument, with the supernatural left precisely balanced against a psychological reading that the text also supports.

entries.name: Elizabeth Hand
entries.description: Four World Fantasy Awards, four Shirley Jacksons, and still under-read.
entries.meta: American, born 1957; her birthplace is given variously as San Diego and Yonkers and is not resolved here. Two Nebulas, **four World Fantasy Awards**, **four Shirley Jackson Awards**, two International Horror Guild awards, plus the Mythopoeic and Tiptree awards in 1996. **Three Bram Stoker nominations and no Stoker win.** She wrote the authorised return to Shirley Jackson's Hill House.
entries.knownFor: Literary horror and dark fantasy of unusual formal range, and a crime series whose protagonist is among the least ingratiating in the field.
entries.signature: Damaged, hard-living women artists observed without redemption arcs, in prose that is precise about landscape and unsparing about them.

works.title: "Last Summer at Mars Hill"
works.note: F&SF, August, which won a World Fantasy Award in 1995 and a Nebula in 1996 as two distinct awards

entries.name: Reggie Oliver
entries.description: The Jamesian tradition's most accomplished living practitioner, and not in fact award-winning.
entries.meta: English, born 1952. Routinely described as award-winning: against the Science Fiction Awards Database he has **zero wins in any of the five major genre awards** — two World Fantasy nominations, one British Fantasy, two Shirley Jackson and two International Horror Guild, and no wins. Two minor prizes are reported and are unconfirmed against any official body. He has been a professional playwright, actor and theatre director since 1975, and the fiction is a second career begun in his fifties — sources routinely invert this.
entries.knownFor: Ghost stories that put theatrical and clerical worlds under a Jamesian lens, published almost entirely through small presses.
entries.signature: A raconteur's voice with an actor's ear for the self-deceiving speaker, and a supernatural that arrives as social embarrassment before it arrives as terror.

works.title: The Dreams of Cardinal Vittorini
works.note: Haunted River, and not the 2012 Tartarus reprint to which it is habitually misdated

works.title: The Complete Symphonies of Adolf Hitler
Out of the Woodshed
works.note: a biography of his aunt Stella Gibbons

entries.name: David J. Schow
entries.description: Coined the word as a joke and spent forty years being defined by it.
entries.meta: American, born 1955 in Marburg, West Germany. World Fantasy Award 1987 for Best Short Story, his only World Fantasy win from three nominations; International Horror Guild award for non-fiction. **One Bram Stoker nomination and zero wins** — the claim that he won for "Pamela's Get" appears in Contemporary Authors and propagates widely, and is false: that year's novelette category was a tie between Alan Rodgers and George R.R. Martin. **He coined "splatterpunk" at the Twelfth World Fantasy Convention in Providence in 1986, as an in-joke rather than a manifesto**, which is the root of the term's definitional instability ever since.
entries.knownFor: Editing the anthology that consolidated the tendency, and for a screenwriting career alongside the fiction.
entries.signature: Hard-boiled velocity and film-literate structure, with the violence staged rather than described.

entries.name: John Skipp
entries.description: Half of the movement's central partnership, and its most durable editor.
entries.meta: American, born 1957. **Two Bram Stokers, both for edited anthologies** — for 2006 and 2011 work — and **no major award for his own fiction**. A World Fantasy nomination in 1990 for Book of the Dead, co-edited with Craig Spector. The commonly stated 1991 end-date for the Skipp and Spector partnership conflicts with joint titles published in 1992 and 1993 and is not settled.
entries.knownFor: With Spector, the rock-and-roll register of 1980s extreme horror, and for Book of the Dead, the anthology that gave prose zombie fiction its modern shape.
entries.signature: Present-tense propulsion and dialogue that sounds spoken, with music and subculture treated as load-bearing rather than as texture.

entries.name: Craig Spector
entries.description: The other half, and the one the record consistently mislays.
entries.meta: American. **His birth date and place are not reliably documented in any library or award source and are not stated here.** **He has no wins in any major award**, individually or jointly — Book of the Dead was a World Fantasy nominee and won nothing. He is frequently credited with the two Bram Stokers that belong to John Skipp alone, both of which postdate the partnership entirely.
entries.knownFor: The collaborative novels of 1986 to 1993, and two solo books that moved toward crime.
entries.signature: Structural discipline underneath the partnership's velocity — the plotting that kept the excess load-bearing.

entries.name: Jack Ketchum
entries.description: A precursor rather than a member, and the field's most argued-over writer.
entries.meta: American, born Dallas William Mayr, 1946–2018. **Four competitive Bram Stokers** — for 1994, 2000 and two for 2003 work — plus **Bram Stoker Lifetime Achievement 2015** and **World Horror Grandmaster 2011**, which are two separate awards and are frequently conflated. He won a Stoker for neither The Girl Next Door nor The Lost. Off Season predates the coinage of splatterpunk by four years, which is why placing him inside the movement is a chronological error. Off Season was edited down before publication and the 1999 Overlook Connection edition restores his preferred text. The Girl Next Door is loosely based on the 1965 murder of Sylvia Likens in Indianapolis — a real case of public court record — and relocates the events to a fictional 1950s suburb, renames every participant and invents its framing narrator; the derivation is verifiable, and any claim that specific incidents in the novel correspond to specific documented events is not.
entries.knownFor: Unmediated depictions of sustained cruelty, defended on the ground that mediation lets the reader off the moral hook — the strongest available version of that argument and the most contested.
entries.signature: Flat, plain reportage sustained at length, with no stylistic cushion between the reader and the event.

entries.name: Richard Laymon
entries.description: Never part of the movement, and a case study in what publishing does to a career.
entries.meta: American, 1947–2001. **One Bram Stoker: Best Novel for 2000 work, awarded posthumously** three months after his death. Seven award entries and that single win. He was American, not British, though he is often taken for British because of where he sold: **American publishers largely declined him on content and sales grounds while he built a substantial readership in the United Kingdom**, a disparity that defined his whole career. The trigger was The Woods Are Dark, cut by nearly fifty pages and rewritten before its 1981 publication; the 2008 restored edition diverges substantially from roughly the eighth chapter onward, making the two versions materially different books.
entries.knownFor: Relentless pace and a refusal of subtext, and for a body of work whose UK reputation and US reputation barely overlap.
entries.signature: Very short chapters, constant forward motion, and a cheerful unwillingness to withhold anything.

works.title: A Writer's Tale
works.note: non-fiction, and the primary source for his own account of the Woods Are Dark episode

entries.name: Billy Martin, published as Poppy Z. Brite
entries.description: Brought a queer, Southern, music-saturated sensibility into a form that had not had one.
entries.meta: American, born 1967. He is a trans man; he began hormone therapy in 2010 and stated a preference for male pronouns in 2011, and he/him is correct throughout including for the earlier period. **The novels were published as Poppy Z. Brite, which is the correct bibliographic attribution and not an error.** British Fantasy Icarus Award for Best Newcomer 1994 is his only major genre win; an International Horror Guild award in 1995 for a co-edited anthology, in that award's first year. **Three World Fantasy nominations and five Bram Stoker nominations, with no wins in either.** He did not stop publishing after transition.
entries.knownFor: New Orleans and the Gulf South as a horror landscape, and for making desire and decay the same subject.
entries.signature: Lush, sensory prose about bodies and food and music, with the violence arriving inside the same register rather than against it.

works.title: Swamp Foetus
works.note: Borderlands Press, reissued in mass market as Wormwood in 1994 and frequently double-counted as two books

entries.name: Edward Lee
entries.description: The extreme small-press wave's defining name, with no awards at all.
entries.meta: American, born 1957. His birthplace is given variously as Bowie, Maryland and Washington, D.C., and an asserted legal name appears in one reference source and is unconfirmed, so neither is stated here. **One Bram Stoker nomination, in 1995, and zero wins in any award** — the "award-winning" epithet attached to him in publisher copy is not supportable. He is a different person from the children's author Edward Edson Lee. He announced his retirement from writing in 2025.
entries.knownFor: Establishing the commercial floor of extreme horror through small and limited-edition presses, largely outside trade publishing.
entries.signature: Escalation as the organising principle, with rural Maryland settings and a deadpan willingness to go further than the previous page.

works.title: The Bighead
works.note: small press, and habitually misdated to a later reprint

entries.name: Brian Keene
entries.description: Restarted prose zombie fiction, and built infrastructure alongside the books.
entries.meta: American, born 1967. **Two Bram Stokers** — Best Non-Fiction for 2001 work and Best First Novel for 2003 work. The dual work-year and ceremony-year convention is why his record is sometimes reported as four rather than two. World Horror Grandmaster 2014. **No World Fantasy Award of any kind.** He is often described as a former Horror Writers Association officer and this is not confirmed by any source, so it is not stated here. He has served on the board of the charity Scares That Care since 2017.
entries.knownFor: The Rising, credited with driving the 2000s resurgence of prose zombie fiction, and for a decade of industry-service work — a market newsletter, then a long-running podcast — that shaped the field as much as the novels.
entries.signature: Fast, plain, unliterary prose with an unexpected streak of theological seriousness underneath the apocalypse.

works.title: Jobs in Hell
works.note: the market newsletter that won his first Stoker

works.title: The Rising
works.note: Delirium Books, with the mass-market edition following in 2004

works.title: Earthworm Gods
works.note: retitled The Conqueror Worms for the 2006 edition and frequently listed as two separate novels

entries.name: Daphne du Maurier
entries.description: Wrote the century's most imitated opening and was patronised for it for fifty years.
entries.meta: English, 1907–1989. DBE 1969; Mystery Writers of America Grand Master 1978, shared with Dorothy B. Hughes and Ngaio Marsh, and frequently misdated to 1977. The "National Book Award" attached to Rebecca is the 1938 American Booksellers Association favourite-novel vote, not the modern prize, which was founded in 1950. **No court ever found her a plagiarist** — the Nabuco claim was never litigated, and the 1948 US suit was dismissed in her favour.
entries.knownFor: Rebecca, which fused the Female Gothic with the modern psychological novel and set the predecessor-wife structure the form still uses.
entries.signature: A narrator whose self-effacement is the trap, in prose so controlled that the cruelty arrives without raising its voice.

works.title: "The Birds"
works.note: and not 1963, which is the film

works.title: "Don't Look Now"
works.note: and not 1973, which is the film

entries.name: Angela Carter
entries.description: Rebuilt the fairy tale from inside its sexual politics.
entries.meta: English, born Angela Olive Stalker, 1940–1992, of lung cancer at fifty-one. John Llewellyn Rhys Prize and Somerset Maugham Award in the late 1960s; the inaugural Cheltenham Prize for Literature 1979; James Tait Black Memorial Prize for Fiction 1984. **She was never nominated for the Booker** — she judged it in 1983 — and no prize bearing her name existed in her lifetime. Her posthumous canonisation produced its own critical backlash, including the argument that The Bloody Chamber stays inside the structures it set out to subvert.
entries.knownFor: The Bloody Chamber, which restored the cruelty the collectors had edited out and made the erotics of the tales the subject rather than the subtext.
entries.signature: Baroque, deliberately artificial prose used with complete precision, so the excess is an argument rather than a texture.

works.title: Fireworks
works.note: and not 1984, which her own estate's page gives in error

entries.name: Toni Morrison
entries.description: Wrote the American ghost story that the American ghost story had been avoiding.
entries.meta: American, 1931–2019. Born Chloe Ardelia Wofford — "Chloe Anthony Wofford" is the published version and not the accurate one. National Book Critics Circle Award 1977; **Pulitzer Prize for Fiction 1988 for Beloved**; **Nobel Prize in Literature 1993**; National Book Foundation Medal 1996; Presidential Medal of Freedom 2012. **Beloved did not win the National Book Award** — it lost the 1987 award, and the statement signed by forty-eight Black writers and scholars in the New York Times Book Review the following January preceded the Pulitzer. She was the first African American and the first Black woman to take the Nobel in Literature, not the first Black laureate.
entries.knownFor: Beloved, in which a haunting is inseparable from the documented historical violence that produced it — the standard against which every trauma-and-the-supernatural novel since is measured.
entries.signature: A withheld central event circled and approached from multiple interiorities until the reader assembles it themselves.

entries.name: Kelly Link
entries.description: Made the unresolved short story a commercially viable form.
entries.meta: American, born 1969. Tiptree Award 1998; World Fantasy Awards for Short Fiction 1999, a professional Special Award 2009 with Gavin J. Grant, and Anthology 2015; **one Hugo, for Best Novelette in 2005**; three Nebulas, including Best Novella and Best Novelette in the same eligibility year, which is often reported as one win; a Shirley Jackson Award 2011; MacArthur Fellowship 2018. **She is a Pulitzer finalist, not a winner**, and the frequently claimed Hugo for Magic for Beginners does not exist.
entries.knownFor: Stories that decline to resolve and are nonetheless satisfying, and for Small Beer Press, which she co-founded and which has carried much of the field's most interesting short fiction.
entries.signature: Deadpan suburban surfaces with the rules of the world quietly wrong, and an ending that stops rather than concludes.

works.title: Get in Trouble
works.note: and not 2016, which is the Pulitzer finalist year

entries.name: Carmen Maria Machado
entries.description: Relocated body horror into the politics of who is believed.
entries.meta: American of Cuban descent, born 1986. For Her Body and Other Parties: the National Book Critics Circle's John Leonard Prize for a first book 2017, a **Shirley Jackson Award for a single-author collection** for 2017 work, the Crawford Award 2018 and a Lambda 2018. For In the Dream House: a Lambda 2020 and the Rathbones Folio Prize 2021. **She was a National Book Award finalist, not a winner**, and has no World Fantasy Award.
entries.knownFor: Her Body and Other Parties, which put queer women's bodies at the centre of the American weird story, and a memoir that used genre apparatus to write about abuse in a same-sex relationship.
entries.signature: Formal invention as argument — a story told as an episode guide, another as a catalogue — with the horror carried by what the form refuses to accommodate.

entries.name: Jeff VanderMeer
entries.description: Made the incomprehensible ecological rather than cosmic.
entries.meta: American, born 1968. Five World Fantasy Awards, three of them shared with Ann VanderMeer and most of them editorial — Novella 2000 as a tie, and Anthology in 2003, 2012 and 2020. **Nebula Best Novel and a Shirley Jackson Award for 2014 work, both for Annihilation.** **Annihilation never won a Hugo and was not even a finalist**, which is among the most-repeated errors about him. He did not coin "New Weird", which is credited to M. John Harrison; he edited the anthology that consolidated it.
entries.knownFor: The Southern Reach books, which took cosmic horror's refusal of comprehension and grounded it in biology and landscape rather than in theology.
entries.signature: Field-report prose — a biologist's register applied to something that will not hold still for it.

works.title: City of Saints and Madmen
works.note: expanded the following year, so single-year citations are unsafe

entries.name: Susanna Clarke
entries.description: Two novels, sixteen years apart, both of them singular.
entries.meta: English, born 1959. For Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell, all in 2005: the **Hugo Award for Best Novel**, the **World Fantasy Award for Best Novel**, the Mythopoeic Fantasy Award and a Locus Best First Novel. For Piranesi: the **Women's Prize for Fiction 2021** and a Kitschies Red Tentacle. **Jonathan Strange was Booker longlisted only**, and Piranesi did not win a Hugo. Chronic fatigue syndrome, which she discusses openly, accounts for the gap between the novels.
entries.knownFor: Restoring the folkloric fae completely — bargains honoured to the letter by a creature entirely without malice as he understands it — and then writing a novel of pure benign estrangement.
entries.signature: Period pastiche with a full scholarly apparatus, and a narrator whose comprehension the reader outpaces.

works.title: The Ladies of Grace Adieu and Other Stories
The Wood at Midwinter
works.note: first broadcast on radio two years earlier

entries.name: Helen Oyeyemi
entries.description: Folklore from several traditions at once, refusing to settle into any of them.
entries.meta: British writer, born in Ibadan, Nigeria in 1984 and raised in London from the age of four. Somerset Maugham Award 2010 for White Is for Witching; Granta Best of Young British Novelists 2013; PEN Open Book Award 2017. **White Is for Witching was a Shirley Jackson finalist, not a winner.** No Booker, Women's Prize, World Fantasy or Bram Stoker.
entries.knownFor: Haunted houses that are also arguments about race, belonging and who a place will accept — the Gothic rebuilt on immigration rather than inheritance.
entries.signature: Multiple narrators including the house itself, in prose that withholds the connective tissue and trusts the reader to supply it.

works.title: The Icarus Girl
works.note: written while she was still at school

works.title: What Is Not Yours Is Not Yours

entries.name: Julia Armfield
entries.description: Body horror and grief in the same sentence, written for the literary shelf.
entries.meta: British, born 1990. The White Review Short Story Prize 2018; the Polari Prize 2023 for Our Wives Under the Sea — the main prize rather than the first-book award, and 2023 rather than the 2024 one headline gave it. Two Goodreads Choice Awards in 2022, which are a reader poll and should be labelled as one. **No Bram Stoker, World Fantasy or Shirley Jackson award, and no Booker or Women's Prize recognition.**
entries.knownFor: Our Wives Under the Sea, in which a partner returns from a deep-sea expedition altered in ways the novel never explains and never needs to.
entries.signature: Domestic accommodation of the impossible — the horror measured in what a household quietly starts doing differently.

works.title: Our Wives Under the Sea
works.note: misdated 2021 from proofs and 2023 from the prize

entries.name: Brian Evenson
entries.description: The American weird tale's most uncompromising living practitioner.
entries.meta: American, born 1966. International Horror Guild Award for a collection 2005; Guggenheim Fellowship 2017; a **Shirley Jackson Award for 2019 work and a World Fantasy Award for Best Collection 2020**, both for the same book. **The Open Curtain did not win the 2007 International Horror Guild novel award** — Conrad Williams took it, and Wikipedia's list reads as a win. **No Bram Stoker.** He publishes tie-in fiction as B.K. Evenson and the bibliographies should not be merged. After a complaint to Latter-day Saint leaders over his first book he **resigned** from Brigham Young University in 1995 and left the church in 2000; he was not fired and no excommunication is documented.
entries.knownFor: Prose horror stripped to affectless surface, in which violence is reported without any framing that would let the reader place it.
entries.signature: Flat declarative sentences, unnamed institutions, and characters whose grasp on their own situation is failing without their noticing.

works.title: Song for the Unraveling of the World

entries.name: Stephen Graham Jones
entries.description: The most decorated horror writer working, and the field's most important Indigenous voice.
entries.meta: American, born 1972; an enrolled member of the **Blackfeet** Tribe of the Blackfeet Indian Reservation of Montana — Blackfeet, never Blackfoot. **Five Bram Stokers and three Shirley Jackson Awards**, taking both Novel awards in the same year for The Only Good Indians and both Novel and Long Fiction categories again the following year; a Nebula for Best Novel and a further Stoker in 2025; a British Fantasy August Derleth Award 2024; an International Horror Guild award 2007. **No World Fantasy Award and no Hugo — he has never been a Hugo finalist.** He is not a 2020 debut: more than thirty books preceded the one that made his name.
entries.knownFor: Slasher structure taken entirely seriously as a form, and horror in which Indigenous experience is the vantage rather than the material.
entries.signature: Close, propulsive, syntactically restless voice that stays inside a character's evasions until the evasion breaks.

entries.name: Paul Tremblay
entries.description: Ambiguity sustained to the last page and beyond it.
entries.meta: American, born 1971; indexed by the Horror Writers Association as Paul G. Tremblay. **Three Bram Stokers** — Best Novel for 2015 and 2018 work and a collection for 2019 — plus a Locus Best Horror Novel 2019 and a British Fantasy August Derleth Award 2017. **He has no Shirley Jackson Award and has never been nominated for one**; he has been a Jackson juror, which is the likely source of the error. No World Fantasy Award. On the 2023 adaptation of The Cabin he prefers his own ending and has also called the film's darker in some respects, so "he hated it" flattens the position.
entries.knownFor: Refusing to adjudicate between the supernatural and the psychiatric, and building the machinery — a reality-television edit, a survivor's blog — that keeps the refusal structural.
entries.signature: Mediated testimony, so the reader receives every account already contested by another.

works.title: The Cabin at the End of the World

entries.name: Victor LaValle
entries.description: Argues with a compromised inheritance in its own form.
entries.meta: American, born 1972 in Queens to a Ugandan mother. **World Fantasy Award for Best Novel 2018 for The Changeling, a tie with Fonda Lee's Jade City**; Bram Stokers in the graphic-novel and long-fiction categories; **Shirley Jackson Awards in 2009 and for The Ballad of Black Tom**, plus a British Fantasy Award for it; a further British Fantasy August Derleth Award and a Locus Best Horror Novel 2018; a Whiting Award, an American Book Award and a Guggenheim. **The Ballad of Black Tom won two awards and lost five** — the Hugo, Nebula, World Fantasy, Bram Stoker and Sturgeon — despite being widely described as having swept.
entries.knownFor: The Ballad of Black Tom, which rebuilds a Lovecraft story from inside the racial politics that story depended on — a conflicted response rather than a homage, and one that postdates the retirement of the World Fantasy trophy rather than causing it.
entries.signature: New York rendered with documentary specificity, and a protagonist whose reasonable choices are the trap.

entries.name: Silvia Moreno-Garcia
entries.description: Mexican Gothic relocated the form's inheritance question onto colonial extraction.
entries.meta: Mexican-Canadian, born 1981 in Baja California. **Her one World Fantasy Award is editorial and shared** — Best Anthology 2016, co-edited with Paula R. Stiles. For Mexican Gothic: a British Fantasy August Derleth Award, a Locus Best Horror Novel and an Aurora Award, all 2021, plus an Ignyte and a Sunburst for 2020. **Mexican Gothic has no Bram Stoker, Shirley Jackson, Hugo or Nebula involvement whatever.** Her master's thesis was on eugenics in Lovecraft, and she publishes Innsmouth Free Press — the editorial career is where the World Fantasy Award comes from.
entries.knownFor: Taking the English country-house Gothic and rebuilding it on a Mexican mining fortune, with the house's rot and the colonial extraction as one mechanism.
entries.signature: Genre pastiche executed straight and then turned, with Mexican history supplying the pressure the borrowed form was missing.

entries.name: Grady Hendrix
entries.description: The field's most useful popular historian, who also writes the novels.
entries.meta: American, born in Charleston, South Carolina; **his birth year is not reliably sourced and is not stated here**. **His entire competitive record is one Bram Stoker, for non-fiction**, for Paperbacks from Hell for 2017 work, plus a Lord Ruthven Award 2021. **He has never won an award for a novel** — The Southern Book Club's Guide was not even a finalist and The Final Girl Support Group lost. No Hugo, Nebula, World Fantasy or British Fantasy award.
entries.knownFor: Paperbacks from Hell, which recovered the 1970s and 1980s horror paperback boom as a subject, and a run of novels built on comic premises that turn out to be sincere.
entries.signature: A high-concept premise played for comedy in the first act and for real loss in the third, with period detail doing the work.

works.title: Paperbacks from Hell
works.note: non-fiction, and popular history with an argument rather than a bibliographic authority

works.title: The Southern Book Club's Guide to Slaying Vampires

entries.name: T. Kingfisher
entries.description: Two names, five Hugos, and the most companionable prose in modern horror.
entries.meta: American, born 1977; she/her. Ursula Vernon is the legal name and carries the children's work, the webcomic Digger and the early short fiction; **T. Kingfisher is the disclosed pen name for adult fantasy and horror**. **Five Hugos across both names** — Best Graphic Story 2012 and Best Novelette 2017 as Vernon, Best Short Story 2021, Best Novel 2023 and Best Novella 2024 as Kingfisher — plus a Nebula for Best Short Story as Vernon and the Andre Norton Award 2020. **She has no Nebula in the four main fiction categories as Kingfisher**: Nettle & Bone won the Hugo and lost the Nebula. No World Fantasy, Bram Stoker or Shirley Jackson award.
entries.knownFor: Retellings that are declared rather than coy — Poe's Usher and Machen's "The White People" both named on the tin — and a first-person voice that is funny without deflating the dread.
entries.signature: A practical, self-deprecating narrator noticing wrong things and continuing to be practical about them.

entries.name: Alma Katsu
entries.description: Historical horror researched by someone who spent a career in intelligence.
entries.meta: American, Japanese-American, born 1959 in Fairbanks, Alaska, after roughly twenty-nine years at the National Security Agency and the Central Intelligence Agency. **One major genre award: a Bram Stoker for Long Fiction for 2022 work.** The Hunger, The Deep and The Fervor were all Best Novel finalists and all lost, and she has no Hugo, Nebula, World Fantasy, British Fantasy or Shirley Jackson award. She writes in two lanes under one name, and the Red Widow books are espionage rather than horror.
entries.knownFor: Attaching supernatural horror to documented historical catastrophe — a wagon party, a liner, an incarceration camp — with the research load-bearing rather than decorative.
entries.signature: Multiple period viewpoints assembled around an event the reader already knows the outcome of.

works.title: The Fervor
works.note: set in the Japanese American incarceration camps and drawing on her family's history

entries.name: Nick Cutter
entries.description: A literary novelist's horror pseudonym, and the more extreme of the two.
entries.meta: Canadian, born 1975 or 1976 — the record differs. **Nick Cutter is the horror name of Craig Davidson**, who publishes literary fiction under his own name and used Patrick Lestewka as an earlier horror pseudonym. **No horror genre award, win or nomination, under the Cutter name.** As Davidson: a Scotiabank Giller Prize **shortlisting** in 2013 — not a win — a Rogers Writers' Trust shortlisting and a Canada Reads finalist placing in 2018.
entries.knownFor: The Troop, which took the boys'-adventure survival story and ran a parasite through it with clinical patience.
entries.signature: Interleaved inquest documents that give away the outcome early, so the reading is a matter of watching it arrive.

entries.name: Josh Malerman
entries.description: A rock musician who wrote one of the decade's most-copied premises.
entries.meta: American, born 1975 in Michigan, and the singer and rhythm guitarist of The High Strung. **A World Fantasy Award for Best Novella in 2024, which is his highest honour and is usually omitted**, and a Bram Stoker for Short Fiction for 2020 work. **Bird Box won neither a Stoker nor a Shirley Jackson Award** — it was a finalist for both and lost. Ten Stoker nominations, one win, and no novel win. The two controversies attached to the 2018 Netflix adaptation belong to the film and not to him.
entries.knownFor: Bird Box, whose perception-as-vector rule converted every ordinary action into a procedure.
entries.signature: A single hard rule applied without exception, and prose that stays at the level of what a blindfolded person can actually verify.

works.title: Bird Box
works.note: and not 2018, which is the film and the commonest error about him

entries.name: Catriona Ward
entries.description: The August Derleth Award's only three-time winner.
entries.meta: British, born in Washington, D.C.; **her birth year is not documented in any source consulted and is not stated here**. **Three British Fantasy August Derleth Awards — 2016, 2019 and 2022** — which makes her the only writer to have taken it three times, and the "two-time winner" in most sources is stale. A **Shirley Jackson Award for Best Novel for Little Eve**, and a Sky Arts Times Breakthrough Award 2022. **There is no Shirley Jackson Award for The Last House on Needless Street**, which lost the World Fantasy Best Novel and was never a Stoker finalist.
entries.knownFor: Structural misdirection sustained across a whole novel, with the reveal reorganising rather than merely surprising.
entries.signature: Multiple narrators whose relationship to each other is itself the withheld information.

works.title: Rawblood
works.note: published in the United States as The Girl from Rawblood, one book rather than two

works.title: The Last House on Needless Street

entries.name: Gemma Files
entries.description: Film criticism, folklore and the weird, in the same career.
entries.meta: British-born Canadian, born 1968 in London and in Toronto from the following year; speaks publicly about being autistic. An International Horror Guild award for Best Short Fiction at the turn of the millennium — the work year and ceremony year are both in circulation; a **Shirley Jackson Award for Best Novel 2015** and a Sunburst Award 2016, both for Experimental Film; **two Bram Stokers for fiction collections, 2021 and 2023**. No World Fantasy, Hugo, Nebula or British Fantasy award. Experimental Film and the Hexslinger books came from ChiZine Publications, which collapsed in late 2019 amid documented allegations of unpaid royalties and abuse — she is an affected author, not an accused one.
entries.knownFor: Experimental Film, which ties film-historical research to a mother's exhaustion so that scholarship and ordinary life compete for the protagonist's attention.
entries.signature: Dense, allusive prose carrying real archival detail, with the folkloric material arriving through a researcher's citations.

entries.name: Cassandra Khaw
entries.description: Prose at maximum density, applied to very short books.
entries.meta: Malaysian, born 1984 in Kuala Lumpur; **they/them**. **One competitive win: a Bram Stoker for a fiction collection for 2022 work.** No Hugo, Nebula, World Fantasy, British Fantasy, Shirley Jackson or Locus award, and **nothing at all for Nothing but Blackened Teeth**, which was a finalist five times over. A former games journalist and games writer.
entries.knownFor: Compressed, highly stylised novellas that put Southeast Asian folklore and Lovecraftian material into the same frame.
entries.signature: Ornate, adjective-forward prose deployed at novella length, where the density is a feature rather than a cost.

works.title: The Dead Take the A Train
works.note: written with Richard Kadrey, and frequently miscredited to Khaw alone

entries.name: P. Djèlí Clark
entries.description: Alternate history with the horror made literal.
entries.meta: American, born 1971 in New York City to Trinidadian parents; the full form is Phenderson Djèlí Clark, with grave accents on both e's, and he publishes academic work as Dexter Gabriel. **Three Nebulas** — Best Short Story 2018, Best Novella 2020 for Ring Shout and Best Novel 2021 — plus four Locus Awards, one of which is Best First Novel rather than Best Novel, a British Fantasy Award 2021 and a BSFA 2024. **He has never won a Hugo**, despite six or more finalist placings and publisher copy that routinely says otherwise, and has no World Fantasy Award.
entries.knownFor: Ring Shout, which makes the Klan literal monsters in 1920s Georgia and engages The Birth of a Nation directly rather than by allusion.
entries.signature: Rigorous alternate-historical scaffolding with a vernacular narrating voice, and the fantastic used to make a documented atrocity legible.

entries.name: Rivers Solomon
entries.description: Inherited trauma written as a literal physical condition.
entries.meta: American, born 1989; **fae/faer and they/them**, in that order; non-binary and intersex, and the she/her that persists in pre-2018 coverage is wrong. A Firecracker Award and a Stonewall Honor 2018; a **Lambda Literary Award 2020 for The Deep, shared four ways**; the **Otherwise Award 2022** for Sorrowland — renamed from the Tiptree in 2019, so it should be called an Otherwise. **No Hugo, Nebula, World Fantasy, Bram Stoker, Shirley Jackson or Locus award**; The Deep was a Hugo and Nebula finalist and lost both.
entries.knownFor: Horror in which the body carries a history the character did not choose, written from inside rather than about.
entries.signature: Interiority under sustained physical duress, with the prose refusing the consolation the plot might have offered.

works.title: The Deep
works.note: credited with Daveed Diggs, William Hutson and Jonathan Snipes of clipping., expanding their song and built on Drexciya's mythology, so sole attribution erases two prior layers

entries.name: Guy de Maupassant
entries.description: Wrote the nineteenth century's most precise account of a mind losing its grip.
entries.meta: French, 1850–1893. No awards, and none possible — any genre award credited to him is a modern artefact. He died of general paresis, the tertiary stage of syphilis, in a private clinic at Passy, having attempted his own life the previous winter — not "insane in an asylum", which is the usual formulation.
entries.knownFor: "Le Horla", the definitive first-person record of an intelligent man reasoning his way toward a conclusion he cannot bear, and for a body of supernatural short fiction underrated beside the realist work.
entries.signature: Diary or deposition form, clinical self-observation, and a narrator whose composure is the horror.

works.title: "La Peur"
works.note: a different story from the 1884 one of the same title

works.title: "Le Horla"
works.note: Gil Blas, 26 October, with an expanded diary version the following May, so there are two versions and not three

entries.name: Gaston Leroux
entries.description: A crime reporter who wrote the locked room and the opera house.
entries.meta: French, 1868–1927. No applicable awards. Le Fantôme de l'Opéra sold moderately and reviewed poorly on publication; its fame is a product of the 1925 Chaney film and the 1986 stage musical, and the preface's claim that the story is true is a fictional device rather than a historical assertion.
entries.knownFor: Founding the locked-room mystery in French, and for an opera-house Gothic whose architecture — cellars, lake, trapdoors — does more work than its phantom.
entries.signature: Journalistic apparatus and documentary sourcing wrapped around material that will not survive the scrutiny it invites.

works.title: Le Mystère de la chambre jaune
Le Parfum de la dame en noir

entries.name: Gustav Meyrink
entries.description: Prague as an occult machine, written by a banker with a criminal record.
entries.meta: Austrian, 1868–1932. Born Gustav Meyer; Meyrink was a pen name he took legally in 1917. No awards. He was charged with fraud as a Prague bank manager in 1902, amid allegations that he was directing the bank's affairs in accordance with spiritualism, and was imprisoned for roughly two months and released — the imprisonment and the ruined career are documented, and neither acquittal nor conviction should be asserted.
entries.knownFor: Der Golem, which is not a retelling of the Rabbi Loew legend but a dream-logic novel of the Prague ghetto in which identity itself is the unstable element.
entries.signature: Hallucinatory urban topography and a narrator who may be inhabiting someone else's memories.

works.title: Der heiße Soldat und andere Geschichten
Der Golem
works.note: serialised 1913 into 1914 with the book in 1915, so give both and never 1914 or 1917 alone

entries.name: Hanns Heinz Ewers
entries.description: A significant weird writer whose politics are not a footnote.
entries.meta: German, 1871–1943. No awards. **He joined the Nazi Party voluntarily on 1 November 1931**, membership number 659,057, and wrote the party's authorised life of Horst Wessel in 1932 — a book that satisfied nobody, since it retained Wessel's relationship with a former prostitute and lacked the expected antisemitic agitation. From 1934, after the Röhm purge, his work was systematically suppressed until almost the whole output was blacklisted. **He was not, on the record, expelled from the party**, his books were not among those burned in May 1933 — he was a party author in good standing that year — and he died isolated in 1943 having never repudiated any of it.
entries.knownFor: Alraune and "Die Spinne", which pair genuine formal invention with a decadent cruelty that the later politics make impossible to read innocently.
entries.signature: Erotic transgression and scientific rationalism collapsed into each other, with an aesthete narrator who declines to be appalled.

entries.name: Jean Ray
entries.description: Belgium's weird master, with a biography he largely invented.
entries.meta: Belgian, 1887–1964. Legal name Raymundus Joannes de Kremer; he published French fantastic fiction as Jean Ray and roughly half his output, in Flemish, as John Flanders. No applicable awards. **He was convicted of embezzlement in 1926 and served roughly two years of a six-year sentence**, which accounts for the gap in his bibliography between 1925 and 1932. The bootlegger and lion-tamer stories attached to him are his own invention.
entries.knownFor: Malpertuis, a house-as-cosmos novel whose reveal reorganises everything preceding it, and a body of maritime and urban weird tales in a register no one else was writing.
entries.signature: Flemish port cities and enclosed houses rendered with claustrophobic specificity, and a plot that turns out to be a container.

works.title: Malpertuis
works.note: and not 1962 or 1971, which are a reissue and the Kümel film

entries.name: Horacio Quiroga
entries.description: The Spanish-language Poe, working from the Misiones jungle.
entries.meta: Uruguayan, 1878–1937, by suicide. No applicable awards. The documented deaths around him should be listed flatly and without editorialising: his father's accidental shooting, his stepfather's suicide in 1896, his first wife's suicide in 1915, and the suicides of two of his children after his own death. **He accidentally shot his friend Federico Ferrando in 1901 or 1902**, while examining a pistol before a duel that Ferrando was to fight — he fought no duel and killed no one deliberately, and the sensationalised versions of this are wrong.
entries.knownFor: Cuentos de amor, de locura y de muerte, and for a body of jungle horror in which the environment is a working antagonist rather than a setting.
entries.signature: Compressed, unadorned realism about death, with the natural world's indifference doing what a monster would do elsewhere.

works.title: Cuentos de amor, de locura y de muerte

entries.name: Julio Cortázar
entries.description: The fantastic as an intrusion into a completely ordinary afternoon.
entries.meta: Argentine, born in Belgium, 1914–1984. Early work as Julio Denis. Prix Médicis étranger 1974 — **no Nobel Prize and no genre award of any kind.** He took French citizenship in 1981 while retaining Argentine nationality. He is a writer of the fantastic rather than a horror writer, a distinction he cared about, and the pack includes him because the technique transfers exactly.
entries.knownFor: Stories in which one impossible fact is introduced without comment and the narrative simply proceeds — the flat register that ambiguous horror has been borrowing ever since.
entries.signature: A conversational middle-class narrator reporting the intolerable in the tone of a minor inconvenience.

works.title: Final del juego
works.note: nine stories, expanded to eighteen in 1964

entries.name: Koji Suzuki
entries.description: Wrote the curse that made transmission a modern horror mechanism.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1957–2026; **he died on 8 May 2026 and is frequently still described as living.** Shared in the Japan Fantasy Novel Award in 1990; the Yoshikawa Eiji Prize for New Writers 1996; a **Shirley Jackson Award for Best Novel for 2012 work**, the first Japanese winner of that category; a Bram Stoker Lifetime Achievement whose year is unresolved. No World Fantasy Award, no Hugo.
entries.knownFor: Ring, whose transmissible curse and hard deadline gave the genre its most-copied structure — and whose mechanism in the novel is a viral and psychic agent rather than anything that crawls out of a television, which is Nakata's 1998 invention.
entries.signature: Procedural investigation under a stated clock, with the sequel reframing the whole apparatus as science fiction.

works.title: Ring
works.note: リング, and not 1998, which is the film, or 2004, which is the English translation

entries.name: Otsuichi
entries.description: Published at seventeen and has been quietly ahead of the field since.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1978. Pen name of Hirotaka Adachi, the name under which he directs films, and he also writes as three further pen names. The 6th Jump Novel Award 1996 and the 3rd Honkaku Mystery Award, fiction division, 2003 — **no Japan Horror Novel Award, no Naoki and no Akutagawa.** Born in October 1978 and awarded in 1996, he was **seventeen** at publication, not sixteen as usually reported.
entries.knownFor: Cruel, formally clean short fiction that alternates between a mode readers call "black Otsuichi" and a gentler one, sometimes inside the same collection.
entries.signature: A withheld structural fact — who is narrating, or when — that reorganises a story of a few thousand words in its last lines.

works.title: Goth
works.note: a mystery novel, which is why it won a mystery award

entries.name: Bora Chung
entries.description: Slavic literature scholarship turned into Korean genre-refusing fiction.
entries.meta: Korean, born 1976. The Yonsei Literature Prize 1998, a Digital Writers' Award distinction 2008, and a Korean SF Award 2014. **She was shortlisted for the International Booker in 2022 and did not win it** — Geetanjali Shree did. No World Fantasy, Shirley Jackson or Bram Stoker award. She was not a debut in 2022: she had been publishing in Korean since 2010 and Cursed Bunny was her fifth book.
entries.knownFor: Cursed Bunny, whose stories move between folk horror, body horror and absurdist fable without settling, and whose politics are economic rather than supernatural.
entries.signature: Fable structure with industrial and bodily specificity, and a moral that arrives without comfort.

works.title: Cursed Bunny
works.note: 저주토끼, and not 2021 or 2022, which are the UK and US editions

entries.name: Yoko Ogawa
entries.description: Quiet horror at literary-prize level, and the field's most damaging misdating.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1962. The **Akutagawa Prize in January 1991**, plus the Yomiuri, Izumi Kyōka, Tanizaki, Noma and Kikuchi Kan prizes and a Medal with Purple Ribbon in 2021; a **Shirley Jackson Award 2008** and an American Book Award 2020. International Booker **shortlisted only** in 2020, and a National Book Award finalist in 2019. No Naoki Prize, no World Fantasy, no Hugo, no Bram Stoker.
entries.knownFor: Fiction in which cruelty is administered in a calm, almost clerical register, and in which institutions do the frightening work.
entries.signature: Precise, cool observation of small physical details, with the violence stated once and not returned to.

works.title: The Memory Police
works.note: 密やかな結晶, and dating it to 2019, the translation year, is the most damaging error available, since the novel predates by twenty-five years the politics it is read as allegorising

works.title: The Ring Finger
works.note: 薬指の標本, which is not Hotel Iris

entries.name: Samanta Schweblin
entries.description: Dread built entirely out of a conversation between two people.
entries.meta: Argentine, born 1978. The Premio Casa de las Américas 2008, the Premio Juan Rulfo 2012, a **Shirley Jackson Award for Best Novella for 2017 work**, and the **National Book Award for Translated Literature in 2022**, which is the win most often omitted. **International Booker: one shortlisting in 2017 and two longlistings, and never a win** — publisher copy frequently implies otherwise.
entries.knownFor: Fever Dream, a novella conducted as a dialogue in which the reader assembles a catastrophe from what one speaker refuses to let the other skip.
entries.signature: Withheld context, an interrogating second voice, and an ecological horror that is never named as such.

works.title: Distancia de rescate
works.note: the translation lag is the trap here, since the English appeared in 2017

entries.name: Mariana Enriquez
entries.description: Argentine horror in which the dictatorship's disappeared are the haunting.
entries.meta: Argentine, born 1973. The Premio Ciutat de Barcelona 2017, the **Premio Herralde de Novela 2019**, and the Premio Iberoamericano de Letras José Donoso 2024. **She was shortlisted for the International Booker in 2021 and did not win.** No World Fantasy, Bram Stoker or Shirley Jackson award. Things We Lost in the Fire was not her debut — she had been publishing for over twenty years.
entries.knownFor: Making Argentina's political violence and its ghosts the same material, with the supernatural offering no consolation and no explanation.
entries.signature: Contemporary Buenos Aires rendered with journalistic exactness, and horror that arrives through poverty, addiction and disappearance rather than beside them.

works.title: Los peligros de fumar en la cama
works.note: and not 2017 or 2021, which are a reissue and the translation

works.title: Las cosas que perdimos en el fuego
Un lugar soleado para gente sombría

entries.name: James Whale
entries.description: Gave Universal horror its wit, and got no award for any of it.
entries.meta: English, 1889–1957, by suicide. **No Academy Award nomination of any kind** — the Adapted Screenplay Oscar associated with Gods and Monsters belongs to Christopher Bram's source novel and its screenwriter, not to Whale. He lived openly as a gay man, but "driven out of Hollywood for being gay" is unsupportable: the career decline follows a 1937 production. His partner suppressed the suicide note for decades, which is why older sources record the drowning as accidental.
entries.knownFor: Bride of Frankenstein, which is the rare sequel that improves on its original by introducing camp, pathos and open theatricality to a form that had been solemn.
entries.signature: Expressionist staging cut with genuine comedy, and a creature given more dignity than anyone around it.

entries.name: Val Lewton
entries.description: Proved that constraint produces better horror than money does, and directed nothing.
entries.meta: Russian-born American, 1904–1951, born Vladimir Ivanovich Leventon. No Academy Award nomination or win in any capacity. **He directed none of his films.** He ran RKO's B-horror unit from 1942 to 1946 under fixed constraints — titles handed down by management, budgets around $150,000, running times under seventy-five minutes — and rewrote every screenplay uncredited, twice taking a writing credit as Carlos Keith.
entries.knownFor: The unit that invented modern suggestion horror, including the bus sequence that named the false scare, on budgets that made showing anything impossible.
entries.signature: Shadow, sound and off-screen space substituting for a monster, with literate scripts and unusual sympathy for their protagonists.

works.title: The Curse of the Cat People
works.note: producer, directed by Gunther von Fritsch and then Robert Wise

entries.name: Alfred Hitchcock
entries.description: Five Best Director nominations and no competitive Oscar.
entries.meta: English, 1899–1980, born in Leytonstone; a US citizen from 1955 who retained British nationality. **He never won a competitive Academy Award**, losing all five Best Director nominations, and Rebecca's Best Picture statuette went to its producer David O. Selznick. He received the honorary Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award in 1968, a DGA Lifetime Achievement the same year, a BAFTA Fellowship 1971, the AFI Life Achievement 1979 and a KBE in the 1980 New Year Honours. Tippi Hedren's allegations of harassment and career sabotage during The Birds and Marnie are her own account, set out in her 2016 memoir, and are disputed by others present.
entries.knownFor: Psycho, which spent its star at the midpoint and reassigned the protagonist role to her killer — the structural manoeuvre that made the modern horror twist possible.
entries.signature: Audience information managed as the primary tool, with suspense generated by what the viewer knows and the character does not.

entries.name: Roman Polanski
entries.description: A major body of work and a criminal case that no reference can omit.
entries.meta: Dual French and Polish citizen, born 1933. **Academy Award for Best Director for The Pianist at the 75th ceremony in March 2003**, which he did not attend and cannot collect in the United States; the Palme d'Or 2002; the Golden Bear 1966; three BAFTAs, ten Césars and two Golden Globes. He was **expelled from the Academy in May 2018, and the 2003 award stands and was not rescinded.** On 10 March 1977, aged 43, he engaged in sexual acts with a thirteen-year-old girl, Samantha Gailey, having given her champagne and part of a Quaalude. He was charged on 24 March 1977 with six felony counts including rape by use of drugs and lewd and lascivious act upon a child under fourteen. **In August 1977 he pleaded guilty in open court to one count of unlawful sexual intercourse with a minor**, the other five dismissed under the bargain; he served forty-two days of a ninety-day diagnostic study; and on **1 February 1978, believing the judge intended to renege on the plea agreement, he fled the United States on the eve of sentencing.** He has never been sentenced, remains a fugitive, and the warrant stands; extradition was refused by Switzerland in 2010 and Poland in 2016. Later allegations by five other women, all denied, have produced no conviction, and he was acquitted in a French defamation action brought over one of them in May 2024. He was not convicted of rape, was not acquitted, and the charges were not dropped — there was no trial. His wife Sharon Tate, eight and a half months pregnant, was murdered with four others in August 1969, which is context and not mitigation.
entries.knownFor: The Apartment Trilogy, which built paranoid horror out of tenancy, neighbours and architecture, and is the direct ancestor of domestic and home-invasion horror.
entries.signature: A protagonist isolated inside a building whose other occupants may or may not be organised against them, with the ambiguity never resolved in the protagonist's favour.

works.title: Rosemary's Baby
works.note: director and screenwriter, from Ira Levin's novel

entries.name: George A. Romero
entries.description: Invented a monster, lost the copyright, and kept working anyway.
entries.meta: American and, from 2009, Canadian, 1940–2017. **Bram Stoker Lifetime Achievement 2015** and a handful of genre honours — **no Academy Award and no major festival prize**, and the honours he holds are lifetime rather than craft awards. The distributor's title change to Night of the Living Dead dropped the copyright notice from the new title cards, forfeiting copyright under the law then in force — **the error was the distributor's, not Romero's.** The film itself never says "zombies"; it says ghouls.
entries.knownFor: Establishing the modern zombie as a crowd rather than a character, and using each film in the sequence to make a different argument about the living.
entries.signature: Regional, low-budget realism and a documentary hand-held eye, with the social argument carried by who in the room is listened to.

works.title: Night of the Living Dead
works.note: director, co-writer with John A. Russo, photographer and editor

works.title: Creepshow
works.note: director only, written by Stephen King

entries.name: John Carpenter
entries.description: Composer, editor, writer and director, and never an Academy Award.
entries.meta: American, born 1948. A Saturn Award 1998, the **Carrosse d'Or at Cannes in 2019** — a directors'-guild honour in the Directors' Fortnight rather than a competition prize — a career award from the Los Angeles critics in 2024 and a Walk of Fame star in 2025. **He has never won an Academy Award**, and there is no Venice Golden Lion for him. The Oscar-winning 1970 short he worked on was directed by James R. Rokos and its statuette went to its producer; Carpenter co-wrote, edited and scored it and received nothing.
entries.knownFor: Halloween, which codified the slasher, and The Thing, whose assimilation rule remains the genre's best-designed threat.
entries.signature: Widescreen composition with the frame's negative space weaponised, and his own synthesiser scores doing the work an orchestra would do elsewhere.

works.title: Halloween
works.note: director, co-writer with Debra Hill, composer

works.title: The Thing
works.note: director only, scored by Ennio Morricone

works.title: Christine
works.note: director and composer, written by Bill Phillips

entries.name: Wes Craven
entries.description: Reinvented the slasher twice, ten years apart.
entries.meta: American, 1939–2015. Genre career honours and a Gérardmer grand prize in 1997 — **no Academy Award, no nomination and no major festival prize.** He directed pornographic films in the early to mid 1970s under pseudonyms and acknowledged it, and omitting that is the error rather than including it. **He directed no Nightmare sequel except New Nightmare**, and he directed the Scream films while writing none of them. His account of the Nightmare premise is that it came from newspaper reports of Hmong and Laotian refugees dying in their sleep — not that the film is based on a true story.
entries.knownFor: A Nightmare on Elm Street, which made the dream a jurisdiction, and two separate metafictional turns that revived the form after it had exhausted itself.
entries.signature: Rules stated to the audience and then interrogated, with the film's own conventions treated as the material.

works.title: The Last House on the Left
A Nightmare on Elm Street 3
works.note: co-writer and executive producer, not director

works.title: Scream
works.note: director only, written by Kevin Williamson

entries.name: Tobe Hooper
entries.description: One film that changed the register of American horror permanently.
entries.meta: American, 1943–2017. A state film hall-of-fame induction in 2003 — **no Academy Award, no nomination and no major festival prize, so he should not be called award-winning.** On Poltergeist the directing credit is his and **no arbitration ever removed or altered it**, though authorship is disputed on the record: Spielberg undercut it in the press in May 1982, and a Directors Guild arbitrator ordered the studio to pay Hooper over the size of his credit in the trailer. **The Texas Chain Saw Massacre is not based on a true story** — it borrows skin masks and bone furniture from Ed Gein, a Wisconsin grave robber with two known killings and no chainsaw.
entries.knownFor: A film whose documentary grain, sound design and refusal of a score made grindhouse material feel like recovered evidence.
entries.signature: Heat, noise and exhaustion as the primary texture, with far less on-screen gore than its reputation asserts.

works.title: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre
works.note: director, co-writer with Kim Henkel, co-composer

works.title: Salem's Lot
works.note: director, a two-part television miniseries rather than a feature

works.title: Poltergeist
works.note: credited director, written by Spielberg with Michael Grais and Mark Victor

entries.name: David Cronenberg
entries.description: Made the body the site and stayed there for fifty years.
entries.meta: Canadian, born 1943. A **Special Jury Prize at Cannes in 1996**, created specially by that jury and not the Palme d'Or; the Carrosse d'Or 2006; four Canadian best-director awards; a Silver Bear 1999; the **Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at Venice in 2018**; Companion of the Order of Canada. **He has never won the Palme d'Or and has never been nominated for an Academy Award**, and he did not win an Oscar for The Fly — that film's makeup award went to Chris Walas and Stephan Dupuis.
entries.knownFor: Founding body horror as a coherent mode, and for treating transformation as a clinical process rather than a spectacle.
entries.signature: Medical calm applied to the impossible, with technology and flesh converging and no character quite alarmed enough.

works.title: The Fly
works.note: director and co-writer with Charles Edward Pogue

entries.name: Dario Argento
entries.description: Style as the argument, at the cost of everything else.
entries.meta: Italian, born 1940. **His award record could not be verified as a set from any official listing**, so this card claims only career honours in Italy and states that he has no Academy Award and no major competitive festival prize. **Daria Nicolodi is credited as co-writer of Suspiria** and claimed substantial authorship of it, which Argento has at times minimised — the credit is stated here and the dispute is not adjudicated. The Three Mothers films were not planned as a trilogy from the outset.
entries.knownFor: Suspiria, whose colour, architecture and score subordinate causality entirely to sensation, and for the giallo's transfer into supernatural horror.
entries.signature: Saturated primary colour, elaborate camera movement and set-piece murders staged as choreography.

works.title: Once Upon a Time in the West
works.note: story credit only, with Bernardo Bertolucci

works.title: The Bird with the Crystal Plumage
Dawn of the Dead
works.note: producer, responsible for European financing and the European cut, and he neither directed nor co-directed it

works.title: Demons
works.note: writer and producer, directed by Lamberto Bava

entries.name: Kiyoshi Kurosawa
entries.description: The most formally serious director working in horror, and no relation to Akira.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1955; **no relation to Akira Kurosawa**, which is worth saying explicitly. **Un Certain Regard** prizes at Cannes in 2008 and 2015 — the section matters, since these are not Competition prizes — a best-director award at Rome in 2013, and the **Silver Lion for Best Direction at Venice in 2020**. He has never won the Palme d'Or, the Grand Prix or Competition Best Director. He directed neither Ju-On nor Ringu, and the 2006 American remake of Pulse is not his.
entries.knownFor: Pulse, which found in early network isolation an apocalypse of loneliness, and Cure, which made a detective procedural into a study of suggestion.
entries.signature: Long static takes, figures placed at the edges of wide frames, and dread that accumulates from composition rather than incident.

entries.name: Guillermo del Toro
entries.description: The genre's most decorated director, and not for the film you would guess.
entries.meta: Mexican, born 1964. **Best Picture as producer and Best Director at the 90th Academy Awards in March 2018 for The Shape of Water, and Best Animated Feature at the 95th in 2023** — the first person to win all three — plus the **Golden Lion at Venice in 2017**, three BAFTAs and two Golden Globes. **He personally won nothing for Pan's Labyrinth**: its three Oscars went to its art directors, its cinematographer and its makeup team, and del Toro was nominated for Original Screenplay and lost. His father was kidnapped in Guadalajara in 1997 and held for seventy-two days, after which del Toro left Mexico and has said he will not live there again.
entries.knownFor: Fusing fairy tale with historical atrocity so that the monsters and the fascism are the same argument, and for a creature design practice rooted in physical effects.
entries.signature: Amber and teal, practical creatures with real weight, and a child protagonist whose moral clarity is the film's measure.

entries.name: Jordan Peele
entries.description: Made social horror commercially unignorable in a single film.
entries.meta: American, born 1979. **Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay for Get Out at the 90th ceremony in March 2018**, the first Black winner of that category, plus a Writers Guild award, a Directors Guild first-feature award and a Primetime Emmy in 2016 for sketch comedy. **Get Out did not win Best Picture** — it won one Oscar, for the screenplay, and he lost Best Director at the same ceremony. **He was the fifth Black Best Director nominee, not the first.** He did not direct Candyman, which Nia DaCosta directed from a script he co-wrote.
entries.knownFor: Get Out, whose antagonists are uniformly polite and entirely unnegotiable, and which put the Black protagonist's accurate perception at the centre of the American horror film.
entries.signature: Accumulating social wrongness carried by tone and performance, with the reveal recontextualising a hundred small courtesies.

works.title: Candyman
works.note: co-writer and producer, directed by Nia DaCosta

entries.name: Junji Ito
entries.description: The most influential horror artist alive, and unrecognised at home.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1963. **Four Eisner Awards, all between 2019 and 2022, and all for English-language editions**, plus induction into the Eisner Hall of Fame in 2025 and an Inkpot Award 2023. **He holds no Japanese manga industry award of any kind** — no Shogakukan, no Kodansha, no Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize — and the 1987 prize often credited to him was an honourable mention. Uzumaki was Eisner-nominated in 2003 and 2009 and won neither. He worked for more than thirty years before his first Eisner, so no framing should imply decades of anglophone recognition.
entries.knownFor: Uzumaki, which takes a single geometric shape and treats it as contagious until it has propagated through hair, pottery, bodies and finally a town's architecture.
entries.signature: Immaculate fine-line rendering of ordinary faces and rooms, deformed by one rule applied without exception, on a fixed panel grid that makes the deformation measurable.

entries.name: Kazuo Umezz
entries.description: Horror manga's founder, working forty years before the field caught up.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1936–2024; **he died on 28 October 2024 of gastric cancer**, with the announcement following in early November, which several outlets misreport as the date. **Umezz is his own official romanisation**, used by his foundation and exhibitions, though Umezu is standard Hepburn. The 20th Shogakukan Manga Award in 1974 in the shōnen category — correctly Shogakukan's, since the title ran in that publisher's magazine — the Angoulême Heritage Prize 2018, and a Japanese Agency for Cultural Affairs award 2019. **No Kodansha or Tezuka prize, and he is not in the Eisner Hall of Fame.** He stopped serialising in 1995 because of a repetitive-strain injury to his drawing arm rather than age, and did not stay retired: a new work was announced in 2021 after twenty-seven years, executed as 101 acrylic paintings.
entries.knownFor: The Drifting Classroom, which put a whole primary school into a wasteland and let the children's social order collapse at length and without mercy.
entries.signature: Children rendered with genuine tenderness and then subjected to sustained adult catastrophe, in a stark high-contrast line.

entries.name: Hideshi Hino
entries.description: Ero-guro made personal, by a man born in occupied Manchuria.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1946 in Qiqihar, in Japanese-occupied Manchuria, to settler parents and repatriated after the war. **No award of any kind could be verified** — no Shogakukan, Kodansha, Tezuka, Eisner or Harvey — so he should not be described as award-winning. He directed and wrote **two** entries in the Guinea Pig film series and neither created the series nor directed any other entry. The Charlie Sheen story attached to that series is partly documented and partly contested, and approaching urban legend; on a separate and more serious matter, Hino has stated that the tape found in a notorious offender's collection was a different entry and not his.
entries.knownFor: Autobiographical grotesque — Panorama of Hell narrates its own painter — in which the horror is inseparable from postwar Japanese poverty and displacement.
entries.signature: Wide-eyed, almost childlike cartooning applied to viscera, with a first-person narrator implicating himself.

entries.name: Alan Moore
entries.description: The medium's most decorated writer, and its most consistent critic of its business.
entries.meta: English, born 1953. **Nine Eisner Awards for Best Writer, a Guinness world record**, alongside a further dozen Eisners across album, series and anthology categories; **Eisner Hall of Fame class of 2014**; a **Hugo Award in 1988** in a one-off category; seven Harvey Awards for Best Writer; three Bram Stokers including Lifetime Achievement; an International Horror Guild award 1996. **He has never won a World Fantasy Award.** **He does not own Watchmen and never has** — the rights were to revert once the work went out of print, and it has been kept continuously in print — and he has not disowned the comic itself, only the adaptations, prequels and continued exploitation, requiring since 2005 that his name be removed and his share paid to the artists.
entries.knownFor: Bringing formal rigour and adult moral seriousness to mainstream comics, and for a body of horror work — a swamp monster reconceived, a Ripper novel, a late Lovecraftian sequence — that is consistently underrated beside the superhero material.
entries.signature: Nine-panel discipline, dense caption-and-image counterpoint, and research so heavy the apparatus becomes part of the text.

entries.name: Neil Gaiman
entries.description: An enormous award record, and allegations that a reference work cannot omit.
entries.meta: English, born 1960. **Five Hugos, two Nebulas, five Bram Stokers, at least four Eisners with Hall of Fame induction in 2021, the Newbery Medal 2009, and a World Fantasy Award in 1991 for a Sandman issue — the only comic ever to win one.** More than twenty Locus Awards. No Academy Award; the Coraline nomination belongs to Henry Selick's film. **On the allegations, every element is an allegation, attributed and dated, and he denies non-consensual conduct; there has been no criminal charge and no finding of civil liability.** In July 2024 Tortoise Media reported allegations of sexual misconduct by women in relationships or working arrangements with him. In January 2025 New York magazine published an investigation by Lila Shapiro reporting allegations from eight women, including assault and coercive conduct, and reporting on non-disclosure agreements. He responded the following day denying he had ever engaged in non-consensual sexual activity while acknowledging he "was not always the person I should have been", and in 2026 characterised the allegations as a smear campaign. Three civil suits filed in 2025 by a former nanny alleging rape, sexual assault and human-trafficking violations were **all dismissed** — one voluntarily dropped, and two dismissed on the ground that the case must be pursued in New Zealand, which is a forum ruling and not a ruling on the merits.
entries.knownFor: The Sandman, which made an ongoing comic a literary object, and a body of prose in which folklore is treated as a functioning legal system.
entries.signature: Mythic register carried in plain conversational sentences, with the rules of the other world stated as domestic fact.

entries.name: Emily Carroll
entries.description: Webcomics horror that used the scroll as a structural device before anyone else.
entries.meta: Canadian, born 1983 — Canadian rather than American, which is frequently misstated. **She now publishes as E.M.
