Carroll**, and the earlier books are correctly credited to Emily Carroll. **Two Eisner Awards in 2015**, one for a short story and one in the reprint category; an Ignatz 2015, a British Fantasy Award 2015, Joe Shuster and Doug Wright awards, a Lambda 2024 and a Los Angeles Times Book Prize 2024. No Shirley Jackson, Bram Stoker or Hugo.
entries.knownFor: "His Face All Red" and Through the Woods, which brought folk-tale cruelty into comics with an economy the form had not previously managed.
entries.signature: Flat, saturated colour with negative space used as dread, and page architecture that makes the reader scroll or turn into the reveal.

works.title: Through the Woods
works.note: a collection of previously published webcomics, which is why its Eisner is in the reprint category

works.title: When I Arrived at the Castle

entries.name: Joe Hill
entries.description: Published anonymously to be judged on the work, and was.
entries.meta: American, born Joseph Hillström King, 1972, son of Stephen and Tabitha King. **The pseudonym was publicly identified in 2007, after the first Bram Stoker wins** — which is the point, since the early awards were won without the name. **Four Bram Stokers from eleven nominations**, including Superior Achievement in a First Novel; an **Eisner Award for Best Writer in 2011**, which is his rather than the book's; a **World Fantasy Award for Best Novella in 2006**; five British Fantasy Awards, an International Horror Guild award and two Locus Awards. **Three Shirley Jackson nominations and no wins, and no Hugo.** He is not to be confused with his brother Owen King.
entries.knownFor: Locke & Key, whose locked doors are each a specific rule-bound capability, and a body of prose horror with an unusual gift for premise.
entries.signature: A high-concept object or rule established early and then followed with complete logical patience.

works.title: 20th Century Ghosts
works.note: PS Publishing, and not the 2007 US edition

entries.name: Scott Snyder
entries.description: Brought a prose writer's structure to mainstream horror comics.
entries.meta: American, born 1976. **Three Eisner Awards** — Best New Series 2011, Best Limited Series 2014 and Best Digital Comic 2023 — plus four Harvey Awards, an Eagle Award 2012 and an Inkpot 2019. **No Bram Stoker and no Shirley Jackson.** **Stephen King co-wrote American Vampire for its first five issues only**, contributing the period backup strip while Snyder wrote the main strip throughout and everything after — a collaboration routinely overstated. Wytches remains unfinished.
entries.knownFor: American Vampire, which built a new vampire biology and ran it across a century of American history, and Wytches, which put folk horror into a suburban family.
entries.signature: Long-arc structure with a prose novelist's patience, and a willingness to let a horror premise carry genuine sentiment.

works.title: Voodoo Heart
works.note: a prose collection, his debut and the thing most often omitted

entries.name: Jeff Lemire
entries.description: Writes and draws, and the record keeps forgetting the second half.
entries.meta: Canadian, born 1976. **Three Eisner Awards** — Best New Series in 2017 and 2019 and Best Digital Comic in 2022 — plus a Xeric grant, an Alex Award 2008, two Joe Shuster Awards and two Doug Wright Awards. **He has no Eisner for Essex County**, which is the one most often assumed. He is a cartoonist as well as a writer: several major works are written **and drawn** by him, while others are written only, and conflating the two misdescribes the career.
entries.knownFor: Gideon Falls, whose two protagonists' panel languages are formally incompatible until they are not, and a body of rural Ontario work that is closer to Southern Gothic than to anything else in comics.
entries.signature: Scratchy, unglamorous linework and watercolour, with small-town Canadian settings given the weight American comics reserve for cities.

works.title: Sweet Tooth
works.note: written and drawn, and the comic rather than the later television series

entries.name: Shinji Mikami
entries.description: Built survival horror's commercial template and then rebuilt it.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1965. **No personal industry award could be verified** — no BAFTA Fellowship, no Game Developers Choice lifetime or pioneer award, no academy hall-of-fame induction — and Resident Evil 4's game-of-the-year prizes belong to the game rather than to him. **He did not create Resident Evil alone**: it was heavily indebted to Capcom's own Sweet Home of 1989, and the 1996 team included a planner and a producer whose contributions are documented.
entries.knownFor: Establishing inventory scarcity, fixed cameras and the save-token economy as horror's tension mechanics, and then discarding all three for an over-the-shoulder design that the whole medium copied.
entries.signature: Deliberately awkward control and constrained resources as deliberate design rather than as limitation.

works.title: Ghostwire: Tokyo
works.note: executive producer only, directed by Kenji Kimura

entries.name: Keiichiro Toyama
entries.description: Directed Silent Hill, left immediately, and had no part in what followed.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1970. Two awards for a later game in 2012, **both to the game rather than to him personally**, and no verified individual honour. **He left Konami and Team Silent in 1999, immediately after the first game, and had no involvement in Silent Hill 2 or anything after it** — that game was directed and written by other people, and attributing the series to him is a common and consequential error.
entries.knownFor: Silent Hill, which replaced combat competence with psychological terrain and turned a hardware draw-distance limit into the fog that became the series' identity.
entries.signature: Physical environments that externalise a character's condition, with the transformation rules unstated.

entries.name: Hidetaka Miyazaki
entries.description: Not a horror designer, with one exception that matters.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1974; president of FromSoftware since 2014. **He is not related to Hayao Miyazaki.** A Japanese industry special award 2022 and a government award the same year. **He has not received a BAFTA Fellowship** — the 2025 award went to a composer — **and holds no Game Developers Choice lifetime award**, and Elden Ring's game-of-the-year honours went to the studio and publisher rather than to him. He did not direct two of the games most often credited to him, having supervised one and handed another to a successor.
entries.knownFor: Bloodborne, which is his strongest claim on horror and takes cosmic horror's epistemic damage and makes comprehension a stat.
entries.signature: Environmental storytelling delivered through item descriptions and level geography, with the plot never narrated.

entries.name: Thomas Grip
entries.description: Removed the weapon and proved the form survived without one.
entries.meta: Swedish; **his birth year is not documented and is not stated here.** Co-founder and creative director of Frictional Games, founded in 2007. **No personal award** — Amnesia's three 2011 independent-games prizes went to the game and the studio. The writer on Amnesia was Mikael Hedberg, with Grip co-credited, and the 2013 sequel was developed and written by another studio entirely, with Frictional only publishing it.
entries.knownFor: Amnesia: The Dark Descent, which removed combat altogether and made looking at the threat a mechanical cost — the design that defined a decade of independent horror and of the streaming culture around it.
entries.signature: Physics-driven interaction with objects, a sanity system tied to darkness and sight, and no means of fighting back.

works.title: Amnesia: The Dark Descent
works.note: designer and programmer, written by Mikael Hedberg

entries.name: Sandy Petersen
entries.description: Gave cosmic horror a rule set that fed back into prose for forty years.
entries.meta: American, born 1955. **An Origins Award in 1982 for the 1981 game**, and — a distinction worth keeping straight — **induction into the Origins Hall of Fame in 1990 as a person, with the game itself inducted separately in 1995**; a favourite-designer award 1994 and an ENnie Hall of Fame entry for the game in 2024. He built the game on an existing engine rather than from scratch, and **he did not found Chaosium**, which Greg Stafford did in 1975.
entries.knownFor: The sanity mechanic — making comprehension itself the resource that depletes — which is the single most transferable design idea horror has produced in the last half-century.
entries.signature: Investigation rather than combat as the core activity, with player knowledge as the thing at risk.

works.title: Doom
works.note: every level of the third episode

entries.name: Farnsworth Wright
entries.description: Edited the magazine that made the field, and rejected some of its best work.
entries.meta: American, 1888–1940, dying in June 1940. No awards. He edited Weird Tales from November 1924 to March 1940, across 179 issues. **He did not found the magazine**, which began in 1923 under a different editor. His documented rejections include At the Mountains of Madness and The Shadow over Innsmouth — and he rejected "The Call of Cthulhu" and then **published it in February 1928**, after Donald Wandrei told him, untruthfully, that Lovecraft might place it elsewhere.
entries.knownFor: Printing most of Lovecraft's magazine work, Howard's Conan debut, Clark Ashton Smith, Bloch, Kuttner and C.L. Moore, and launching the cover artists who gave the pulps their visual identity.
entries.signature: A taste for the genuinely strange over the merely frightening, exercised inconsistently and under severe commercial pressure.

entries.name: Donald Wandrei
entries.description: Co-founded the press that saved the canon, and refused its highest honour.
entries.meta: American, 1908–1987; his brother Howard was also a writer and the two are frequently merged. **He was awarded a World Fantasy Life Achievement award in 1984 and refused it** — because he considered Gahan Wilson's Lovecraft bust a demeaning caricature of a man he had personally known, which is a different and effectively opposite motive from the campaign that retired that same trophy three decades later. No Hugo, Bram Stoker or British Fantasy Award. He **co-founded Arkham House with August Derleth in 1939** and co-edited Lovecraft's selected letters.
entries.knownFor: The preservation work, and for a body of cosmic fiction and poetry of his own that the founder's role has largely obscured.
entries.signature: Astronomical scale and a poet's diction applied to pulp material.

entries.name: Ellen Datlow
entries.description: The most decorated editor in the field's history, by a wide margin.
entries.meta: American, born 1949. Fiction editor of Omni from 1981 to 1998 — fiction editor rather than editor-in-chief. **Ten World Fantasy Awards, ten Hugos, nine Bram Stokers, eighteen Locus Awards, five Shirley Jackson Awards, two International Horror Guild awards and a Karl Edward Wagner Award.** **There is no 2012 Hugo** among them, which one source asserts, and her World Fantasy total is neither eleven nor nine. Roughly half the World Fantasy wins are **joint with Terri Windling**, so solo credit on those is wrong, and the two long-running year's-best series she has edited are separate series with different publishers rather than one renamed.
entries.knownFor: Two decades of the year's-best volumes that are the field's institutional memory, and a run of original anthologies that has introduced much of its current generation.
entries.signature: Catholic taste with a bias toward the quiet and the formally strange, and a track record of buying writers before anyone else does.

works.title: The Year's Best Fantasy and Horror
works.note: twenty-one volumes to 2008, with Terri Windling

works.title: The Best Horror of the Year

entries.name: Kirby McCauley
entries.description: Agented the field into existence and edited one anthology that mattered enormously.
entries.meta: American, 1941–2014. A World Fantasy Special Convention Award 1979 and a **World Fantasy Award for Best Anthology 1981** — one anthology win, not several. No Bram Stoker, no Hugo. He **co-founded the World Fantasy Convention in 1975 and helped create the World Fantasy Awards**, as one of several architects rather than the sole founder, and as an agent he represented much of the field at the moment it became commercially large.
entries.knownFor: Dark Forces, an all-original anthology whose contents included the first publication of King's "The Mist" — not, as usually stated, the 1985 collection.
entries.signature: Editorial ambition on the scale of a permanent anthology rather than an annual, with original commissions rather than reprints.

entries.name: Stephen Jones
entries.description: Twenty-one British Fantasy Awards, the largest individual total in the field.
entries.meta: English, born 1953. **Twenty-one British Fantasy Awards**, a Karl Edward Wagner Award 2006, **three World Fantasy Awards and possibly a fourth**, five Bram Stokers of which **four are for non-fiction rather than anthologies**, and three International Horror Guild awards. **He has never won a Hugo**, despite an assertion to the contrary that is propagating into biographies. Solo credit is wrong on several of his co-edited series, and his long-running year's-best series has been renamed twice while remaining one continuous run that databases split into three.
entries.knownFor: The year's-best series that has run for more than three decades, and a body of reference and art books that constitute much of the field's popular scholarship.
entries.signature: Completist editorial apparatus — necrologies, market reports, exhaustive headnotes — that makes each volume a record of the year rather than a selection from it.

works.title: Best New Horror
works.note: editor, the first five volumes with Ramsey Campbell

entries.name: Dennis Etchison
entries.description: A short-story writer first, and one of the form's finest.
entries.meta: American, 1943–2019. **A World Fantasy Award for Best Short Fiction in 1982 — a tie with Stephen King** — and two further World Fantasy Awards for anthologies in 1993 and 2002; three British Fantasy Awards for short fiction; **Bram Stoker Lifetime Achievement 2017 and no competitive Stoker** despite four nominations; **zero International Horror Guild wins** from five nominations, despite a claim to the contrary in circulation. Every competitive award he holds is for short fiction or for an anthology he edited, and none is for a novel. He wrote film novelisations as Jack Martin.
entries.knownFor: Southern California as a horror landscape of laundromats, freeways and all-night diners, populated by people who have come loose from anything.
entries.signature: Affectless dislocation and an unnameable dread, with the supernatural often never confirmed at all.

entries.name: Karl Edward Wagner
entries.description: Edited the year's-best for fifteen years and has an award named after him.
entries.meta: American, 1945–1994. He held a medical degree with psychiatric residency training that he left, so he trained and never practised. A World Fantasy Special Award 1976 and **Best Novella 1983 as a tie**; three British Fantasy short-fiction awards and the **British Fantasy Society's Special Award in 1983** — which he did win, under its old name, and **the award was renamed in his honour in 1997, after his death**, so the tempting formulation that he could not have won the award named for him is wrong. No Bram Stoker of any kind. His death is attributable to alcoholism with heart and liver failure.
entries.knownFor: Editing fifteen volumes of the year's-best horror across the 1980s and early 1990s, and a body of short fiction — "Sticks" above all — that is far better than his sword-and-sorcery reputation suggests.
entries.signature: Physical grimness and structural precision, with folk-horror imagery arriving inside otherwise realist stories.

works.title: Darkness Weaves with Many Shades
works.note: badly cut on first publication, with the restored text following in 1978, so cite both

entries.name: The Castle of Otranto
entries.author: Horace Walpole
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: The founding text, and a hoax before it was a genre. Walpole issued it on 24 December 1764 with an 1765 title page, presenting it as a translation by…
entries.text: The founding text, and a hoax before it was a genre. Walpole issued it on 24 December 1764 with an 1765 title page, presenting it as a translation by one invented Englishman from another invented Italian, and the critical reception reversed sharply once he admitted authorship in the second edition — the same reviewers who had praised a medieval curiosity now found the same book absurd. That second edition supplied the subtitle "A Gothic Story", which is where the genre's name enters English. What the novel actually contributes is machinery rather than psychology: the animate portrait, the labyrinthine castle, the usurped inheritance, the prophecy that fulfils itself through the attempt to evade it. Read it for the apparatus and for the useful lesson that the form began as a stunt its author could not quite defend.

entries.name: Vathek
entries.author: William Beckford
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: The Gothic's orientalist wing, and a publication history stranger than most novels. Beckford wrote it in French, and it first appeared in June 1786 in…
entries.text: The Gothic's orientalist wing, and a publication history stranger than most novels. Beckford wrote it in French, and it first appeared in June 1786 in an unauthorised anonymous English translation by Samuel Henley, presented as taken from an Arabic manuscript; Beckford's own French text followed the next year. The result is a book whose original language, first appearance and attribution were all misrepresented at once. Its contribution to horror is the descent structure — a protagonist whose appetite for knowledge and sensation carries him progressively downward to a hall of the damned — and an ending that offers no rescue and no repentance. It is also genuinely funny for most of its length, which is the part its imitators consistently fail to reproduce.

entries.name: The Mysteries of Udolpho
entries.author: Ann Radcliffe
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: The book that made the Gothic a commercial category and set the terms of its central argument. Radcliffe's method — the explained supernatural, in…
entries.text: The book that made the Gothic a commercial category and set the terms of its central argument. Radcliffe's method — the explained supernatural, in which every apparent haunting is rationalised before the end — is often reported as a failure of nerve and is better read as a deliberate position: terror is produced by suspense and uncertainty rather than by confirmation, and confirmation ends it. The novel's real technical contribution is duration. Extended landscape description functions as a delaying mechanism, so that dread accumulates in the reader across long stretches in which nothing happens, and the reader's own impatience becomes part of the effect. Austen's parody in Northanger Abbey is affectionate and accurate, and reading them together is the fastest way to understand what the form was doing.

entries.name: The Monk
entries.author: Matthew Gregory Lewis
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Radcliffe's opposite number, published anonymously in March 1796 — not 1795, as is frequently printed — and written by a man of nineteen who put his…
entries.text: Radcliffe's opposite number, published anonymously in March 1796 — not 1795, as is frequently printed — and written by a man of nineteen who put his name and his parliamentary seat on the second edition and then expurgated the fourth under threat of prosecution. Where Radcliffe rationalises, Lewis confirms: the supernatural is real, the damnation is literal, and the sexual and violent content is delivered without cutaway at a speed that leaves the machinery visibly creaking. It matters because it establishes that the Gothic could be genuinely transgressive rather than decorous, and because the outrage it caused is the first instance of a pattern the genre repeats every few decades. The two settlements it opened with Udolpho — explained or confirmed — are still the choice every horror writer makes in their first act.

entries.name: Frankenstein
entries.author: Mary Shelley
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: The genre's most complete moral argument, published anonymously with a preface by Percy Shelley and first carrying her name only in 1823. Two facts…
entries.text: The genre's most complete moral argument, published anonymously with a preface by Percy Shelley and first carrying her name only in 1823. Two facts govern any serious use of it. First, there are two substantially different texts — the 1818 original and the 1831 revision most readers actually meet — and citing "Frankenstein" without specifying which is ambiguous. Second, the creature is the novel's most articulate voice and its best case, which relocates the horror onto its maker and keeps it there; every adaptation that silences him weakens the argument to the point of losing it. It founded science-fiction horror, established the created-being tradition, and demonstrated at the outset that a monster given language becomes a problem rather than a threat.

entries.name: The Vampyre
entries.author: John Polidori
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: The short piece that made the vampire an aristocrat, and did so out of the same Villa Diodati summer that produced Frankenstein. Its significance is…
entries.text: The short piece that made the vampire an aristocrat, and did so out of the same Villa Diodati summer that produced Frankenstein. Its significance is almost entirely typological: before it, the folkloric revenant is a bloated peasant corpse dug up by a village; after it, the vampire is titled, travelled, socially adept and predatory within polite society — which is the figure Le Fanu and Stoker inherit and every subsequent version argues with. The story was published attributed to Byron, which Polidori and Byron both had reason to resent, and its central figure is a recognisable and unflattering portrait of Byron himself. For a writer, it is the clearest demonstration in the canon that a monster's social class is a design decision with consequences that outlast the story.

entries.name: Melmoth the Wanderer
entries.author: Charles Maturin
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: The Gothic's last major statement and its most theologically serious. Maturin nests narratives inside narratives so that the reader descends through…
entries.text: The Gothic's last major statement and its most theologically serious. Maturin nests narratives inside narratives so that the reader descends through frames toward a bargain that is offered repeatedly, under conditions of increasing desperation, and refused every time — which is the novel's actual argument, since the refusals are what establish that damnation cannot be transferred to someone who has not consented. The structure is demanding and the prose is unfashionable, and both are why it has survived: Balzac and Baudelaire admired it long after English taste had moved on, and Wilde took its title character's name as his own after prison. Read it for the frame architecture, which is the most ambitious in the pre-modern canon.

entries.name: The Fall of the House of Usher
entries.author: Edgar Allan Poe
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: The demonstration of Poe's own compositional theory: a single predetermined effect, every element subordinated to it, and a length calibrated to one…
entries.text: The demonstration of Poe's own compositional theory: a single predetermined effect, every element subordinated to it, and a length calibrated to one sitting. Its lasting contribution is the fusion of house, family and body into a single failing organism, so that the building's fissure, the line's extinction and the protagonists' physical collapse are one event described three ways — which is the haunted-house tradition's founding idea and remains its most efficient. The narrator's uselessness is deliberate and instructive: he observes, rationalises, and is unable to intervene in anything, which makes him the ancestor of every ineffective witness the genre has used since. Note also how little happens, and how completely the atmosphere is doing the work.

entries.name: Varney the Vampire
entries.author: Attribution disputed
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: The penny-dreadful serial that ran to enormous length and settled much of the vampire's modern furniture — the fangs, the entry at the window, the…
entries.text: The penny-dreadful serial that ran to enormous length and settled much of the vampire's modern furniture — the fangs, the entry at the window, the hypnotic gaze, the reluctant and self-loathing predator. **Its authorship is genuinely unresolved**: long attributed to Thomas Peckett Prest, reassigned to James Malcolm Rymer by Helen R. Smith's 2002 bibliographic work on Lloyd's advertising and compositor evidence, and not settled beyond dispute even now, so a reference work should name both and adjudicate neither. As craft it is repetitive, padded and paid by the line, and that is exactly what makes it useful: it is the clearest available case study in how serial economics shape a monster, and in how much of what a genre treats as ancient tradition was in fact invented for weekly instalments.

entries.name: The String of Pearls
entries.author: Attribution disputed
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: The serial that introduced Sweeney Todd, running in a penny periodical from late 1846 into 1847 and expanded around 1850 with a different ending. It…
entries.text: The serial that introduced Sweeney Todd, running in a penny periodical from late 1846 into 1847 and expanded around 1850 with a different ending. It shares Varney's authorship problem and the same scholarly reassignment toward Rymer, and it carries a second and more instructive caution: **Sweeney Todd has no documented historical basis.** The claim that he was a real barber is a later invention, repeatedly asserted and repeatedly unsupported, and the most cited book making the case has been rejected by scholars. For a writer, this is the genre's best example of fiction acquiring a false documentary past — the same mechanism that produced the Angels of Mons and the Amityville claims, running a century earlier.

entries.name: Jane Eyre
entries.author: Charlotte Brontë
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Published as by "Currer Bell", and the Female Gothic's central text whether or not it is read as horror. Its contribution is the attic — a woman…
entries.text: Published as by "Currer Bell", and the Female Gothic's central text whether or not it is read as horror. Its contribution is the attic — a woman confined, unnamed for most of the book, and audible before she is visible — and the structural fact that the heroine's judgement is sound throughout while everyone around her insists it is not. That combination is the machinery of gaslighting rendered as plot, and it is the direct ancestor of Rebecca, of the modern domestic thriller and of the psychological-horror narrator whose reliability is the reader's problem. The novel's later reception, in which the attic's occupant is read from her own side rather than the narrator's, is itself part of what the book now teaches.

entries.name: Wuthering Heights
entries.author: Emily Brontë
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Published in December 1847 as by "Ellis Bell", and still the least assimilable book in the English canon. Its horror is not the ghost at the window,…
entries.text: Published in December 1847 as by "Ellis Bell", and still the least assimilable book in the English canon. Its horror is not the ghost at the window, striking as that is, but the sustained presence of a cruelty the novel declines to explain, condemn or resolve — there is no moral frame available to the reader, and the narrative supplies none. The nested narration is the mechanism: a tenant reports a housekeeper's account, which keeps the reader at two removes from events nobody in the book can adequately describe, and makes every judgement provisional. It is also the canon's clearest case of posthumous reputation management, since Charlotte's 1850 preface and her edited second text shaped how it was read for a century.

entries.name: The Old Nurse's Story
entries.author: Elizabeth Gaskell
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Published in the Christmas number of Dickens's Household Words, and the best early demonstration of what the seasonal magazine slot actually produced.…
entries.text: Published in the Christmas number of Dickens's Household Words, and the best early demonstration of what the seasonal magazine slot actually produced. Gaskell gives the narration to a servant, which is the story's whole design: the nurse has full access to the household's crime and no standing whatever to name it, so the reader receives the family's history through someone structurally forbidden to interpret it. The apparition is a child at a window in the snow, and the horror is the pull it exerts on a living child — a haunting that wants company rather than justice. It is short, it was written to be read aloud, and it establishes the class dimension that the English ghost story never quite loses.

entries.name: The Woman in White
entries.author: Wilkie Collins
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Serialised from November 1859, with the volume following the next year, and the founding text of the sensation novel — horror's closest structural…
entries.text: Serialised from November 1859, with the volume following the next year, and the founding text of the sensation novel — horror's closest structural neighbour. Collins assembles the book from testimony, each witness limited to what they can personally attest, so that the reader does the collation and the gaps between depositions carry what no narrator would state. That apparatus is what Stoker takes wholesale for Dracula and what the entire found-document tradition is still rebuilding with cameras. The novel's other bequest is the substitution plot and the private asylum, which put a sane woman's identity at the mercy of paperwork — the legal machinery that the Female Gothic had gestured at and Collins makes procedural.

entries.name: Uncle Silas
entries.author: Sheridan Le Fanu
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Published in 1864 — not 1865, as is frequently given — and expanded from a story Le Fanu had published twenty-six years earlier, with the setting…
entries.text: Published in 1864 — not 1865, as is frequently given — and expanded from a story Le Fanu had published twenty-six years earlier, with the setting relocated from Ireland to England at his English publishers' insistence. That commercial compromise is worth knowing, because presenting the book as an English novel misrepresents both its origins and its author's career. What it does supremely is the locked-house menace conducted entirely through manners: a young heiress placed in the guardianship of a relative whose intentions are legible to the reader long before she can act on them, with the threat carried by hospitality, courtesy and the impossibility of accusing a host. Its closest modern descendant is the domestic thriller rather than the ghost story.

entries.name: The Signal-Man
entries.author: Charles Dickens
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Published in the Mugby Junction Christmas number of All the Year Round, and the most technically precise short ghost story of its century. Dickens…
entries.text: Published in the Mugby Junction Christmas number of All the Year Round, and the most technically precise short ghost story of its century. Dickens grounds the whole thing in occupational detail — the cutting, the signal, the bell, the shift pattern — so that the apparition is measured against a working man's absolute competence at a job with no margin for error. The horror is therefore epistemological rather than spectral: the signalman's problem is that he is receiving a warning he cannot act on, in a system where his authority to act is exactly defined and does not extend to this. Dickens had survived the Staplehurst rail crash the previous year, which is context rather than explanation.

entries.name: Carmilla
entries.author: Sheridan Le Fanu
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Serialised from December 1871 into the following year — the flat "1872" citation is incomplete — and a quarter-century ahead of Dracula, which it…
entries.text: Serialised from December 1871 into the following year — the flat "1872" citation is incomplete — and a quarter-century ahead of Dracula, which it directly shaped. Its contribution is intimacy: the predator is resident in the household, the relationship is mutual and affectionate, and the erotic charge is neither coded nor incidental but the mechanism by which the predation works. That makes it structurally different from every vampire narrative that treats seduction as a means to feeding, and it is why the story has been continuously rediscovered by readers Stoker's version does not serve. The framing device — a case in a physician's papers — is Le Fanu's standard move and lets the account be simultaneously clinical and unresolved.

entries.name: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
entries.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Issued in the United States on 5 January 1886, four days ahead of the London edition — a rare case where the American date has priority. It is…
entries.text: Issued in the United States on 5 January 1886, four days ahead of the London edition — a rare case where the American date has priority. It is constructed as a legal and medical mystery whose solution the modern reader already knows, which is itself instructive: the book was written for an audience to whom the transformation was a genuine revelation, and reading it with that gone reveals how much of the effect survives on structure alone. Its lasting contribution is the divided self as a physical condition rather than a metaphor, and the specifically bourgeois horror of a respectable man's appetites acquiring a separate body and a separate address. The story that Stevenson's first draft was burned rests on family testimony and has no documentary support.

entries.name: Hauntings
entries.author: Vernon Lee
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Four stories by a writer whose day job was aesthetic theory, and the collection where the haunting becomes a problem of connoisseurship. Lee's…
entries.text: Four stories by a writer whose day job was aesthetic theory, and the collection where the haunting becomes a problem of connoisseurship. Lee's revenants arrive through art objects — a portrait, a voice, a piece of music — and the scholar-narrators are vulnerable precisely because their expertise makes them susceptible: they want the past, they have trained themselves to respond to its traces, and the traces respond back. That inversion of the antiquarian formula, where knowledge is a defence, is the collection's central move and is not much imitated even now. The prose is dense and the stories are slow, and both are the point.

entries.name: The Great God Pan
entries.author: Arthur Machen
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: First published in a shorter form in 1890 and substantially revised for the 1894 book that is almost universally cited as its first appearance.…
entries.text: First published in a shorter form in 1890 and substantially revised for the 1894 book that is almost universally cited as its first appearance. Machen's proposition — that evil is a positive metaphysical fact rather than an absence, and that the ordinary surface of the world is a courtesy extended to us — is the founding statement of cosmic horror as a philosophical position rather than a set of monsters, and Lovecraft acknowledged the debt directly. The technique is transmission at several removes: a doctor's notes, a coroner's report, a chain of witnesses each reporting what someone else saw, so that the central event is never assembled and never has to be. It was received as obscene, which tells you the transmission worked.

entries.name: The Picture of Dorian Gray
entries.author: Oscar Wilde
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Published in a magazine in 1890 and expanded for the 1891 volume after the first version was attacked as immoral, with Wilde adding both defensive…
entries.text: Published in a magazine in 1890 and expanded for the 1891 volume after the first version was attacked as immoral, with Wilde adding both defensive material and the preface that is now quoted more than the book. Its horror mechanism is the externalised ledger: corruption is real, cumulative and recorded, but recorded somewhere the corrupted man can lock away — which makes deferral rather than sin the actual subject, and makes the final reversal require no explanation at all. For a writer it is the cleanest demonstration in the canon of a single supernatural rule, stated once, obeyed absolutely, and permitted to generate the entire plot without further intervention.

entries.name: The King in Yellow
entries.author: Robert W. Chambers
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Only the first four stories are weird fiction; the rest of the volume is Parisian art-student romance, and knowing that is part of using the book…
entries.text: Only the first four stories are weird fiction; the rest of the volume is Parisian art-student romance, and knowing that is part of using the book properly. Its device is the contaminating text — a play that damages whoever finishes it, never reproduced, its effects reported only by people already damaged — which is the purest form of the withheld artefact and the direct ancestor of every cursed tape, film and website since. Chambers took Carcosa, Hastur and Hali from Ambrose Bierce, where they are not horrors at all; Lovecraft did not read the book until 1927 and borrowed only two elements from it. The systematised mythos built on it afterwards is largely August Derleth's invention.

entries.name: Dracula
entries.author: Bram Stoker
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Published on 26 May 1897, and the most complete demonstration of assembled-document narration in the language. The cast are compulsive recorders —…
entries.text: Published on 26 May 1897, and the most complete demonstration of assembled-document narration in the language. The cast are compulsive recorders — journals, phonograph cylinders, shorthand, telegrams, newspaper cuttings — and the plot is literally the collation of those records into a usable weapon, which makes the novel's structure and its story the same thing. The technology is contemporary and specific rather than decorative, the gaps between documents do work no narrator could, and every found-footage film since has been rebuilding this apparatus with a camera. One caution: the claim that "Dracula's Guest" is an excised opening chapter comes from Florence Stoker's 1914 preface and is rejected by the leading scholars.

entries.name: The Turn of the Screw
entries.author: Henry James
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Serialised in Collier's Weekly from January 1898, with the book following that October, so the familiar 1898 volume date postdates the first appearance…
entries.text: Serialised in Collier's Weekly from January 1898, with the book following that October, so the familiar 1898 volume date postdates the first appearance by eight months. The apparitionist and hallucinationist readings remain genuinely unsettled rather than solved, and Edmund Wilson's Freudian account is frequently presented as the answer when it is one position among several. What makes it permanently useful is that the ambiguity is structural rather than coy: James supplies enough for either reading and not enough for both, and the governess's syntax becomes more elaborate exactly as her claims become less supportable, so the prose is the evidence. Every ambiguous-narrator horror novel since is working in its shadow.

entries.name: Ghost Stories of an Antiquary
entries.author: M.R. James
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: The form's technical manual, by a medievalist who wrote the stories to read aloud to friends at Christmas and published most of them first in the…
entries.text: The form's technical manual, by a medievalist who wrote the stories to read aloud to friends at Christmas and published most of them first in the collections rather than in magazines. The recurring shape is exact: a scholar on an ordinary errand disturbs something catalogued, one wrong detail is noticed in passing, and the apparition when it arrives is described in tactile terms — hair, cloth, dampness, a face that is wrong to touch rather than to see. James also set out his own rules in print, and they still function as a checklist: a familiar setting, a gradual intrusion, no occult apparatus, and no explanation offered. Almost everything the English ghost story has done since is either following this or arguing with it.

entries.name: The Willows
entries.author: Algernon Blackwood
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: First published in a collection rather than a magazine, which is worth noting because Blackwood is a collection-first author and is routinely misdated…
entries.text: First published in a collection rather than a magazine, which is worth noting because Blackwood is a collection-first author and is routinely misdated on the assumption that he is not. Two competent men on a canoeing trip encounter a landscape that has developed intentions, and the entire story is carried by the argument between them about what is happening — one understands sooner, neither can act, and nothing is ever seen clearly. Lovecraft called it the finest weird tale in English and the judgement holds: the presences are never described, the mechanism is never explained, and the dread is generated almost entirely by two men adjusting their behaviour to a conclusion they will not state aloud.

entries.name: The House on the Borderland
entries.author: William Hope Hodgson
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: Frequently misdated to 1907, and the earliest full statement of deep-time cosmic horror in English. Hodgson's structure is a recovered manuscript…
entries.text: Frequently misdated to 1907, and the earliest full statement of deep-time cosmic horror in English. Hodgson's structure is a recovered manuscript within a frame, and its extraordinary central movement accelerates time until the sun dies and the solar system runs down — an effect no one had attempted at that length, and which converts a siege narrative into a cosmological one without changing register. The swine-creatures that occupy the first half are conventional; the time-lapse is not, and it is the reason the book survives. Note that Lovecraft did not read Hodgson until 1934, sixteen years after Hodgson's death, which inverts the influence relationship people usually assume.

entries.name: Carnacki the Ghost-Finder
entries.author: William Hope Hodgson
entries.awards: None — no literary prize existed
entries.description: The stories appeared in The Idler across 1910 and are habitually misdated to the 1913 collection. Carnacki is the occult detective done properly, and…
entries.text: The stories appeared in The Idler across 1910 and are habitually misdated to the 1913 collection. Carnacki is the occult detective done properly, and the reason is that his caseload is mixed: some investigations end supernatural, several end in hoaxes, and he is sometimes simply wrong. That willingness to let the specialist fail is what the character contributes and what most of his descendants discard, since a detective whose every case is genuine collapses into a monster-of-the-week. The electric pentacle is period technology treated as laboratory apparatus rather than as magic, which is a small but permanently useful move: it makes the protection falsifiable, and therefore makes its failure mean something.

entries.name: The Night Land
entries.author: William Hope Hodgson
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: One of the strangest books in the canon and one of the least readable, and both facts are instructive. Hodgson imagines a far future in which the sun…
entries.text: One of the strangest books in the canon and one of the least readable, and both facts are instructive. Hodgson imagines a far future in which the sun is dead, humanity survives inside a vast pyramid, and the surrounding darkness is populated by watching things that have been waiting for a very long time — an image of deep-time siege that nothing else in the period approaches. The execution is the problem: he wrote it in a pseudo-archaic register sustained across enormous length, and the romance plot at its centre is tedious even to admirers. It is the clearest case in the collection of a work whose ideas outran its author's technique, and it has been more influential through summary and homage than through direct reading.

entries.name: Supernatural Horror in Literature
entries.author: H.P. Lovecraft
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: The essay that gave the field its first critical self-understanding, revised across the following decade and still the document most genre histories…
entries.text: The essay that gave the field its first critical self-understanding, revised across the following decade and still the document most genre histories are quietly built on. Its opening proposition — that the oldest and strongest emotion is fear, and the oldest and strongest fear is of the unknown — is quoted more than anything else Lovecraft wrote, and its survey established the canon that Arkham House then physically reprinted. Two cautions for use. It is a partisan document rather than a neutral survey, promoting the writers Lovecraft was in correspondence with; and it is where the anglophone field's reading list was set by one man's taste, which is part of why that list stayed so narrow for so long.

entries.name: The Colour Out of Space
entries.author: H.P. Lovecraft
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: Published in Amazing Stories in September 1927 — **not Weird Tales**, which is among the most persistent errors in his bibliography — and by his own…
entries.text: Published in Amazing Stories in September 1927 — **not Weird Tales**, which is among the most persistent errors in his bibliography — and by his own judgement his best story. The contaminant has no form, no intention and no negotiable interface: it arrives, it persists in soil and water, and it alters what grows and lives there, indifferent to ownership and to the family's increasingly desperate attempts to farm around it. That indifference is the purest available statement of the cosmic position, and it is achieved without a single entity, cult or invented book. For a writer it demonstrates that the mode's power comes from the absence of an addressable antagonist rather than from scale.

entries.name: The Call of Cthulhu
entries.author: H.P. Lovecraft
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: Weird Tales, February 1928, after the editor had rejected it and then been told — untruthfully, by Donald Wandrei — that Lovecraft might place it…
entries.text: Weird Tales, February 1928, after the editor had rejected it and then been told — untruthfully, by Donald Wandrei — that Lovecraft might place it elsewhere. Its structure is the contribution: an executor assembling a dead relative's papers, so that the reader receives a cult, a sculpture, a police report and a ship's log as separate fragments and does the collation themselves. The entity is barely present and is better for it. The story is also where the racial anxieties running through the work become inseparable from the mechanism, since the cult is located among non-white and immigrant populations by design rather than by accident, and any serious use of the story has to hold both facts at once.

entries.name: The Dunwich Horror
entries.author: H.P. Lovecraft
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: The most conventional of the major stories and the most useful for studying his weaknesses. It has a monster, a countermeasure, a competent scholar and…
entries.text: The most conventional of the major stories and the most useful for studying his weaknesses. It has a monster, a countermeasure, a competent scholar and a victory — the full apparatus his best work refuses — and the result is a story that is more satisfying and considerably less frightening than The Colour Out of Space. Its degenerate-family material is also the clearest instance of the eugenic anxiety that runs through the work, presented without irony. Read it alongside the Colour to see exactly what explanation and a winnable fight cost a cosmic-horror premise, which is the single most transferable lesson in the whole Lovecraft corpus.

entries.name: The Hounds of Tindalos
entries.author: Frank Belknap Long
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: Weird Tales, March 1929, and not 1946, which is the date of the Arkham House collection named after it. Long's contribution was to make the geometry…
entries.text: Weird Tales, March 1929, and not 1946, which is the date of the Arkham House collection named after it. Long's contribution was to make the geometry itself the threat: pursuers that move through the angles of time rather than through space, so that a curved room is a defence and a corner is a breach. That gave the shared apparatus a vocabulary Lovecraft had not supplied, and it remains one of the very few genuinely original monster designs the circle produced. The prose is chatty and the frame is creaky, and the idea has outlived both — which is a useful thing for a writer to notice about which parts of a story survive.

entries.name: Shambleau
entries.author: C.L. Moore
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: Weird Tales, November 1933, and a debut that arrived with no visible apprenticeship. Moore brought a genuine erotics of dread into a magazine that had…
entries.text: Weird Tales, November 1933, and a debut that arrived with no visible apprenticeship. Moore brought a genuine erotics of dread into a magazine that had not previously known what to do with one: the encounter is sustained, mutual and physically specific, and the horror is inseparable from the attraction rather than following it. The prose is colour-saturated and sensuous in a way nobody else in the pulps was attempting, and it is applied to something the narrator cannot look at directly. It also matters that she was writing under initials to hide the work from her employer rather than her sex from readers, since the standard version of that story has obscured how visible she actually was.

entries.name: At the Mountains of Madness
entries.author: H.P. Lovecraft
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: Serialised in Astounding Stories across February, March and April 1936 **after Weird Tales rejected it** — the frequent attribution to Weird Tales is…
entries.text: Serialised in Astounding Stories across February, March and April 1936 **after Weird Tales rejected it** — the frequent attribution to Weird Tales is wrong and propagates through otherwise careful sources. Its method is scientific procedure: an Antarctic expedition, a dissection, an architectural survey, and a slow reconstruction of a non-human history from physical evidence. The famous move is the reversal in which the discovered civilisation becomes sympathetic — "they were men!" — and the true horror is relocated onto what that civilisation had itself built and could not control. It is the best available demonstration that comprehension can deepen cosmic horror rather than defusing it, provided each answer opens a worse question.

entries.name: The Shadow over Innsmouth
entries.author: H.P. Lovecraft
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: The only book of his fiction published in his lifetime, in a small and badly produced edition. As craft it is his most propulsive work — the night in…
entries.text: The only book of his fiction published in his lifetime, in a small and badly produced edition. As craft it is his most propulsive work — the night in the hotel and the flight through the town are genuine suspense writing, which is rare for him — and its structure of arrival, investigation, pursuit and revelation is the template for a great deal of later folk horror. It is also the story in which the racial mechanism is least deniable: the horror is hybridisation and inherited taint, the reveal is ancestral, and the final transformation is presented as a fate. A reference work that recommends it, as this one does, has to say both things in the same paragraph.

entries.name: The Outsider and Others
entries.author: H.P. Lovecraft
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: Not a story but an object, and one of the most consequential in the field: the Arkham House omnibus that August Derleth and Donald Wandrei founded a…
entries.text: Not a story but an object, and one of the most consequential in the field: the Arkham House omnibus that August Derleth and Donald Wandrei founded a press in order to publish, two years after Lovecraft's death, when no commercial house would collect a pulp writer nobody outside the magazines had heard of. It established the small press as horror's preservation mechanism, a pattern that has held for eighty-five years. It also began the process by which Derleth's editorial framing became inseparable from the work, and the chain of title Arkham asserted over the corpus remains genuinely disputed and unresolved.

entries.name: Out of Space and Time
entries.author: Clark Ashton Smith
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: The Arkham House collection that made Smith available as a body of work rather than as scattered magazine appearances, and the place most readers still…
entries.text: The Arkham House collection that made Smith available as a body of work rather than as scattered magazine appearances, and the place most readers still meet him. Its texts carry a caution: Smith's magazine publications were cut by editors who found him excessive, and the versions here and in later scholarly editions differ, so citing a Smith story without specifying which text is imprecise. What the collection demonstrates is a register nobody else achieved — baroque diction and corrosive irony held in exact balance, so that catastrophe arrives as an aesthetic event. He was a published poet from 1912, before Lovecraft published fiction, and reading him as a disciple gets the sequence backwards.

entries.name: Who Fears the Devil?
entries.author: Manly Wade Wellman
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: The Silver John stories, collected by Arkham House after a decade in the magazines, and the most convincing use of American folk tradition the pulp era…
entries.text: The Silver John stories, collected by Arkham House after a decade in the magazines, and the most convincing use of American folk tradition the pulp era produced. Wellman's wandering balladeer meets the supernatural with regional knowledge and a silver-strung guitar, and the material is collected rather than invented — the ballads, the beliefs and the remedies are real and treated as working technology. The first-person Appalachian voice is sustained without condescension across the whole sequence, which is harder than it looks and is where most regional horror fails. For a writer building from folklore, this is the model that shows what specificity buys you.

entries.name: Conjure Wife
entries.author: Fritz Leiber
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: First published in Unknown Worlds in April 1943 — **not 1953, which is the book** — and the sharpest single premise of mid-century American horror: a…
entries.text: First published in Unknown Worlds in April 1943 — **not 1953, which is the book** — and the sharpest single premise of mid-century American horror: a sociology professor discovers that his wife practises protective magic, persuades her to stop, and finds out what her practice had been holding off. The novel's real subject is the faculty politics of a small college, and the witchcraft operates entirely through it, which makes the supernatural a description of how academic power actually moves rather than an intrusion into it. It also anticipates by decades the domestic-conspiracy structure Levin would perfect, with the crucial difference that the husband here is a fool rather than a conspirator.

entries.name: Dark Carnival
entries.author: Ray Bradbury
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: His first book, from Arkham House, and the collection in which American horror acquires a lyric voice. The stories are short, image-driven and built on…
entries.text: His first book, from Arkham House, and the collection in which American horror acquires a lyric voice. The stories are short, image-driven and built on childhood perception — the jar, the crowd that gathers at accidents, the small-town October — and the effect depends on metaphor doing work that plot would do elsewhere. Much of the contents was later revised into The October Country, so the two books overlap without being interchangeable and the texts differ. It matters historically as the point at which the genre demonstrated it could carry prose ambition without abandoning the pulps, and matters practically as the best short course in horror written from a child's-eye vantage.

entries.name: The Lottery
entries.author: Shirley Jackson
entries.awards: O. Henry Prize Stories selection, 1949
entries.description: The New Yorker, 26 June 1948 — and not 1949, which is the collection. It is the most-taught short story in American literature and the most…
entries.text: The New Yorker, 26 June 1948 — and not 1949, which is the collection. It is the most-taught short story in American literature and the most misremembered: there is no supernatural element, no explanation of the ritual's purpose, and no villain, and the horror is entirely administrative — the box, the slips, the roll-call, the children gathering stones in advance. The reader response was substantial and hostile, and Jackson's own account gives roughly three hundred letters of which she counted thirteen as kind. For a writer, it is the definitive demonstration that a community's unexamined procedure is more frightening than any monster, and that withholding the reason is not a gap but the subject.

entries.name: I Am Legend
entries.author: Richard Matheson
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: The book that moved horror into the suburb and rebuilt the vampire as an epidemiological problem. Matheson gives his last man a bacteriology, a…
entries.text: The book that moved horror into the suburb and rebuilt the vampire as an epidemiological problem. Matheson gives his last man a bacteriology, a research programme and a resource economy, so the novel is procedural for most of its length — garlic tested, mirrors tested, hypotheses discarded — and the horror is loneliness administered daily rather than delivered in scenes. The title's meaning is the reversal that makes it permanent: the protagonist ends the book understanding that he is the aberration and the monster in the new world's folklore. It founded the modern apocalypse narrative, and Romero has always credited it as the direct source of Night of the Living Dead.

entries.name: The Body Snatchers
entries.author: Jack Finney
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: Serialised in Collier's across three issues in late 1954, with the Dell paperback the following year. **The title is The Body Snatchers**; "Invasion…
entries.text: Serialised in Collier's across three issues in late 1954, with the Dell paperback the following year. **The title is The Body Snatchers**; "Invasion of" is the 1956 film's title, retro-applied to later reissues, and citing a 1955 "Invasion of the Body Snatchers" gets both the name and the date wrong. The premise is the purest form of the replacement horror: the people are unchanged in every observable respect and something is nevertheless gone, which makes detection a matter of intimacy rather than evidence. The persistent reading as McCarthyism allegory is reception history — neither Finney nor the film's makers reported intending one — and the novel is more disturbing read as being about nothing but the loss itself.

entries.name: The October Country
entries.author: Ray Bradbury
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: The revised and expanded successor to Dark Carnival, and the volume through which most readers actually encounter Bradbury's horror. The revisions are…
entries.text: The revised and expanded successor to Dark Carnival, and the volume through which most readers actually encounter Bradbury's horror. The revisions are substantial enough that the two books are not interchangeable, and the newer texts are generally tighter and slightly less strange. What it collects is a specific and enormously influential mode: Midwestern childhood in which wonder and dread are the same emotion, small-town Octobers, and a metaphorical density that carries material which would be unbearable stated plainly. Almost every subsequent American writer who has put a child at the centre of a horror story is working somewhere downstream of this book.

entries.name: The Shrinking Man
entries.author: Richard Matheson
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: Body horror before the term existed, and structurally the most rigorous thing Matheson wrote. A man diminishes at a fixed rate, and the novel simply…
entries.text: Body horror before the term existed, and structurally the most rigorous thing Matheson wrote. A man diminishes at a fixed rate, and the novel simply follows the consequences: the house becomes a wilderness, the domestic cat becomes a predator, a spider becomes an antagonist requiring tactics, and his marriage fails in a way the book treats as seriously as the physical danger. The discipline is that nothing is arbitrary — every scene is derived from the single premise applied at a different scale — and the ending refuses both rescue and despair. For a writer it is the best available demonstration of the consequence cascade: one rule, propagated honestly, generating an entire novel.

entries.name: Psycho
entries.author: Robert Bloch
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: Published in 1959 — the 1958 date given in one standard reference is wrong. Bloch's contribution is relocation: horror leaves the castle and the remote…
entries.text: Published in 1959 — the 1958 date given in one standard reference is wrong. Bloch's contribution is relocation: horror leaves the castle and the remote village for a motel off a rerouted highway, and the monster is a man with a business and a mother problem. The Ed Gein connection is real and routinely overstated — Bloch lived some thirty-five miles from the case, did not know its details when he began, and had nearly finished the book when the crimes broke, so the premise is drawn from the idea of such a man rather than from the biography of one. The novel's structural reversal, spending its apparent protagonist early, is what Hitchcock kept and what the genre has been reusing ever since.

entries.name: The Haunting of Hill House
entries.author: Shirley Jackson
entries.awards: National Book Award for Fiction, finalist, 1960
entries.description: The haunted-house novel against which the others are measured, and a **finalist** for the National Book Award rather than a winner, which is a frequent…
entries.text: The haunted-house novel against which the others are measured, and a **finalist** for the National Book Award rather than a winner, which is a frequent inflation. Jackson refuses throughout to let the house's malice be separated from Eleanor's need: every apparent manifestation is simultaneously an accurate reading of a lonely woman's psychology, and neither interpretation can be discarded without breaking the book. The opening and closing paragraphs give the house its own sentence and its own agency, and the prose accelerates and fragments as Eleanor's grip fails, so the reader experiences the deterioration rather than being told about it. Seventy years of the subgenre have been arguing with it rather than improving on it.

entries.name: Something Wicked This Way Comes
entries.author: Ray Bradbury
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: The carnival novel, and the fullest statement of Bradbury's central proposition that childhood's wonder and its terror are the same faculty pointed…
entries.text: The carnival novel, and the fullest statement of Bradbury's central proposition that childhood's wonder and its terror are the same faculty pointed differently. Its temptation mechanism is unusually well designed — the carousel offers age or youth, and every character's desire for it is specific and sympathetic — which makes the moral stakes real rather than asserted. The father is the book's genuine achievement: a middle-aged man whose weapon against the supernatural is acceptance of his own mortality, which is a far stranger and better idea than the fight it replaces. It is also where the horror-as-Americana mode that Stephen King inherited was set.

entries.name: We Have Always Lived in the Castle
entries.author: Shirley Jackson
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: Her last completed novel and her most technically extreme. The narration comes from inside a settled and thoroughly unsettling logic that the book…
entries.text: Her last completed novel and her most technically extreme. The narration comes from inside a settled and thoroughly unsettling logic that the book never breaks frame to explain or apologise for, so the reader assembles the family's history from a voice that sees no reason to present it as remarkable. The horror is social rather than supernatural — a village's sustained cruelty toward two women, escalating to something like a pogrom — and the ending's contentment is the effect: the reader's recognition of what that contentment consists of does all the work. It is the purest example in the collection of an unreliable narrator whose distortion is consistent, learnable and never once acknowledged.

entries.name: Rosemary's Baby
entries.author: Ira Levin
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: The novel that made the horror paperback a mainstream category, and a masterpiece of economy — short chapters, no ornament, and a reader kept exactly…
entries.text: The novel that made the horror paperback a mainstream category, and a masterpiece of economy — short chapters, no ornament, and a reader kept exactly half a step behind a protagonist nobody believes. Its achievement is that the conspiracy is indistinguishable from ordinary social pressure: the obstetrician, the neighbours, the husband's career and the standard dismissal of a pregnant woman's account of her own body would produce the same experience with no supernatural element at all. Levin also releases repeatedly into social comedy and domestic detail without ever lowering the threat, which is the tension-valve technique executed at professional level. The ending is a settlement so consistent with everything preceding it that it reads as inevitable.

entries.name: The Exorcist
entries.author: William Peter Blatty
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: The book that proved horror could occupy the bestseller list for a year, and a far more patient novel than its reputation suggests. Blatty spends…
entries.text: The book that proved horror could occupy the bestseller list for a year, and a far more patient novel than its reputation suggests. Blatty spends roughly half its length on neurology, psychiatry and police procedure, so the supernatural arrives only after the medical apparatus has been genuinely exhausted rather than dismissed — which is why the theology, when it comes, functions as a last resort rather than a premise. Its second achievement is the priest: a man whose crisis is loss of faith and whose expertise is therefore useless to him. It derives from a documented 1949 exorcism case, and the case and the fiction are constantly and unhelpfully conflated.

entries.name: Hell House
entries.author: Richard Matheson
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: Matheson's deliberate answer to Hill House, and the useful counter-position even where it is the lesser book. Where Jackson refuses to specify,…
entries.text: Matheson's deliberate answer to Hill House, and the useful counter-position even where it is the lesser book. Where Jackson refuses to specify, Matheson supplies apparatus, physics and a stated mechanism — a machine that will drain the house's energy, a documented history, an explanation that holds. The result is a novel that is more explicit in every sense and considerably less frightening, which is precisely why the pair should be read together: it is the clearest controlled experiment the genre offers on what explanation costs. It is also a significant escalation in sexual content for mainstream horror, and marks the point where the paperback market's appetite began outrunning its restraint.

entries.name: The Other
entries.author: Thomas Tryon
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: An actor's first novel and one of the decade's best, built on a structural withholding that the book earns rather than deploys. Tryon spends an…
entries.text: An actor's first novel and one of the decade's best, built on a structural withholding that the book earns rather than deploys. Tryon spends an unhurried first act establishing a 1930s Connecticut farm community in full — the grandmother, the games, the harvest, the heat — so that when the arrangement is revealed the reader has to reinterpret a world they have been enjoying rather than merely a plot they have been following. The nostalgia is not decoration but the mechanism. It is also the founding text of the evil-child cycle that ran through the following decade, and the one with the least interest in explaining itself.

entries.name: Burnt Offerings
entries.author: Robert Marasco
entries.awards: None — the category did not exist
entries.description: The house that restores itself in exact proportion to its occupants' decline, and the template most subsequent haunted-house novels are working from…
entries.text: The house that restores itself in exact proportion to its occupants' decline, and the template most subsequent haunted-house novels are working from whether or not they know it. Marasco's discipline is that the horror is tracked entirely through household detail — fresh paint appearing, a fixture repaired, wallpaper renewed — so the reader monitors a home-improvement schedule and understands what it costs before the family does. The summer-rental premise supplies both the isolation and the reason nobody leaves, and the mother's increasing devotion to the house is a possession narrative that never once uses the word. Marasco published only one further novel, which is why the frequent claim that this was his only book is wrong.

entries.name: Harvest Home
entries.author: Thomas Tryon
entries.awards: None confirmed
entries.description: Tryon's second novel and the book that established folk horror's American register a year before *The Wicker Man* did it on film. A city couple move to…
entries.text: Tryon's second novel and the book that established folk horror's American register a year before *The Wicker Man* did it on film. A city couple move to a New England village that is prosperous, welcoming and organised around an agricultural calendar nobody explains to them, and the novel's method is to let the reader accumulate the rules by observation until the omissions become the loudest thing in the book. It runs long and *Kirkus* said so at the time — "too much corn to husk before the last loaded third" — but the length is doing work, because the horror is that the arrangement is functioning and has been for generations. Stephen King predicted in 1976 that libraries would still be rebinding it in forty years, which is a useful reminder that the boom's bestsellers were not uniformly disposable.

entries.name: The Rats
entries.author: James Herbert
entries.awards: None
entries.description: The British counter-tradition, and the cleanest demonstration in the collection that a novel can succeed commercially while being critically despised.…
entries.text: The British counter-tradition, and the cleanest demonstration in the collection that a novel can succeed commercially while being critically despised. Herbert — an advertising art director whose wife typed the manuscript and who was turned down by nine publishers — writes East End London with specificity and then eats it, in set-piece deaths given to characters introduced pages earlier for that purpose. The technique is the vignette structure, later standard in creature horror: a named stranger, a paragraph of ordinary life, an attack. Its first printing of 100,000 sold out in three weeks. Two cautions for use: it was notorious for hostile reviews, not acclaim, and retrospectives that read the sales as critical success invert the record; and Herbert's much-quoted fifty-four-million lifetime sales figure is career-wide, not this book's.

entries.name: Carrie
entries.author: Stephen King
entries.awards: None
entries.description: The short, structurally inventive book that funded everything after it. Its epistolary apparatus — commission testimony, a book-length academic study,…
entries.text: The short, structurally inventive book that funded everything after it. Its epistolary apparatus — commission testimony, a book-length academic study, news reports — surrounds the narrative with the aftermath, so the reader knows from early on that the town burns and reads the middle as a countdown rather than a mystery, which is a documented-fragment technique the genre had not used at this pitch since Stoker. The commercial facts are the reason it belongs here: a $2,500 Doubleday advance, a first printing of 30,000, hardcover sales of roughly thirteen to seventeen thousand copies — and then $400,000 for the mass-market rights from NAL, of which King's half was $200,000. Careful phrasing is required on one point: this is King's first **published** novel, not his first written. *The Long Walk* was begun in 1966–67 and appeared in 1979 under the Bachman name.

entries.name: The Manitou
entries.author: Graham Masterton
entries.awards: None confirmed
entries.description: Included as a specimen rather than a recommendation, because it is the period's most efficient illustration of a failure mode this pack takes…
entries.text: Included as a specimen rather than a recommendation, because it is the period's most efficient illustration of a failure mode this pack takes seriously: the Native American revenant deployed as a monster with no interest in the tradition it claims to draw on. A three-hundred-year-old Algonquian medicine man gestates in a woman's neck as a tumour, and the book proceeds as a possession-and-exorcism plot with a substituted mythology. It was a genuine commercial success and spawned sequels, and the reason to look at it is to see how completely the appropriation registered as unremarkable in 1975 — which is the context every later corrective, from *The Only Good Indians* backwards, is arguing against. Bibliographic care needed: this is a **UK Neville Spearman hardcover, 1975**; the US Pinnacle paperback is 1976 and secondary sources date the work variously to 1976 and 1977. It was Masterton's first horror novel but nowhere near his first book.

entries.name: ’Salem’s Lot
entries.author: Stephen King
entries.awards: World Fantasy Award, Best Novel — 1976 nominee (lost)
entries.description: *Dracula* relocated to a dying Maine mill town, and the transposition is the whole argument: the vampire works because the community was already…
entries.text: *Dracula* relocated to a dying Maine mill town, and the transposition is the whole argument: the vampire works because the community was already hollow, its economy gone, its houses emptying, its residents individually unwilling to notice each other's absence. King's structural decision is to spend the first third on the town as a social organism — a rotating cast, small cruelties, who is sleeping with whom — so that the infection has something to spread through. The title is elided from Jerusalem's Lot and the apostrophe is canonical; the setting has no connection to Salem, Massachusetts, and copy that implies a witch-trial lineage is inventing one. The paperback rights went for a reported $550,000, the number that converted King from a promising newcomer into the market's centre of gravity.

entries.name: Interview with the Vampire
entries.author: Anne Rice
entries.awards: None confirmed
entries.description: The pivot from vampire-as-threat to vampire-as-narrator, and every sympathetic-monster novel of the following half-century is downstream of it. The…
entries.text: The pivot from vampire-as-threat to vampire-as-narrator, and every sympathetic-monster novel of the following half-century is downstream of it. The formal choice does the work: Louis speaks into a tape recorder, at length, and the reader is placed in the interviewer's seat, receiving an account that is self-justifying, unreliable and impossible to interrupt. Immortality is presented as duration rather than power — the problem of what to do with centuries — and Claudia, a child's body with an adult's mind and appetites, is the most disturbing thing in the book precisely because she is a victim of the sympathetic protagonist. The composition history is worth stating accurately: the novel grew from a short story written around 1968–69, was rewritten as a 338-page draft in about five weeks in 1973, and was then expanded by roughly two hundred pages.
