The legal history matters as craft history. **Florence Stoker** sued, and in **July 1925** the court ordered all prints and negatives destroyed; multiple prints survived regardless, which is why the film exists. It entered the worldwide public domain in 2019 — a copyright status, not an honour.

entries.name: Frankenstein (1931 film)
entries.author: James Whale
entries.awards: None — no Academy Award nominations
entries.description: The film that fixed the popular image of the creature so firmly that Shelley's articulate, self-educating being has never fully recovered — flat head,…
entries.text: The film that fixed the popular image of the creature so firmly that Shelley's articulate, self-educating being has never fully recovered — flat head, neck bolts, heavy tread, and a vocabulary of grunts. Its craft value is Karloff's performance, which generates sympathy without dialogue and locates the horror in the creature's incomprehension rather than in its malice; the drowning of the child Maria is the scene the whole tradition of the misunderstood monster descends from. Credit precision: the film derives from **both** Shelley's novel **and** John L. Balderston's adaptation of Peggy Webling's 1927 stage play, and Balderston is the name most often dropped. It won nothing and received no Academy Award nomination, which is the single most common false claim made about it.

entries.name: Freaks
entries.author: Tod Browning
entries.awards: None — it was a commercial and reputational disaster
entries.description: MGM cast performers from the working sideshow circuit as themselves and built a revenge plot around them, and the result destroyed Browning's career…
entries.text: MGM cast performers from the working sideshow circuit as themselves and built a revenge plot around them, and the result destroyed Browning's career while producing the most ethically complicated film in the horror canon. Its craft argument is inverted from the audience's expectation: the sideshow performers are the moral community, bound by a code the "normal" trapeze artist violates, and the wedding-feast sequence — "one of us, one of us" — works because the acceptance being offered is sincere. The final transformation is nonetheless the film betraying its own thesis, converting the people it humanised into instruments of body horror. Cut heavily after disastrous previews, with roughly thirty minutes lost and presumed destroyed, and **banned in the UK from 1932 until 1963**. Added to the National Film Registry in 1994 — a preservation listing, not an award.

entries.name: Cat People
entries.author: Jacques Tourneur
entries.awards: None
entries.description: The film that proved a horror picture could be made for almost nothing by refusing to show anything, and the entire suggestion-based tradition is…
entries.text: The film that proved a horror picture could be made for almost nothing by refusing to show anything, and the entire suggestion-based tradition is downstream of it. Produced by **Val Lewton — who produced and did not direct**, a distinction this pack enforces everywhere — and written by DeWitt Bodeen, it withholds its transformation completely and generates its two most famous sequences out of a swimming pool and a walk beside a park wall. The second of those gave the industry the term **"Lewton bus,"** for a shock resolved into a mundane source: the hiss the audience takes for a big cat is a bus's air brakes. RKO's own figures show it in solid profit; the "it saved the studio" claim rests on a much larger estimate and should be treated as folklore. National Film Registry, 1993.

entries.name: Les Diaboliques
entries.author: Henri-Georges Clouzot
entries.awards: Prix Louis Delluc, 1954
entries.description: A wife and a mistress conspire to murder the man who abuses them both, and the body disappears from the swimming pool — a plot Clouzot derived from…
entries.text: A wife and a mistress conspire to murder the man who abuses them both, and the body disappears from the swimming pool — a plot Clouzot derived from Boileau-Narcejac's *She Who Was No More*, having reportedly acquired the rights just ahead of Hitchcock, an anecdote widely repeated and worth attributing rather than asserting. Its permanent contribution is the closing title card asking the audience not to reveal the ending, which established the spoiler-protection campaign as a marketing form, and the bathroom sequence, which is the template for the reveal-in-still-water shot the genre has used ever since. The craft lesson is patience: the film spends most of its length as a study of institutional cruelty in a shabby provincial school, so the horror when it arrives has a fully built world to happen in. The Delluc is a **1954** prize, awarded before the January 1955 release.

entries.name: Peeping Tom
entries.author: Michael Powell
entries.awards: None
entries.description: A focus-puller murders women with a blade mounted on his camera's tripod and films their faces as they die, so that the audience watches through his…
entries.text: A focus-puller murders women with a blade mounted on his camera's tripod and films their faces as they die, so that the audience watches through his viewfinder and is implicated in the apparatus. Released the same year as *Psycho* and destroyed by the reviews where Hitchcock's film was celebrated, it is the more radical work: it identifies the camera itself as the instrument of violence and offers no detective, no explanation the film endorses, and no comfortable distance. Written by **Leo Marks**, a wartime cryptographer, and scored by Brian Easdale. One myth to retire: Powell's career was **not** ended overnight and the film was not permanently withdrawn — it played nationally, was re-released in 1961–62, and Powell went on to make *The Queen's Guards*, *They're a Weird Mob* and *Age of Consent*. What he lost was Rank and Korda backing. Being British, it is ineligible for the National Film Registry.

entries.name: Onibaba
entries.author: Kaneto Shindō
entries.awards: None confirmed
entries.description: Two women in a fourteenth-century civil war survive by killing wounded samurai in a sea of susuki grass and selling their armour, and the film is the…
entries.text: Two women in a fourteenth-century civil war survive by killing wounded samurai in a sea of susuki grass and selling their armour, and the film is the strongest available demonstration that a landscape can be the antagonist. The grass is taller than the actors, moves constantly, hides everything and is shot in high-contrast black and white so that the frame is almost entirely restless texture — a visual solution to isolation that requires no set. The demon mask that will not come off, and what is beneath it when it does, is folk horror in its purest transactional form: a punishment that is also a physical fact. The sexual frankness and the class analysis are inseparable from the horror rather than decorating it. Its award record is single-sourced and thin; state none rather than guessing, and note that as a Japanese film it cannot carry a National Film Registry year.

entries.name: Night of the Living Dead
entries.author: George A. Romero
entries.awards: None
entries.description: The film that invented the modern zombie without once using the word, and the most influential independent horror production ever made. Romero…
entries.text: The film that invented the modern zombie without once using the word, and the most influential independent horror production ever made. Romero directed, shot and co-wrote it with **John A. Russo**; the producers were Russell Streiner and Karl Hardman. Its rules — reanimation, the bite as vector, destruction of the brain, the siege in a farmhouse, the group that destroys itself faster than the dead can — became a genre grammar within a decade. Duane Jones's casting as the competent, surviving Black lead in 1968, and the ending in which he is shot by a posse and disposed of with meathooks, is the reason the film has never stopped being read politically, whatever Romero said about the casting being colour-blind. The copyright fact, which is constantly garbled: this was **not** a lapsed renewal. Distributor Walter Reade changed the title from *Night of the Flesh Eaters* and physically removed the copyright notice, which under the 1909 Act forfeited copyright **on release in 1968**. National Film Registry, 1999.

entries.name: The Wicker Man
entries.author: Robin Hardy
entries.awards: Saturn Award, Best Horror Film — 6th Saturn Awards, 24 February 1979
entries.description: Folk horror's defining text, written by Anthony Shaffer, loosely derived from David Pinner's novel *Ritual* (1967) — loosely being the operative word,…
entries.text: Folk horror's defining text, written by Anthony Shaffer, loosely derived from David Pinner's novel *Ritual* (1967) — loosely being the operative word, since Shaffer deliberately departed from it. A devout Presbyterian policeman investigates a missing child on a Hebridean island and finds a functioning pagan community that is cheerful, sexually relaxed, agriculturally motivated and entirely open with him. The structural brilliance is that nobody lies: every answer Howie receives is true, and his own certainty is the mechanism that carries him to the wicker frame. It is the model for the horror plot in which the investigator's virtues are the trap. Two bibliographic cautions. The 2013 "Final Cut" runs 91 minutes and is **shorter** than the 2001 cut at 99, so it is not the most complete version; and the story that the negative was buried under the M4 motorway is uncorroborated legend.

entries.name: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre
entries.author: Tobe Hooper
entries.awards: Avoriaz Fantastic Film Festival, Special Jury Prize, 1976
entries.description: Almost no blood, one on-screen death by chainsaw, and a reputation as the most brutal film ever made — which is the whole lesson. Hooper substitutes…
entries.text: Almost no blood, one on-screen death by chainsaw, and a reputation as the most brutal film ever made — which is the whole lesson. Hooper substitutes texture for gore: heat, insect noise, bone furniture, a house that smells through the screen, and a final act of sustained screaming that exhausts rather than shocks. The dinner sequence is the most successful piece of sound-design horror of the decade. Credit precision: **Kim Henkel and Hooper share a joint story-and-screenplay credit**, Henkel billed first — there is no split between story and screenplay to report. The "based on a true story" claim is a marketing device; the only real connection is Ed Gein's furniture and skin-work, and Gein was a Wisconsin grave-robber and murderer of two, not a Texan chainsaw family. Added to the National Film Registry in December 2024, which is recent enough that most reference copy still says it is not.

entries.name: Suspiria
entries.author: Dario Argento
entries.awards: None
entries.description: The most purely aesthetic horror film in the canon, in which plot is subordinated to colour and sound so completely that the narrative can be described…
entries.text: The most purely aesthetic horror film in the canon, in which plot is subordinated to colour and sound so completely that the narrative can be described in three sentences and the experience cannot be described at all. An American ballet student arrives at a German dance academy run by a coven, and Argento lights the interiors in saturated primary reds, greens and blues achieved through coloured gels and printing, giving the film a chromatic intensity that later stocks and processes could not reproduce. The score is by the band credited on screen as **"The Goblins," with Argento himself co-credited** — a fact routinely dropped — and it is mixed at a level that makes it an aggressor rather than an accompaniment. For a writer the transferable point is that atmosphere can carry a film with a nearly vestigial plot, and that this is a trade, not a free gain.

entries.name: Halloween
entries.author: John Carpenter
entries.awards: None — Saturn Award, Best Horror Film nominee, lost to *The Wicker Man*
entries.description: The film that codified the slasher, written by Carpenter and **Debra Hill** and produced by Irwin Yablans on a budget documented variously between…
entries.text: The film that codified the slasher, written by Carpenter and **Debra Hill** and produced by Irwin Yablans on a budget documented variously between $300,000 and $325,000. Its innovations are formal rather than gory: the extended opening POV shot that withholds the killer's identity and age, the use of anamorphic widescreen to hide a figure in the corner of a suburban frame, and a synthesiser score in 5/4 that Carpenter composed himself in three days. Michael Myers has no motive and no dialogue, and the film's refusal to supply either is what the franchise then spent forty years undoing. Two facts to state carefully: Carpenter's $10,000 flat fee came **with ten per cent of profits**, so the fee-only story misleads; and Carpenter's only Academy Award is a 1970 Live Action Short win as co-writer, editor and composer, on which the statuette went to the producer. He has never been nominated as a director. National Film Registry, 2006.

entries.name: Alien
entries.author: Ridley Scott
entries.awards: Academy Award, Best Visual Effects — 52nd ceremony, 1980; BAFTA, Best Film Music (Jerry Goldsmith); Hugo Award, Best Dramatic Presentation; Saturn Awards for Best Science Fiction Film, Best Direction and Best Supporting Actress
entries.description: A haunted-house film in a spaceship, and the cleanest demonstration in the pack that a genre transplant works when the new setting supplies genuine…
entries.text: A haunted-house film in a spaceship, and the cleanest demonstration in the pack that a genre transplant works when the new setting supplies genuine constraints. The Nostromo is a working vessel crewed by contractors arguing about bonuses, so the horror lands on people with no heroic apparatus, and the corridors, ducts and airlocks generate the geography a haunted house would. Giger's biomechanical design is inseparable from the film's real subject — the creature's life cycle is a sequence of forced impregnations and violent births, applied first to a man, which is the source of the unease no later sequel recovered. Screenplay by **Dan O'Bannon** alone per the Writers Guild; story by O'Bannon and Ronald Shusett. Award care: it has exactly **one** Oscar; Art Direction was a nomination, and Goldsmith's Academy Award is for *The Omen* (1976) and is habitually slid onto this film.

entries.name: The Thing
entries.author: John Carpenter
entries.awards: None — two Saturn nominations, both lost
entries.description: A commercial and critical failure on release that is now the standard against which practical creature effects are measured, and the pack's best case…
entries.text: A commercial and critical failure on release that is now the standard against which practical creature effects are measured, and the pack's best case study in reputation lagging quality by a decade. Written by **Bill Lancaster**, with effects by **Rob Bottin** and a score by **Ennio Morricone** — not by Carpenter, a credit error so common it is worth stating twice. Its structural achievement is the paranoia engine: an organism that perfectly imitates its host means every character is a possible antagonist and no test the men devise is trustworthy, so the drama is entirely about verification. The blood-test sequence is the most efficient suspense set-piece of the decade because the audience understands the rules exactly. It opened 25 June 1982, **two weeks after *E.T.*** and on the same day as *Blade Runner*, into an audience that had just been given a benign alien. Morricone's Razzie was a nomination, not a win.

entries.name: Videodrome
entries.author: David Cronenberg
entries.awards: Genie Award, Best Achievement in Direction, 1984 — a tie with Bob Clark for *A Christmas Story*
entries.description: The most prescient horror film of its decade and the fullest statement of body horror as an intellectual position rather than a special-effects mode. A…
entries.text: The most prescient horror film of its decade and the fullest statement of body horror as an intellectual position rather than a special-effects mode. A sleazy cable programmer chasing a torture broadcast develops a vaginal slit in his abdomen into which videotapes are inserted, and the film's proposition — that media is not consumed but incorporated, and that the flesh will reorganise itself around what it watches — reads now as a description rather than a metaphor. Cronenberg's discipline is that hallucination and event are never distinguished after the first act, so the viewer loses the same footing Max does. Rick Baker's effects work is the reason the transformations still function. Award care: the Genie was a **tie**, which a source consulted in isolation will render as a loss; and Cronenberg has never been nominated for an Academy Award, the Oscar in his filmography belonging to Chris Walas and Stephan Dupuis for *The Fly*.

entries.name: A Nightmare on Elm Street
entries.author: Wes Craven
entries.awards: Avoriaz Fantastic Film Festival, Critics Award, 1985
entries.description: The slasher's most elegant premise, because it solves the subgenre's structural problem: if the killer attacks in dreams, then sleep is the deadline…
entries.text: The slasher's most elegant premise, because it solves the subgenre's structural problem: if the killer attacks in dreams, then sleep is the deadline and safety is impossible by definition. Craven wrote and directed, and Robert Shaye produced for New Line, a company the film effectively built. The craft value is in the constraint the premise imposes — every set-piece must be plausible as a dream and lethal in reality, which forces invention where a masked-stalker film would repeat itself. Freddy Krueger is also the point at which the silent slasher acquired a personality, a decision the sequels turned into stand-up comedy and which the first film keeps genuinely frightening. Craven cited contemporaneous newspaper reports of Southeast Asian refugees dying in their sleep as his starting point. Credit precision: he directed **none** of the numbered sequels, co-wrote *Dream Warriors* (1987), and wrote and directed *Wes Craven's New Nightmare* (1994). National Film Registry, 2021.

entries.name: Hellraiser
entries.author: Clive Barker
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Barker directing his own novella, and the rare adaptation that is a different work rather than a lesser one — the film foregrounds the Cenobites the…
entries.text: Barker directing his own novella, and the rare adaptation that is a different work rather than a lesser one — the film foregrounds the Cenobites the book keeps marginal, and in doing so creates an iconography that outran everything else about it. Its lasting contribution is the transactional cosmology: a puzzle box that is a request form, beings who fulfil the request exactly and consider themselves neither cruel nor kind, and a hell that is a service industry. The domestic plot underneath — a woman murdering men in her attic to reconstitute her lover from blood — is the film's actual engine and is where its sexual candour lives. Two credit notes. The Cenobites are never named as such in the film, and "Pinhead" appears nowhere in it. And it is Barker's feature debut as director but not his first work behind a camera, following earlier shorts. Its awards line is empty.

entries.name: Ringu
entries.author: Hideo Nakata
entries.awards: None confirmed
entries.description: The film that made J-horror a global category and set the visual grammar — the long black hair, the jerking movement, the drowned monochrome palette,…
entries.text: The film that made J-horror a global category and set the visual grammar — the long black hair, the jerking movement, the drowned monochrome palette, the vengeful female ghost with a legitimate grievance. Nakata's decisive change from Suzuki's novel is to make the protagonist a woman and a mother, to reduce the procedural explanation, and to give Sadako a physical emergence through the television screen that the book does not have; virtually every English-language description of "the novel *Ring*" is in fact describing this film. Screenplay by **Hiroshi Takahashi**. The craft point worth stealing is the film's use of duration: the videotape is shown early, in full, and the audience is then made to wait out seven days with a character who has seen it. No Japanese award for it could be established from any source, and the frequently asserted Japanese Academy Prize should be treated as false until proven.

entries.name: The Blair Witch Project
entries.author: Daniel Myrick & Eduardo Sánchez
entries.awards: Independent Spirit Award, John Cassavetes Award, 2000
entries.description: Found footage's commercial breakthrough and the most successful marketing campaign in horror history, which are two separate achievements that must not…
entries.text: Found footage's commercial breakthrough and the most successful marketing campaign in horror history, which are two separate achievements that must not be merged. The film itself is a genuine formal experiment: three actors improvising from notes, filming themselves, given deteriorating instructions by directors who were tracking them through the woods, and a monster that is never shown because there was never a budget to show one. The final shot works because the film has spent eighty minutes establishing a piece of folklore about a corner. The campaign — a website presenting the footage as recovered, missing-person materials, actors listed as deceased on IMDb — created a genuine ambiguity in the audience about whether the film was fiction. Award correction: it **won nothing at Sundance**, where it merely premiered; the "Sundance winner" claim is the standard error, and its real prize is the Cassavetes Award for a feature made under $500,000.

entries.name: Audition
entries.author: Takashi Miike
entries.awards: Rotterdam International Film Festival, FIPRESCI Prize and KNF Award, 2000
entries.description: A widower stages a fake film casting session to find a wife, and for two-thirds of its length the film is a restrained, well-mannered drama about…
entries.text: A widower stages a fake film casting session to find a wife, and for two-thirds of its length the film is a restrained, well-mannered drama about middle-aged loneliness — which is the structural device, not a slow start. The tonal break is one of the most violent in cinema, and it works because everything that precedes it is played straight and because the woman's revenge is legible as a response to exactly the objectification the audition premise embodies. The sack in the apartment is the best single use of a static shot in modern horror. Release facts: world premiere at Vancouver on 2 October 1999, **Japanese general release 3 March 2000**, and its Rotterdam prizes are 2000 — a card that dates the awards to 1999 has compressed the sequence. The much-repeated walkout stories are real in outline; Miike's own account names only "a film festival," and the quotation is "you are sick," which is worth getting right before repeating.

entries.name: Martyrs
entries.author: Pascal Laugier
entries.awards: None — Gérardmer nominee only
entries.description: The most argued-about film of the New French Extremity, and the pack's hardest case in the question of whether extreme content can carry a metaphysical…
entries.text: The most argued-about film of the New French Extremity, and the pack's hardest case in the question of whether extreme content can carry a metaphysical argument. It begins as a revenge film, converts at the midpoint into something else entirely, and spends its final act on a systematic programme of suffering administered by an organisation seeking empirical evidence of an afterlife. Whether the film earns its ending is a genuine and unresolved critical disagreement: it is defended as the only horror film to take transcendence-through-suffering seriously as a proposition, and attacked as an elaborate rationalisation for filming a woman being tortured for forty minutes. A reference pack that pretends this is settled is not being useful. Award correction: it **did not premiere at Cannes** and won nothing there — it had a Marché du Film trade screening in May 2008, which is a sales event, not an official selection. The substantive story is its French classification battle, not its prizes.

entries.name: The Babadook
entries.author: Jennifer Kent
entries.awards: AACTA Awards, 4th ceremony, 29 January 2015 — Best Film (shared with *The Water Diviner*), Best Direction and Best Original Screenplay, all to Kent
entries.description: Grief horror's defining modern text, and the clearest demonstration that a monster can be a diagnosis without the film becoming a lecture. A widow…
entries.text: Grief horror's defining modern text, and the clearest demonstration that a monster can be a diagnosis without the film becoming a lecture. A widow raising a difficult son alone finds a pop-up book in the house, and the creature it describes behaves exactly as the book promises — but the film's real subject is a mother who resents her child and cannot say so, and whose exhaustion is filmed with an unsparing attention the genre rarely gives to caregiving. Kent's final act is the pack's model for the ending that refuses exorcism: the thing is not destroyed, it is housed in the basement and fed, because that is what living with grief actually looks like. It grew from Kent's short *Monster* (2005). Two award corrections: it **won nothing at Sundance**, where its premiere was in a non-competitive strand; and its AACTA Best Film was a **tie**, the first time Australia's top film prize was shared.

entries.name: Get Out
entries.author: Jordan Peele
entries.awards: Academy Award, Best Original Screenplay — 90th ceremony, 4 March 2018; Writers Guild of America Award; Academy Award nominations for Best Picture, Best Director and Best Actor, all lost
entries.description: The most commercially and critically successful horror film of its decade and the one that most decisively reopened the genre to social argument. A…
entries.text: The most commercially and critically successful horror film of its decade and the one that most decisively reopened the genre to social argument. A Black man meets his white girlfriend's family and encounters not hostility but enthusiasm — praise for his genetics, admiration for his physique, a bidding auction conducted as a garden party — and the film's mechanism is that every escalation is delivered as a compliment. The Sunken Place is the rarest thing in modern horror, a new image that entered the general vocabulary within months. Peele wrote, directed and is a credited producer, and became the first Black winner of the Best Original Screenplay Oscar. Citation care: it is a **2017 film that won at the 2018 ceremony**, and writing either year unqualified will mislead. Daniel Kaluuya's Academy Award is for *Judas and the Black Messiah* and is routinely slid onto this film.

entries.name: Hereditary
entries.author: Ari Aster
entries.awards: Gotham Award, Best Actress (Toni Collette), 2018; no Academy Award nominations
entries.description: A family disintegrates after a grandmother's death, and the film's structural gamble is to spend its first hour as a domestic drama about grief and…
entries.text: A family disintegrates after a grandmother's death, and the film's structural gamble is to spend its first hour as a domestic drama about grief and blame so precisely observed that the audience forgets what they bought a ticket for. The dinner-table confrontation is the most quoted scene and is not supernatural at all. Aster's formal signature — dollhouse framing, static wide shots held past comfort, an editing pattern that cuts on the wrong beat — makes the family look like objects being arranged, which the ending retrospectively confirms. Its most discussed sequence, the accident and the drive home, works because it withholds the reaction shot for an entire night. Two award facts worth carrying: it received **zero Academy Award nominations**, and Toni Collette's Oscar nomination is for *The Sixth Sense* nineteen years earlier — the "Collette snub" discourse exists precisely because the nomination never came. Its CinemaScore of D+ is a useful reminder that opening-weekend audience grades measure expectation mismatch, not quality.

entries.name: The Twilight Zone
entries.author: Rod Serling
entries.awards: Hugo Award, Best Dramatic Presentation — 1960, 1961 and 1962, three consecutive wins
entries.description: The anthology that taught American television how to do short-form dark fantasy, and the single most efficient teaching text in this pack for the twist…
entries.text: The anthology that taught American television how to do short-form dark fantasy, and the single most efficient teaching text in this pack for the twist ending — because roughly half of its 156 episodes demonstrate the device working and the other half demonstrate exactly how it fails. Serling created it, hosted it, and wrote or co-wrote more than ninety instalments, using the science-fictional frame to get racial and political material past network standards that would have blocked it in a realist drama. Its best horror episodes — "The Hitch-Hiker," "Living Doll," "The Invaders," "Time Enough at Last" — all run on the same engine: a single premise stated plainly, escalated for twenty minutes, and closed with a reversal that recontextualises rather than negates. Two card cautions: it ran on **CBS from 1959 to 1964** and the three revivals are separate productions; and the 1963 Academy Award for *An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge* belongs to that French short and its director, not to the series that later bought and aired it.

entries.name: Twin Peaks
entries.author: David Lynch & Mark Frost
entries.awards: two Primetime Emmy Awards from 18 nominations — costume design and single-camera picture editing; three Golden Globes
entries.description: The series that made prestige-horror television possible by fusing a murder investigation, a small-town soap and an oneiric supernatural cosmology…
entries.text: The series that made prestige-horror television possible by fusing a murder investigation, a small-town soap and an oneiric supernatural cosmology without labelling any of the three. Its craft contribution is tonal permission: a scene can be funny, unbearable and inexplicable in sequence without the show apologising, and the Red Room sequences established that a television budget can produce genuine dream-logic if the design is committed enough. Laura Palmer is the model for the dead girl who is nonetheless the protagonist — the investigation reconstructs a person rather than a case. It is also the standard cautionary example of the mystery that must not be solved: network pressure forced the killer's identity in season two, and the show lost its engine immediately. Award precision: eighteen Emmy nominations produced exactly **two wins**, both craft, which is a useful corrective to the assumption that reputation and trophies track each other.

entries.name: Ghostwatch
entries.author: Stephen Volk
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Broadcast once, on **BBC1 on Saturday 31 October 1992** in the *Screen One* drama strand, and never repeated on British television since. Written by…
entries.text: Broadcast once, on **BBC1 on Saturday 31 October 1992** in the *Screen One* drama strand, and never repeated on British television since. Written by Stephen Volk and produced by Richard Broke, Ruth Baumgarten and Derek Nelson, it presents itself as a live investigation into a north London poltergeist, fronted by real BBC presenters playing themselves, with a phone number on screen that connected to a recorded message. It was pre-recorded weeks earlier; nothing about it was live. Its craft achievement is the slow accretion of wrongness inside a format the audience trusts absolutely — the figure standing in the background of a shot nobody comments on is the single most copied device in found-footage horror since. The aftermath is inseparable from the work and must be stated carefully: the broadcast drew a very large volume of complaints, the Broadcasting Standards Commission ruled on it on 29 June 1995, and the Denham family's complaint concerning their son's death was rejected by the Commission, a decision that was then subject to judicial review. Its record is entirely controversy; it won nothing.

entries.name: The X-Files
entries.author: Chris Carter
entries.awards: Peabody Award, 1996; 15 Primetime Emmy wins from 61 nominations
entries.description: Nine seasons that ran two shows at once, and the pack's best case study in the structural tension between arc and episode. The mythology episodes built…
entries.text: Nine seasons that ran two shows at once, and the pack's best case study in the structural tension between arc and episode. The mythology episodes built a conspiracy that eventually collapsed under its own accumulated promises; the standalone "monster of the week" episodes are where the horror is, and several of them — "Home," "Squeeze," "Irresistible," "Ice" — are among the best hours of televised horror ever made. Its lasting formal contributions are the believer/sceptic pairing as an engine for exposition that never feels like exposition, and the demonstration that a network drama could sustain genuine dread on a weekly schedule by keeping its monsters small, local and specific. The lesson for a serialised writer is the one the show learned the hard way: an arc that withholds indefinitely trains the audience to stop believing an answer exists. Award note: it never won Outstanding Drama Series despite the fifteen wins, all of which are in other categories.

entries.name: Les Revenants
entries.author: Fabrice Gobert
entries.awards: International Emmy Award, Best Drama Series, 2013 — the first French series to win it; Peabody Award, 2014
entries.description: The dead return to a French alpine town, unaware that they died, physically unchanged and expecting to resume their lives — and the series' entire…
entries.text: The dead return to a French alpine town, unaware that they died, physically unchanged and expecting to resume their lives — and the series' entire method is to refuse the outbreak. Nobody is infectious, nobody is hostile on arrival, and the horror is administrative and emotional: a mother who has grieved and rebuilt now has her daughter back at the age she died, a husband has remarried, a town has moved on. Gobert's control of pace is the craft lesson, since the show extracts genuine dread from long static shots of a dam, an empty road and a swimming pool with almost no incident. Mogwai's first-season score is a substantial part of the effect and is credited as such. It is the strongest available argument that the return-of-the-dead premise has been almost entirely wasted on siege plots, and it is where later grief-horror television took its register from.

entries.name: Hannibal
entries.author: Bryan Fuller
entries.awards: None — one Primetime Emmy nomination, for Special Visual Effects in 2016, and no wins
entries.description: The most visually extreme thing ever broadcast on American network television, and a rare case of an adaptation improving on its source by relocating…
entries.text: The most visually extreme thing ever broadcast on American network television, and a rare case of an adaptation improving on its source by relocating the emphasis. Fuller's move is to make Will Graham's empathy a clinical liability rather than a gift, and to render the murders as tableaux so aestheticised — antlered bodies, a human cross-section, a totem of corpses — that the audience is implicated in finding them beautiful before it registers what it is looking at. The dinner sequences do the same work in a lower key, and the show's central relationship is a courtship conducted entirely in food and diagnosis. Its craft value is the demonstration that stylisation can carry content that literalism could never get past a censor. Its award record is the field's standard example of a critically adored series shut out by the Television Academy: one nomination, in a technical category, in its final year.

entries.name: Channel Zero
entries.author: Nick Antosca
entries.awards: None — Saturn and Fangoria nominations only
entries.description: Four seasons of six episodes each on Syfy, each adapting a single internet-native horror story, and the pack's key text on how creepypasta moves into a…
entries.text: Four seasons of six episodes each on Syfy, each adapting a single internet-native horror story, and the pack's key text on how creepypasta moves into a professional medium. The sources are specific and worth citing correctly: season one adapts **Kris Straub's "Candle Cove"** (2009), originally posted as a threaded forum conversation and converted into the season's framing device; season two adapts **Brian Russell's "The No-End House"**; season three, **Butcher's Block**, adapts **Kerry Hammond's "Search and Rescue Woods"** — not a story of the season's own name, which is the trap; and season four, **The Dream Door**, adapts **Charlotte Bywater's "Hidden Door."** The craft interest is expansion: a creepypasta is typically a premise and an image with no second act, and the seasons succeed or fail exactly on whether they find a human situation to hang the image on. Season one and season three do; the show is uneven by design. It has no wins and should not be called award-winning.

entries.name: Midnight Mass
entries.author: Mike Flanagan
entries.awards: Bram Stoker Award, 2022, in a screenplay category
entries.description: A limited series in which a declining island community receives a charismatic new priest and a sequence of apparent miracles, and the vampire is never…
entries.text: A limited series in which a declining island community receives a charismatic new priest and a sequence of apparent miracles, and the vampire is never once named as such — the show's central proposition is that the theology and the parasitism describe the same thing, and it allows both readings to remain fully coherent to the end. Its formal signature is the monologue: several episodes hand a character four or five uninterrupted minutes on faith, addiction, guilt or what they believe happens at death, and the series stakes its pace on the belief that an audience will sit still for that. It is also the pack's best study of religious horror written from inside rather than from suspicion, since the congregation's belief is treated as real, load-bearing and worthy of respect even as it is exploited. Development note worth carrying: Flanagan conceived it as a novel, failed to sell it as a film in 2014, and kept it alive as a prop book written by Kate Siegel's character in *Hush* (2016) and again in *Gerald's Game* (2017).

entries.name: Tales from the Crypt
entries.author: William Gaines & Al Feldstein
entries.awards: None — the comics award apparatus postdates the run by three decades
entries.description: EC's flagship horror title, and the body of work that provoked the American comics industry into censoring itself out of the form for a generation.…
entries.text: EC's flagship horror title, and the body of work that provoked the American comics industry into censoring itself out of the form for a generation. Gaines published and Feldstein edited and wrote, and the house style is the most rigorously moral in the genre's history: an ironic-retribution engine in which the punishment is always proportionate, always physical, and always derived from the offence, delivered by a horror host whose relish is part of the contract with the reader. That structure is the direct ancestor of the anthology form from *Twilight Zone* to *Creepshow*. Bibliographic care: **there is no issue #1** — the title inherited its numbering and runs from **#20 (Oct/Nov 1950) to #46 (Feb/Mar 1955)**. Its ending is the field's founding censorship story: the 1954 Senate subcommittee hearings, Gaines's disastrous testimony, and the Comics Code that followed made the line unpublishable rather than illegal, which is a distinction worth preserving.

entries.name: Saga of the Swamp Thing
entries.author: Alan Moore
entries.awards: None verified
entries.description: The run that proved mainstream American comics could sustain literary horror, and the direct cause of everything Vertigo later became. Moore's tenure…
entries.text: The run that proved mainstream American comics could sustain literary horror, and the direct cause of everything Vertigo later became. Moore's tenure runs from **#20 (January 1984) to #64 (September 1987)**, excepting issues 59 and 62, drawn principally by Stephen Bissette, John Totleben and later Rick Veitch. The pivot is "The Anatomy Lesson" (#21), which discards the existing premise entirely: the creature is not a man transformed into a plant but a plant that absorbed a dead man's consciousness and believes it was once human, a reveal that converts a monster book into a study of an identity built on a false memory. Its other permanent effect was procedural — the run dropped the Comics Code seal and demonstrated a commercially viable adult market outside it. Two credit corrections: Swamp Thing was created by **Len Wein and Bernie Wrightson** in *House of Secrets* #92 (July 1971), and no award for the run could be verified, the Eisners having begun in 1988, after it ended.

entries.name: Hellblazer
entries.author: Jamie Delano
entries.awards: None verified
entries.description: The longest-running horror comic in the American mainstream and the pack's model for occult detection written as social realism. John Constantine is a…
entries.text: The longest-running horror comic in the American mainstream and the pack's model for occult detection written as social realism. John Constantine is a working-class Liverpudlian con man with a small, unreliable magical competence, a body that ages in real time across three hundred issues, and a documented habit of getting his friends killed — an antihero defined by consequence rather than by cool. Delano's founding run, issues **#1–40**, sets the register: Thatcher's Britain, the miners' strike, yuppie demonology and a horror that is continuous with the political economy rather than an intrusion into it. Publisher precision matters here: it is a **DC Comics** title from #1, moving to the Vertigo imprint only from **#63 (March 1993)**, and Constantine himself was created by Moore, Bissette and Totleben in *Saga of the Swamp Thing* #37 (June 1985) — not by Delano. No award for the title could be verified; later writers' Eisners are for other work.

entries.name: Black Hole
entries.author: Charles Burns
entries.awards: Harvey Award, Best Graphic Album of Previously Published Work, 2006; Ignatz Award, Outstanding Anthology or Collection, 2006; Angoulême Essentials selection, 2007
entries.description: Serialised across a decade and set among Seattle teenagers in the mid-1970s, where a sexually transmitted infection produces individually specific…
entries.text: Serialised across a decade and set among Seattle teenagers in the mid-1970s, where a sexually transmitted infection produces individually specific mutations — a tail, a shedding skin, a second mouth in the throat — and the afflicted drift into an encampment in the woods. Its achievement is that the metaphor is never resolved into a single referent: it reads as AIDS, as puberty, as social exile, as addiction, and Burns refuses to adjudicate. The art is the argument, in a high-contrast black and white where the ink masses are so heavy that the white areas read as wounds, and where the dream sequences use recurring cut-and-split imagery to make the biological horror feel adolescent rather than clinical. It is the strongest available demonstration that body horror is most effective when the transformation is socially legible before it is physically dangerous. Do not attach an Eisner to it; the verified record is Harvey, Ignatz and Angoulême.

entries.name: Uzumaki
entries.author: Junji Ito
entries.awards: None — Eisner Award nominations in 2003 and 2009, no wins
entries.description: A town becomes obsessed with the spiral, and the premise's absurdity is precisely what makes it the most instructive horror manga in the pack: Ito…
entries.text: A town becomes obsessed with the spiral, and the premise's absurdity is precisely what makes it the most instructive horror manga in the pack: Ito takes a shape rather than a monster and derives every consequence, so hair coils, bodies coil, a lighthouse coils, people compress themselves into snail shells, and the town's architecture eventually reveals what it has always been. The craft lesson is exhaustiveness — a horror premise becomes inescapable when it is applied without exception, and a writer's instinct to vary the threat is usually a failure of nerve. Ito's line work is the other half: an obsessively even, almost clinical hatching that makes the impossible read as documentary. Two award corrections that matter, because "Eisner-winning Uzumaki" is in wide circulation: **Uzumaki won nothing**, taking two Eisner nominations only, and Ito's four Eisners are for *Frankenstein*, *Remina*, *Venus in the Blind Spot* and *Lovesickness*, all for English-language editions. His verified Japanese honour is a 1987 Kazuo Umezu Prize honourable mention.

entries.name: Locke & Key
entries.author: Joe Hill & Gabriel Rodríguez
entries.awards: Eisner Award, Best Writer (Joe Hill), 2011; British Fantasy Award, Best Graphic Novel, 2012, for *Keys to the Kingdom*
entries.description: A family moves into a New England house after the father's murder and finds keys that do specific, literal, wonderful things — one opens your own head…
entries.text: A family moves into a New England house after the father's murder and finds keys that do specific, literal, wonderful things — one opens your own head so items can be added or removed, one turns you into a ghost, one changes your sex, one lets you walk through any door in the world. The series is the pack's best demonstration of a magic system used as a horror engine rather than a power fantasy, because every key's benefit has an exact and foreseeable cost, and the antagonist's strategy is simply to understand the rules better than the children do. Rodríguez's clean, warm, densely detailed art is essential to the effect: the house is drawn as a real, liveable place, so the wrongness inside it has somewhere to land. It is also a genuine study of childhood grief with a body count. Its two Hugo appearances were nominations, not wins.

entries.name: Through the Woods
entries.author: Emily Carroll
entries.awards: two Eisner Awards, 2015 — Best Graphic Album (Reprint) and Best Short Story, for "When the Darkness Presses"; British Fantasy Award, Best Comic/Graphic Novel, 2015
entries.description: Five short comics in the fairy-tale register, and the most formally intelligent use of the page as a horror instrument in the contemporary field.…
entries.text: Five short comics in the fairy-tale register, and the most formally intelligent use of the page as a horror instrument in the contemporary field. Carroll builds her panels so that a reader's eye is led into darkness and made to scroll or turn to find what is in it, uses long vertical black gutters as spaces where something is standing, and sets text in irregular hand-lettered blocks that drift as the narration becomes less trustworthy. "His Face All Red," the collection's centrepiece, is a perfect short horror story: a brother returns from a hole in the woods, is unmistakably himself, and is unmistakably not. The palette — red, black, white, occasional sick greens — is doing the same work Suspiria's does in cinema. For a prose writer the lesson is about withholding as a spatial decision rather than a verbal one. Do not attach Carroll's later prizes for *A Guest in the House* to this book.

entries.name: Alone in the Dark
entries.author: Infogrames
entries.awards: European Computer Trade Show, 1993 — Best Graphics, Most Original Game and Best French Game of the Year; Consumer Electronics Show, 1993 — Best Foreign Game
entries.description: Created by **Frédérick Raynal** at Infogrames and released in Europe in 1992, with the US release following in 1993, this is the origin point for the…
entries.text: Created by **Frédérick Raynal** at Infogrames and released in Europe in 1992, with the US release following in 1993, this is the origin point for the survival-horror form even though the term did not exist for another four years. Its technical device is the one the genre then used for a decade: polygonal characters composited over pre-rendered two-dimensional backgrounds, which let a small team build a Louisiana mansion with cinematic fixed camera angles at a time when a fully three-dimensional interior was impossible. The fixed camera is the craft point — it is a limitation converted into a horror instrument, because the designer controls exactly what is off-screen. The Lovecraftian content is explicit and licensed in spirit rather than in fact. Claim precision: it is the first survival horror game in the pre-rendered-background lineage, not the first fully three-dimensional one, which is *Overblood* (1996).

entries.name: Resident Evil
entries.author: Capcom
entries.awards: Electronic Gaming Monthly Readers' Picks — PlayStation Game of the Year; Sony Computer Entertainment — Best PlayStation Game Overall
entries.description: Released in Japan as *Biohazard* and retitled for the West, this is the game that named the genre: its opening narration calls it "a survival horror,"…
entries.text: Released in Japan as *Biohazard* and retitled for the West, this is the game that named the genre: its opening narration calls it "a survival horror," and the phrase was taken up as a category label from there. Its design is a scarcity system, and the scarcity is the horror. Ammunition, healing items and inventory slots are all limited; saving requires a consumable ink ribbon; and the mansion is a lock-and-key puzzle box that must be traversed repeatedly, so the player's knowledge of a cleared corridor becomes a resource that the game can then invalidate. The dogs-through-the-window sequence is the most efficient jump scare in the medium precisely because it violates a route the player had learned to trust. The fixed cameras and tank controls are usually described as dated; they are better understood as deliberate friction, and every remake that removes them trades fear for competence.

entries.name: Silent Hill 2
entries.author: Konami
entries.awards: None documented
entries.description: The medium's strongest argument that horror can be psychological in a rigorous rather than a decorative sense. James Sunderland receives a letter from…
entries.text: The medium's strongest argument that horror can be psychological in a rigorous rather than a decorative sense. James Sunderland receives a letter from his dead wife asking him to meet her in a town neither of them can be in, and the town supplies him with monsters that are legible expressions of his own guilt — including one whose design is an explicit statement about his sexual frustration that the game never explains and never needs to. The fog is a technical limitation on draw distance converted into the defining aesthetic of a franchise. Akira Yamaoka's score, built from industrial noise, prepared piano and metal impacts, is inseparable from the effect. Credit corrections: the director is **Masashi Tsuboyama**, and **Keiichiro Toyama directed only the first game**, leaving Team Silent in 1999 — the attribution of the sequel to him is a persistent error. Release order is also inverted from the assumption: North America on 25 September 2001, Japan two days later.

entries.name: Fatal Frame
entries.author: Tecmo
entries.awards: None documented
entries.description: The purest J-horror game and the one with the most elegant central mechanic in the genre: the only weapon is a camera, and to damage a ghost the player…
entries.text: The purest J-horror game and the one with the most elegant central mechanic in the genre: the only weapon is a camera, and to damage a ghost the player must frame it, hold the shot as it approaches, and release at the last possible moment. Fear and effectiveness are therefore the same variable — the closer the player lets the thing come, the more damage the photograph does — which is a design solution horror games have never bettered. The setting is a Japanese manor with a ritual history involving rope, and the archival material scattered through it does the exposition without a narrator. Title and release facts need care, since it has three names in three territories: **Japan as *Zero*, 13 December 2001; North America as *Fatal Frame*, 27 February 2002; Europe as *Project Zero*, 30 August 2002**, with the European PS2 edition published by Wanadoo Edition rather than Tecmo.

entries.name: Dead Space
entries.author: EA Redwood Shores
entries.awards: BAFTA Games Awards, 2009 — Use of Audio and Original Score (Jason Graves)
entries.description: *Alien* and *Event Horizon* fused into a survival-horror shooter, and the pack's model for interface design as a horror decision. Dead Space has no…
entries.text: *Alien* and *Event Horizon* fused into a survival-horror shooter, and the pack's model for interface design as a horror decision. Dead Space has no heads-up display: health is a glowing spine on the suit, ammunition is projected in front of the weapon, and the inventory is a hologram that hangs in the world while the game continues around it — so the player can never look away to a menu and be safe. Its combat rule is the other innovation: the Necromorphs must be dismembered limb by limb rather than shot centre-mass, which retrains a decade of shooter reflex and makes every encounter deliberate. The sound design is the reason it won what it won, particularly the vacuum sequences where the score and the impacts continue while the diegetic audio drops away. Studio note: EA Redwood Shores was renamed **Visceral Games** in 2009, so award citations from that year onward read under the new name.

entries.name: Amnesia: The Dark Descent
entries.author: Frictional Games
entries.awards: Independent Games Festival, 2011 — Excellence in Audio, Technical Excellence, and the Direct2Drive Vision Award
entries.description: The game that established defencelessness as a viable design and effectively created the modern hide-and-run horror genre. The player has no weapon at…
entries.text: The game that established defencelessness as a viable design and effectively created the modern hide-and-run horror genre. The player has no weapon at any point, a lantern with finite oil, and a sanity meter that degrades in darkness and degrades faster while looking directly at a monster — so the two survival imperatives, stay lit and do not look, are in direct opposition to each other and to hiding. That triangulation is the whole design and it is elegant enough to have been copied for fifteen years. Its physics-driven interaction, in which doors and drawers are dragged open with the mouse rather than opened with a button, converts every entry into a slow physical act the player performs under pressure. Frictional's earlier *Penumbra* series (2007–2008) developed the engine and much of the vocabulary. Award care: its three IGF wins do **not** include the Grand Prize, which is the standard misattribution.

entries.name: Outlast
entries.author: Red Barrels
entries.awards: None documented
entries.description: Found footage as a game mechanic executed with total commitment: the player is a journalist inside an asylum with a camcorder, the camcorder's night…
entries.text: Found footage as a game mechanic executed with total commitment: the player is a journalist inside an asylum with a camcorder, the camcorder's night vision is the only way to see in the dark, and the batteries are finite — so the resource being rationed is vision itself, and the act of looking is the act of spending. Everything the player does that increases their safety also increases the rate at which safety runs out, which is the tightest expression in the medium of the horror-scarcity principle. Its weakness is the other half of the design: the chase sequences are largely trial-and-error, and death is frequent enough to erode dread into irritation, which is a documented failure mode worth studying. Its institutional setting also carries the genre's oldest ethical problem, since it treats psychiatric patients as monsters, and a card that recommends its mechanics should say so.

entries.name: P.T.
entries.author: 7780s Studio
entries.awards: None
entries.description: A free playable teaser released without announcement on the PlayStation Store, released under the pseudonymous studio name **7780s Studio** and…
entries.text: A free playable teaser released without announcement on the PlayStation Store, released under the pseudonymous studio name **7780s Studio** and published by Konami, revealed on completion to be a trailer for a *Silent Hill* game by Hideo Kojima and Guillermo del Toro that was subsequently cancelled. It is the most influential horror game of its decade despite being roughly an hour long and no longer purchasable — delisted in 2015 and playable only on consoles where it was already installed. The design is a single L-shaped corridor that loops, changing in small increments each time: a photograph alters, a door is ajar, a radio says something new, a figure is present in a bathroom that was empty. That is the entire game, and it demonstrates that repetition with variation is a more reliable horror engine than novelty. Its unavailability is now part of its meaning, and the preservation problem it represents is worth stating on any card that recommends it.

entries.name: Alien: Isolation
entries.author: Creative Assembly
entries.awards: BAFTA Games Award, Audio Achievement, 2015; Game Developers Choice Award, Best Audio, 2015
entries.description: Developed by Creative Assembly and published by **SEGA**, and the only adaptation in this pack that improves on its source's genre by returning it to…
entries.text: Developed by Creative Assembly and published by **SEGA**, and the only adaptation in this pack that improves on its source's genre by returning it to one. Where every previous *Alien* game had been a shooter about killing many aliens, this is a survival game about avoiding one, driven by an adaptive artificial intelligence that learns the player's habits: hide under the same desk twice and it checks there. That single design decision produces the fear the films generate and the games never had, because the threat cannot be solved, only postponed. The reconstruction of the 1979 film's analogue-futurist production design — CRT monitors, chunky switchgear, magnetic tape — is the other achievement, and its audio work, from the motion tracker's ping to the ventilation, is why it won what it won. Four BAFTA nominations produced one win; British Game was a nomination.

entries.name: SOMA
entries.author: Frictional Games
entries.awards: None — Golden Joystick nominations for Best Original Game, Best Storytelling and Best Visual Design
entries.description: The most intellectually serious horror game yet made, and the one that most fully justifies the medium's claim to do something prose cannot. Set in an…
entries.text: The most intellectually serious horror game yet made, and the one that most fully justifies the medium's claim to do something prose cannot. Set in an underwater research facility after an extinction event, it uses its monsters sparingly and spends its real effort on a philosophical problem it forces the player to enact rather than contemplate: if a mind can be copied, the copy is not a transfer, and every act of continuation in the game creates one person who goes on and one who is left behind. The player makes that decision repeatedly, in the first person, with the abandoned version audible. Its horror is therefore conceptual and inescapable, since the fear is about the player's own continuity rather than about the thing in the corridor. Frictional's decision to allow a mode with the monsters disabled is a rare and honest acknowledgement that the game's argument survives without its threats.
